rows.text: The distinction that matters is between a single prompt and response and a task an agent sees through to the end. A chatbot that answers one question is not agentic. A system that reads a support ticket, looks up the order, drafts a refund and issues it is agentic. Nobody scripted that exact sequence in advance. Engineering teams build this pattern because it automates the cross-system judgement calls that used to need a person. Security reviewers and boards ask about it separately from the model itself, because the risk changes once a system can act, not only speak. A wrong sentence in a chat reply is embarrassing. A wrong action against a live order or a payment has already happened by the time anyone notices, because nothing stood between the decision and the outcome.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It comes up the moment a pitch or a product description says "agent" instead of "assistant". A security reviewer's next question is almost always what the agent can do without asking first. The reviewer asks because that is where the real exposure sits, not the model choice. A board hears "agentic" and correctly hears "this thing takes actions on its own." That is a different risk conversation than a chatbot that only produces text. ## What to do about it List every action an agent can take, not just what it can say, and sign off on each as a separate risk. Set a real limit on what it can do without a person confirming first, especially anything that spends money, touches a customer record, or sends something external. Log every tool call, so a bad outcome traces to a specific decision. Evals belong here: test the whole action chain, not just the model's replies.

rows.text: AI governance sits above the technology itself. It covers who owns each AI system, what data it may touch, which use cases are off limits, and who signs off before a system reaches customers. That shows up as a register of the systems in use, a policy engineers actually follow, and a review step before anything new goes live. A customer's procurement team asks for it during a security review. A board asks after a pilot nears production, once someone raises who is liable for a bad call. Regulators ask for pieces of it too, through frameworks like the NIST AI RMF and standards like ISO/IEC 42001. In practice, it changes three things. Someone specific owns each AI system, instead of it belonging to whichever team built it. A new system needs sign-off before it touches customer data. A written answer exists the day a customer or auditor asks for one.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up An insurer asks who owns AI risk before writing a policy. A board member reads about an AI failure elsewhere and asks what would happen here. An investor's due-diligence checklist now has a line for it too. Write down who is responsible for each system, and who would notice if it started producing worse answers. ## AI governance framework: the parts and where standards ask for each An AI governance framework is the set of roles, records and routines around your AI systems. It gives each system an owner, a risk tier, a release check and a review date. The table lists nine parts and the [NIST AI RMF](/glossary/nist-ai-rmf) and [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act) passages that ask for them. | Part | What the company has to show | Where a framework asks for it | | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Accountability | A named owner per system, and an executive who answers for AI risk decisions | [NIST GOVERN 2.1, 2.3](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf). AI Act [Article 17(1)(m)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27/eng) for [providers](/glossary/provider-vs-deployer) of [high-risk systems](/glossary/high-risk-ai-system). Article 26(2), [human oversight](/glossary/human-oversight) by people with competence, training and authority, for deployers of those systems | | Inventory | An [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) with each system, its owner, its data and its risk tier | NIST GOVERN 1.6 | | Policy | Written AI policies, and proof that people follow them | NIST GOVERN 1.2, 1.4. AI Act Article 17(1) for providers of high-risk systems | | Risk assessment and tiering | A risk tier per system, and a written assessment for the riskiest, such as an [AI impact assessment](/glossary/ai-impact-assessment) or a [DPIA](/glossary/dpia) | NIST GOVERN 1.3. AI Act Article 9 for providers of high-risk systems, Article 27 for some deployers of high-risk systems | | Approval before release | A named approver, test results and a go or no-go decision before launch | NIST MANAGE 1.1, GOVERN 4.3. AI Act Article 9(8) and Article 17(1)(d) for providers of high-risk systems | | Monitoring and incidents | What is watched after launch, who reviews it and who is called when it fails | NIST GOVERN 4.3, MANAGE 4.1, 4.3. AI Act Article 17(1)(h), [post-market monitoring](/glossary/post-market-monitoring), and (i), [serious incident](/glossary/serious-incident-reporting) procedures, for providers of high-risk systems. Article 26(5) for deployers of those systems | | Third parties | Each AI vendor, its [sub-processors](/glossary/sub-processor) and its terms on data use | NIST GOVERN 6.1, 6.2 | | People and training | Who has had AI risk training, and when | NIST GOVERN 2.2. AI Act Article 4, support for AI literacy, for providers and deployers of any AI system | | Review and retirement | A review date per system, and a way to switch one off or replace it | NIST GOVERN 1.5, 1.7, MANAGE 2.4. AI Act Article 9(2), regular review, for providers of high-risk systems | [NIST AI RMF 1.0](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf) is voluntary and says its actions are not a checklist, so the middle column is example evidence. These subcategory IDs come from that January 2023 text, which [NIST says](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) it is revising. The table cites the [consolidated EU AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27/eng) of 27 July 2026, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. Under Article 113, the table's duties for high-risk systems apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and from 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. Article 4 applies from 2 February 2025. [ISO sells the text](https://www.iso.org/standard/81230.html) of [ISO/IEC 42001](/glossary/iso-iec-42001), the standard for an [AI management system](/glossary/ai-management-system), so the table cites no clause. The [FAQ on NIST, ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act](/faq/what-do-nist-ai-rmf-iso-iec-42001-and-the-eu-ai-act-require) says what each requires of a company your size. ## AI governance policy: what goes in it and who signs it An AI governance policy records who may approve, run and retire AI systems, and what each one must show first. Write one short section per decision: - Scope: which systems, staff and vendors it covers, including [shadow AI](/glossary/shadow-ai) - Roles: the policy owner, the approving executive and each system's owner - Register: where the [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) lives and who updates it - Risk tiers: how a system gets a tier and what that tier requires - Approval: who approves a new system or major change, and on what evidence - Data: which [data classification](/glossary/data-classification) tier may reach which tool - Oversight: who watches each system and who may stop it ([human oversight](/glossary/human-oversight)) - Vendors: what a vendor discloses before purchase, including its [sub-processors](/glossary/sub-processor) - Incidents: who is told, in what order, and who rules an incident serious - Training: who is trained on AI risk, and where it is recorded - Review: the review date, early-review triggers and the version history Under the [NIST AI RMF](/glossary/nist-ai-rmf), [GOVERN 2.3](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf) says executive leadership takes responsibility for decisions about AI risk. The GOVERN overview in NIST AI RMF 1.0 adds that governing authorities can determine the overarching policies. [Article 17(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27/eng) of the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act) has [providers](/glossary/provider-vs-deployer) of [high-risk systems](/glossary/high-risk-ai-system) write their [quality management system](/glossary/ai-management-system) down as policies, procedures and instructions. Point (m) adds an accountability framework for the responsibilities of management and other staff. Neither NIST GOVERN 2.3 nor Article 17(1) says who signs a policy, so this part is advice. Name one policy owner, have one executive approve the policy and set a review date. In the [AI Governance Starter Kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit), a named AI risk owner keeps the register and each employee who uses an AI tool for work signs the separate [acceptable use policy](/blog/ai-acceptable-use-policy-for-a-50-person-company). Make that AI risk owner your policy owner too. ## What to do about it Start with a one-page register: every AI system in use, who owns it, what data it touches, and whether customer data leaves the building. Assign one named owner per system, not a team. Add a single sign-off step before a new system reaches production. Map what you already do against the NIST AI RMF or ISO/IEC 42001. Do this so you have a recognised structure to point at, not to get certified immediately.

rows.text: The EU AI Act calls this a fundamental rights impact assessment. Article 27 requires it from deployers that are public-law bodies or private entities delivering a public service. It also applies to any deployer using a high-risk system to score creditworthiness. The same goes for pricing life and health insurance. The assessment has to name the process the system sits inside, how often it runs, and which people or groups it is likely to affect. It has to describe the human oversight in place, and the governance and complaint routes that take effect if a risk appears. The deployer sends the finished assessment to the national market surveillance authority. Article 27 lets this assessment build on an existing data protection impact assessment rather than repeat it. Where the two overlap, the newer document only has to add what the DPIA does not already answer.

rows.text: For almost every high-risk system, the provider checks its own work against the rules and signs a declaration, with no outside reviewer involved. Only biometric-identification systems sometimes need an independent outside checker, a "notified body," to sign off instead. Article 43 sets this split by Annex III area, the EU AI Act's list of high-risk use cases. Every area except biometric identification uses Annex VI, the self-check route with no notified body involved. Biometric identification uses Annex VII's notified-body route wherever harmonised standards are not fully applied or do not yet exist. Harmonised standards are the detailed technical rules the Commission recognises as proof of compliance. The assessment is not a one-time formality. Any substantial change to a system after launch triggers a new one, under whichever route applied the first time. The one exception is a system that keeps learning after deployment. A provider can plan for that drift in advance and record it in the technical documentation before the first assessment. Later changes that stay within that plan do not reopen the process.

rows.text: NIST's own method for federal systems ties each category to a real question, not a subjective label. The question is what actually happens to confidentiality, integrity or availability if this breaks. That means naming who could see this data, alter it, or take it offline. Every new tool a company adopts multiplies the places a given tier could leak from. That is why the scheme has to live inside the AI register, not beside it. Without a scheme, two employees facing the same document reach different answers. The wrong answer usually only surfaces after the data has already left the building through a chat prompt.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It is the first practical question underneath any AI acceptable use policy. Can this go into that tool? Nobody can answer that until someone has labelled what this actually is. A security reviewer asks for the classification scheme by name, not as an abstract principle. The scheme is what turns a policy from a statement of intent into something an employee can actually follow on a Tuesday afternoon. ## Data classification policy: what it contains and who signs it A data classification policy states the tiers a company uses, who assigns each label, and what each label allows, including which AI tools may receive which tier. Write one short section per decision: - Purpose and scope: why the policy exists, and which data, people and tools it covers, including [shadow AI](/glossary/shadow-ai) - Roles: who owns each dataset and assigns its label, and who owns the policy - Tiers: the tier names, the test that puts data in each, and the default for unlabelled data - Records: where each label is written down, including the highest tier each AI tool may receive in the [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) - Handling: what each tier allows, which AI tools, vendors and [sub-processors](/glossary/sub-processor) may receive it, and which [guardrails](/glossary/guardrails) enforce the rules - Exceptions: who may approve one, for how long, and where it is logged - Review: the review date, and the changes that trigger an earlier review - Sign-off: who approves the policy, and on what date [NIST FIPS 199](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.199.pdf), published in February 2004, applies to US federal information and systems. It defines three levels of potential impact from a loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability: low, moderate and high. The tests in the example table borrow its words limited, serious and severe. Adapt the tiers, tests and rules to your own data. | Tier and test | Example data | Rule for AI tools | | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | | Public: a leak does no harm | Published pages, press releases | Any tool in the AI register | | Internal: a leak does limited harm | Meeting notes, internal procedures | Tools in the register, on company accounts only | | Confidential: a leak does serious harm | Customer data, personal data, source code | Tools the register approves for this tier | | Restricted: a leak does severe harm | Credentials, API keys, health data | None, unless the AI risk owner approves a tool in writing | A scheme needs an explicit rule for special categories of personal data, such as health data. [Article 9(1) of the GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj/eng) prohibits processing them unless a condition in Article 9(2) applies. Article 35(3)(b) names large-scale processing of these categories as a case that requires a [DPIA](/glossary/dpia). OWASP's [LLM02:2026 Sensitive Information Disclosure](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-genai-llm-top-10-2026/) lists credentials, API keys and trade secrets as protected information. It treats tool-call arguments, logs and reasoning traces as disclosure surfaces that need "the same classification and redaction rules". It also says to enforce no-train and no-retain rules technically, "rather than policy text alone". So the policy's scope should cover those channels as well as the prompt. In the [AI Governance Starter Kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit), the AI risk owner signs the data classification table together with whoever owns the data. Put those two names on the policy's sign-off line. Employees who use AI tools for work sign the separate [acceptable use policy](/blog/ai-acceptable-use-policy-for-a-50-person-company), which points at these tiers. NIST's federal method also names who takes part. In [NIST SP 800-60 Volume 1 Revision 1](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/60/v1/r1/final), published in August 2008, a four-step process identifies information types, selects provisional impact levels, reviews and adjusts them, then assigns the system's category. The roadmap table lists information owners in steps one, three and four. NIST's Revision 2 is still an [initial working draft](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/60/r2/iwd), published in January 2024. Control RA-2 in [NIST SP 800-53 Revision 5](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final) covers approval. It asks the organisation to document each categorisation with its rationale, and to verify that an authorizing official, or that person's designated representative, reviews and approves the decision. As an example mapping, the signatures on the data classification table stand in for that approval. Keep the rationale for each tier beside them. NIST SP 800-60 also says to revisit a categorisation at least every three years, or when the system or its supporting business lines change significantly. Set your own interval, and name the changes that trigger an earlier review. ## What to do about it Keep the scheme small. Three or four tiers is enough for most companies, and a scheme nobody can remember gets ignored the same as none. Map every AI tool in the register to which tiers may reach it. Make the most important rule explicit: customer data and secrets never go into an unclassified tool. The [AI Governance Starter Kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit) already includes this table, mapped to what may reach a vendor.

rows.text: GDPR Article 35 makes this review mandatory, not a judgement call, in three situations. One is large-scale profiling with legal or similarly significant effects. Another is large-scale processing of special-category data, such as health or biometric records. The third is systematic large-scale monitoring of a public space. Most consequential AI systems land in the first of these by default. The assessment has to describe the processing and why it is necessary. It has to assess the risk to the people concerned and set out the measures that reduce it. Where the company has appointed a data protection officer, the company must consult that officer while it carries out the assessment. Signing off afterward does not count. Where the system is high-risk under the EU AI Act, Article 26 also refers to the DPIA. A deployer must draw on the information the provider supplies under Article 13 when carrying out this GDPR assessment. The two obligations end up sharing evidence, not separate files.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up Almost any AI system worth building processes personal data, which makes a DPIA the default question rather than an edge case. Legal or procurement asks for it specifically once a system moves from a prototype to something touching real customer records. People often confuse it with the newer AI Act impact assessment. That is why explaining the difference is usually the more useful answer than either document alone. ## When monitoring staff triggers one Article 35(3) names three cases, but Article 35(1) asks for a DPIA wherever processing is likely to result in a high risk to people. The Article 29 Working Party's 2017 guidelines list criteria that point to high risk. Systematic monitoring is one. Data about vulnerable people is another, and employees may count as vulnerable because of the power imbalance. Meeting two criteria means a DPIA in most cases. Whether a dashboard of AI tool usage counts as systematic monitoring depends on how person-level it is. That is an inference, not a regulator's ruling. ## DPIA template: the headings and fields to copy A DPIA template follows [Article 35(7) GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj/eng), which sets four minimum contents. They are a description of the processing and its purposes, an assessment of necessity and proportionality, an assessment of the risks, and the measures that address them. The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) adopted a [DPIA template](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2026-05/edpb_dpia_template_2026_v1_en.docx) on 10 March 2026 and [consulted on it](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/public-consultations/template-for-data-protection-impact-assessment_en) until 9 June 2026. The EDPB's [announcement](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/news/enhancing-compliance-and-consistency-edpb-adopts-dpia-template_en) says using it is not mandatory. The consultation page still offered the first version on 10 November 2026. The template has seven sections: 0. Overview of the processing - controllers and joint controllers, with the data protection officer (DPO) contact - each processor and [sub-processor](/glossary/sub-processor), with its tasks - processing name, launch date and end date - technical sheet: team, reasons for the DPIA, scope, completion date, validation date, publication plan 1. Systematic description of the processing - each personal data item, with data type, data subject category and special category flag (add your [data classification](/glossary/data-classification) tier) - purposes, secondary uses and their compatibility - nature, scope and context, including cross-border processing and international transfers - phases from collection to deletion, with a data-flow diagram - supporting assets, such as hardware, software, APIs and models, and people - approved codes of conduct 2. Analysis of the processing - legal basis for each purpose, and the Article 9(2) reason for each special category - per data item: need, recipients, retention period, quality threshold - measures for the Article 5(1) principles, data subject rights, consent, processors, transfers, design and default, and security, each marked planned, partially implemented or implemented 3. Considerations on necessity and proportionality - threats from the processing working as designed, with risk sources and impact - necessity: effective and least intrusive, with evidence and alternatives - proportionality: benefits weighed against the impact on rights 4. Risk assessment and management - threats from accidental, unlawful or abnormal events, at least illegitimate access, undesired modification and disappearance of data - method, then per risk: likelihood, severity, modulating factors, level, acceptable or not - additional measures, residual risk, and a plan with responsible team and timeline 5. Involvement of interested parties - DPO opinion and how it was implemented (Article 35(2)) - views of data subjects or their representatives, or why they were not involved (Article 35(9)) 6. Conclusion and decision - rejected, consult the supervisory authority, approved, or approved with conditions The EDPB's [explainer](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2026-05/edpb_dpia_template_explainer_2026_v1_en.pdf) says a responsible official, such as the managing director, must formally approve the DPIA. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), the UK regulator, publishes a [sample DPIA template](https://ico.org.uk/media2/migrated/2553993/dpia-template.docx) in its [guidance on the UK GDPR](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/accountability-and-governance/data-protection-impact-assessments-dpias/how-do-we-do-a-dpia/). Add its sign-off block after section 6. Each item takes a name, position and date: - measures approved by - residual risks approved by, after consulting the supervisory authority if a high risk remains (Article 36(1)) - DPO advice provided, with a summary of it - DPO advice accepted or overruled by, with reasons if overruled - consultation responses reviewed by, with reasons if the decision departs from individuals' views - who keeps the DPIA under review (Article 35(11)) Record each DPIA's review date in your [AI register](/glossary/ai-register). Check a finished DPIA against Annex 2 of the Article 29 Working Party's [DPIA guidelines](https://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/article29/redirection/document/47711). It lists four criteria for an acceptable DPIA: a systematic description, necessity and proportionality, managed risks, and involved interested parties. For an AI system, add these fields. The first two come from the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act) and, under [Article 113](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27/eng) as amended, apply to [high-risk AI systems](/glossary/high-risk-ai-system) from 2 December 2027 for Annex III and from 2 August 2028 for Annex I: - provider information: the Article 13 instructions for use, which Article 26(9) tells the [deployer](/glossary/provider-vs-deployer) to use for the DPIA, including intended purpose, accuracy, known or foreseeable risks to fundamental rights, input data specifications and [human oversight](/glossary/human-oversight) measures - [AI impact assessment](/glossary/ai-impact-assessment): where Article 27 applies, the DPIA sections that already meet its obligations, for cross-reference under Article 27(4) - automated decisions: where model output alone decides something with legal or similarly significant effect, the Article 22(2) ground (contract, authorising law or explicit consent) and its safeguards ## What to do about it Write the DPIA before the system is built, not after, since a risk found during design is cheap to change. The same risk found after launch usually is not. Start from what the system actually collects and why, then fill in the template above. Consult the data protection officer while there is time to act. The [AI Governance Starter Kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit) lays out the same data classification a DPIA starts from.

rows.text: Formally Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Act entered into force on 1 August 2024. It sorts AI systems into a risk ladder, from banned practices, to a high-risk category, to a lighter set of transparency duties. High-risk covers things like hiring, credit and law enforcement. The lighter duties apply to systems such as chatbots. The Act leaves everything else largely unregulated. Obligations scale with the tier. High-risk systems carry duties such as a conformity assessment, technical documentation, human oversight, and registration in an EU database. The Act applies to any company whose AI system is used in the EU, not only companies based there. That is why a US-based startup with European customers cannot treat this as someone else's problem. In practice, the Act changes what "we did not think about that" costs. For a high-risk use case, a company now needs a documented risk assessment and a named point of human oversight. The company also needs evidence of both, ready before a regulator or a customer's legal team asks.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It comes up the moment a company has, or wants, a customer in the EU, regardless of where it is based. A customer's legal team asks which risk tier your product falls into before they sign, because their own exposure depends on your answer. A board asks about it once a competitor gets fined, or a customer raises it at renewal. The Act follows the AI system's users, not the provider's registered address. ## What to do about it Work out which risk tier each AI system falls into. Most products used inside a normal business are not high-risk. A few categories, hiring and credit among them, almost always are high-risk and deserve a real legal read. For anything near the high-risk category, start the paperwork now: a risk assessment, a named oversight point, and technical documentation. For everything else, keep the register entry current, so the answer is a lookup, not a scramble.

rows.text: The comparison that matters is to an ordinary test suite. There is one difference: the system under test can give a different answer each run. A typical eval is a set of inputs with known good answers or a scoring rule. It runs automatically whenever the prompt, the model or the surrounding code changes. The team tracks the pass rate over time rather than a single pass or fail. Engineering teams build them because "it worked when I tried it a few times" does not survive a prompt change six months later, once nobody remembers which cases mattered. Security reviewers and boards ask about them because an eval suite is the concrete answer to "how do you know it still works." Without an eval suite, that question has no answer better than trust. In practice, evals change how a team ships. A prompt or model change runs through the same suite every time. A drop in the pass rate blocks a release, the same way a failing test would.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up A security reviewer or a technical board member asks the same question they would of any release process. What stops a bad change from reaching customers? For a normal codebase, the answer is a test suite. For an AI feature, the honest answer is either an eval suite or "we check by hand." That second answer does not hold up once a product has more than a couple of prompts. ## What to do about it Write down twenty to fifty real cases the system must handle correctly. Draw them from actual support tickets or usage, not invented examples, and include a few you know are hard. Score each case automatically where you can, and by a human reviewer where you cannot. Track the pass rate over time rather than treating one run as final. Run the suite before every prompt or model change ships.

rows.text: In practice a guardrail is one of three things. A topic restriction limits what the model will engage with. An output filter limits what a user sees. An action gate controls what the system may do without a check first. OWASP, an independent security-standards group, publishes its own mitigation list for prompt injection. rows.text: A system reaches the category one of two ways. Article 6(1) covers the first: a safety component of a product already regulated under EU product-safety law, or that product itself. Medical devices and machinery are examples. That product-safety law already requires third-party conformity assessment. Annex III covers the second: eight listed use-case areas, among them biometric identification, employment decisions, credit scoring and law enforcement. Article 6(2) makes a system high-risk just by falling into one of those areas, with no product-safety law involved at all. A system inside Annex III can still escape the label under Article 6(3), for four narrow reasons. One is a limited procedural task, such as reformatting an application into a standard template. Another is improving a human decision already made, such as tidying a report's wording without changing its recommendation. A third is detecting a deviation without replacing human judgement, such as flagging an unusual transaction for a fraud analyst to review. The fourth is a preparatory task ahead of someone else's assessment, such as gathering a loan applicant's documents before a human underwriter looks at them. None of the four applies to profiling: a system that profiles individual people is high-risk regardless.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It is the first question every other AI Act obligation depends on. A customer's legal team or an investor's due diligence checklist asks it before anything else about the system. A board hears it phrased more simply, as "are we in the category that gets the heavy paperwork, and who decided." Getting the classification wrong either way has a real cost, either missed obligations or needless process on a system that never required it. ## What to do about it Run the classification test on each system separately, not on the company as a whole. One product can be high-risk while another, built the same month, is not. Write the decision down, including the reasoning for a not-high-risk conclusion, since an authority can ask to see it later. This classification is exactly what the [AI readiness and risk assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment) produces for every system in the inventory, not just the ones already suspected.

rows.text: The concept sits on a spectrum, from full autonomy at one end to human-in-the-loop at the other. With human-in-the-loop, a person must actively approve each step before it happens. Human-on-the-loop sits in between: a person can intervene but does not have to act. Where a system falls on that spectrum is a design decision, not a fixed property of the technology. For anything that can affect a person's money, employment or legal standing, this decision is one of the first things a customer's security team or a regulator asks about. Article 14 of the EU AI Act requires "effective" human oversight for high-risk systems: oversight that can genuinely catch and correct a bad output, not a person who clicks approve without reading it. In practice, this decides where a company can safely remove a person from a workflow, and where it still needs one.

rows.text: ISO/IEC's joint technical committee for artificial intelligence wrote it. It specifies requirements for an AI management system: the recurring policies, roles and processes that govern how an organisation develops, provides or uses AI. It uses the same Plan-Do-Check-Act structure as other ISO management-system standards, such as ISO/IEC 27001 for information security. Unlike the NIST AI RMF, a free framework, ISO/IEC 42001 is a standard that an accredited third party can audit and certify a company against. Enterprise customers and procurement teams ask for it, or ask how your company compares with it. They ask because certification gives them a documented, externally checked answer instead of a vendor's own claim. Working towards the standard means three things: writing down a risk-assessment method, running an inventory of AI systems, and reviewing that inventory on a schedule. None of that requires certification itself.

rows.text: Every call to any model passes through one place, instead of going straight from application code to a vendor's API. A company can then control who may call a model, and log every prompt and response for an audit trail. It can also redact sensitive data before it leaves the building. It can apply rate and cost limits, and fail over to a different provider if one goes down. Without a gateway, API keys end up scattered across a codebase, and nobody holds a full log of what the company sent to a vendor. A data leak through a prompt stays invisible until a customer or regulator finds it first. Engineering teams adopt one to stop rebuilding the same authentication and logging code in every project that touches a model. It also gives a direct, specific answer to a vendor questionnaire's question about how the company controls model access. That beats a description of several applications each doing it inconsistently.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up A security questionnaire almost always asks how the company controls and logs access to the model provider. "Each team manages its own API key" is a poor answer. A board or customer asks a version of the same question after a well-publicised leak elsewhere. In that leak, a prompt carrying sensitive data reached a third-party model unlogged. Without a gateway, nobody can produce every prompt sent to a vendor last month. ## What to do about it Put one gateway in front of every model call before adding a second application that talks to a model, not after. Route all API keys through it rather than into individual codebases, and log every request and response. Redact anything that looks like a customer identifier or a secret before it leaves. Solid open-source and hosted options already exist, so this is rarely worth building in house. ## The gateway as a governance control A written policy says what staff may do with a model. A gateway is the control that enforces it, because every model call passes through one place where the policy runs. It decides who may call which model, strips sensitive data before it leaves, applies rate limits, and logs each request and response. That log is the evidence a security questionnaire asks for: it shows the policy ran, not only that it exists. The limit is coverage: a gateway controls only the calls that go through it, so an application that calls a vendor directly sits outside the control. The [LLM Gateway Governance Config](/resources/llm-gateway-governance-config) gives a policy file format for one.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up In this site's reading, it comes up when a team connects an [agentic workflow](/glossary/agentic-workflow) to its own systems and a security reviewer asks what the agent can touch. "Open protocol" can sound like a safety claim. It is not one. A 2026 sheet from the US National Security Agency (NSA) says MCP's security posture "remains uneven and highly dependent on implementation discipline rather than protocol guarantees". The sheet cites the November 2025 revision of the specification. ## What to do about it The model picks which tool to call, and text it reads can steer that choice. That is [prompt injection](/glossary/prompt-injection). The MCP project's security policy says a report that an LLM invoked an unexpected tool is not an MCP vulnerability. So the limits go in the host and the servers, as [guardrails](/glossary/guardrails) in code. Give each server only the access its task needs. That is least privilege. The NSA sheet recommends that tool execution be constrained and sandboxed. I start every new tool read-only. Any action that writes, spends money or touches personal data needs approval from a named person. Credentials live with the [gateway](/glossary/llm-gateway) or the server, never in the prompt, and they rotate every quarter. ## Before a third-party server connects I pin the exact version of a third-party server and review its source before it connects. rows.text: The format comes from a 2018 paper. The paper proposed model cards as a response to models shipping with no consistent account of how their makers had actually tested them. A rigorous card reports evaluation broken out by group: race, geographic location, sex, skin type. It also breaks out intersections, such as age combined with race, instead of one blended figure that hides where performance drops. NIST's risk management framework expects the same thing in substance. A model should be explained, validated and documented, not simply shipped. A vendor who has actually done that evaluation work typically wants to show the results, since they usually help on some axis. One who cannot produce a card has most likely skipped the evaluation itself, not just the paperwork describing it.

A card makes two vendors comparable on the same axes, rather than on whatever each chose to advertise. A technical due-diligence review reads the limitations section specifically. rows.text: Article 53 of the EU AI Act turned this from a private claim into a published one for general-purpose models. Providers must publish a sufficiently detailed summary of training content, following a template the AI Office issued. That summary covers the scale of the data, and whether it includes licensed material, scraped web content, user data or synthetic data. For a smaller company building on someone else's model, provenance is a due-diligence question, not a publishing duty. Work through it before signing, not after. That distinction decides who actually reads the summary, and when. The company reads the summary before it signs a contract, not after a customer's legal team goes looking for where the data came from.

rows.text: The framework sets out four functions an organisation applies to an AI system. GOVERN covers policy and accountability, while MAP covers understanding context and risk. Testing and metrics fall under MEASURE. Acting on what it found is MANAGE's job. It is not a law, and it is not sector specific. A bank, a hospital and a ten-person startup can all use the same structure. NIST says it offers flexibility to organisations of all sizes, so small companies can use it too. US procurement teams, and increasingly non-US ones, ask about it. They ask because the framework gives a common vocabulary for a question that used to have no fixed answer. That question is how you know your company actually manages an AI system's risks, not just discusses them once. In practice, adopting the framework means someone can point to a specific function, and to a specific piece of evidence behind it. That beats a general assurance that everything is under control.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It comes up in almost every vendor security questionnaire, and in board packs once a company runs more than one AI system. A customer's risk team wants a framework they recognise, not a bespoke description of your process. They want it because it lets them compare you against every other vendor they review. A board wants the same thing for a different reason: a structure to ask questions against, rather than trusting that engineering thought of everything. ## NIST AI RMF framework: the four functions and what each asks for The NIST AI RMF framework has two parts: Part 1 frames AI risk and describes seven trustworthiness characteristics, and Part 2 holds the Core of four functions and the profiles. The Core divides the functions into nineteen categories and seventy-two subcategories, which [NIST AI 100-1](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf) lists in four tables. | Function and size | What NIST asks, by category | Examples of evidence you may already hold (not NIST text) | | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | GOVERN: 6 categories, 19 subcategories | Working policies, accountable and trained people, workforce diversity and inclusion, a risk-aware culture, outside feedback, rules for third-party risk | [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) with an owner per system (GOVERN 1.6, 2.1), [AI acceptable use policy](/blog/ai-acceptable-use-policy-for-a-50-person-company) (GOVERN 1.4), training records (GOVERN 2.2), vendor review procedure (GOVERN 6.1) | | MAP: 5 categories, 18 subcategories | Context and purpose documented, the system categorised, benefits and costs set against benchmarks, every component mapped for risk, impacts on people characterised | Intended-use statement per system (MAP 1.1), vendor documentation of limits (MAP 2.2), written procedure for [human oversight](/glossary/human-oversight) (MAP 3.5), risk assessment of likelihood and size of each harm (MAP 5.1) | | MEASURE: 4 categories, 22 subcategories | Metrics chosen and applied, the system evaluated against the trustworthiness characteristics, risks tracked over time, feedback on the measurement gathered | [Eval suite](/glossary/evals) with test cases and pass rates (MEASURE 2.1, 2.3), monitoring of the live system (MEASURE 2.4), security test report (MEASURE 2.7), user problem and appeal channel (MEASURE 3.3) | | MANAGE: 4 categories, 13 subcategories | Risks ranked and answered, plans that raise benefit and cut harm, third-party risks managed, response, recovery and communication plans documented and monitored | Go or no-go sign-off (MANAGE 1.1), risk decisions to mitigate, transfer, avoid or accept (MANAGE 1.3), switch-off or rollback steps (MANAGE 2.4), incident log (MANAGE 4.3) | The seven trustworthiness characteristics in Part 1 are valid and reliable, safe, secure and resilient, accountable and transparent, explainable and interpretable, privacy-enhanced, and fair with harmful bias managed. MEASURE evaluates a system against them. GOVERN is where [AI governance](/glossary/ai-governance) sits in the framework. NIST calls it cross-cutting and says it is infused through the other three functions. MAP, MEASURE and MANAGE can be applied to a specific system at a specific lifecycle stage. NIST says most users start with MAP once GOVERN is in place, then continue to MEASURE or MANAGE. NIST adds that the process should be iterative. NIST describes the framework as voluntary, and says its actions are not a checklist and not necessarily an ordered set of steps. An organisation may select some categories and subcategories or apply all of them. NIST's [Playbook](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/playbook/) adds suggested actions for each subcategory, and an organisation may borrow as many or as few suggestions as fit its use case. Read a subcategory's full wording before you claim a document answers it. Profiles apply the Core to a setting. [NIST AI 600-1](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf) is the Generative AI Profile, published in July 2024. It defines twelve risks that generative AI creates or worsens, and lists suggested actions under only some subcategories. A Current Profile records how you manage AI today, and a Target Profile records the outcomes you want. Comparing the two likely reveals your gaps. The counts and mappings here follow NIST AI RMF 1.0, published in January 2023. NIST's [AI RMF page](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework), last modified 13 August 2026, still offers it for download. The same page says NIST is revising the framework as part of the White House AI Action Plan. NIST's [Playbook page](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/playbook/) says the Playbook will be updated after the revision. Record which version your mapping uses. To compare the framework with [ISO/IEC 42001](/glossary/iso-iec-42001) and the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act), read the [FAQ on what each requires](/faq/what-do-nist-ai-rmf-iso-iec-42001-and-the-eu-ai-act-require). ## What to do about it Read the four functions once, properly, rather than skimming a summary. Map what you already do against GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE and MANAGE, and write down the gaps honestly. You do not need to implement all of it before you can talk about it. A short document lists what you have, your review step, and what you still owe against each function. That document beats a claim of full compliance with nothing behind it.

rows.text: An agentic workflow is a system that also calls tools to look things up or take actions on its own. Its record has to extend further. It needs every tool call made along the way, and what each one returned, not just the final input and output. A wrong outcome usually traces back to one step in a longer chain. Skipping tool-call logging leaves exactly that step unrecorded. Observability differs from a simple uptime dashboard. It can show a system is running while saying nothing about whether one specific answer, given to one specific person, was actually right. NIST's risk management framework calls this its Measure function: a system only counts as measured if it keeps being tested and tracked after release, not just before.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up A customer or an internal investigation asks: show me exactly what happened in this one case. A system with only aggregate metrics cannot answer. That is precisely the gap a security review is testing for when it asks about monitoring. It also comes up after a customer complaint that a specific answer was wrong. The honest response depends entirely on whether that exact exchange was ever recorded. ## What to do about it Log the full input, every step the system took including tool calls, and the output for every real request, not a sample. Keep those logs long enough to support an investigation. Make sure any one case can be pulled up by its own reference, rather than only appearing inside an average. This logging, plus a cost-per-outcome view, ships from the first release in the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint).

rows.text: Article 72 requires a documented monitoring system, sized to the technology and the risk of the specific system. It has to actively and systematically collect and analyse data on how the system performs once it is actually in use. Deployers feed into it directly, since Article 26 requires them to monitor the system on their end and report back to the provider. That way, the provider is not relying on its own visibility alone. The monitoring plan is not a separate document. Article 72 makes it part of the system's technical documentation, built and updated alongside it, not added after a complaint. A pattern the monitoring finds also feeds the next duty in the chain. That duty is to decide whether what happened counts as a serious incident that requires a report.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up Does anyone keep watching this system, or was it tested once and left alone? That is the specific question a customer's security team or a regulator asks after any AI failure story in the press. A board hears it as reassurance that a problem would surface through a defined process rather than a customer complaint reaching the news first. Providers who can only describe pre-launch testing, and nothing after, usually have no answer. ## What to do about it Write the monitoring plan before launch, since a plan invented after a problem appears is not the same thing. In the plan, say what you measure, who reviews it and how often. Build a route for deployer-reported issues to reach the provider. A monitoring system that never hears from the people using it day to day is monitoring very little. The [Fractional CAIO Retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) I run keeps this review on a fixed schedule, not only when a customer complains.

rows.text: Direct injection comes from whoever is typing into the box, phrased to override the model's own hidden starting instructions, its system prompt. Indirect injection is the more dangerous form. It arrives inside content the model retrieves on its own: a webpage it is summarising, a resume it is screening. No attacker ever touches the model directly. Multimodal systems add a further variant, since an instruction can hide inside an image processed alongside ordinary text. It has kept that position through every edition of the list, most recently the 2026 revision. The reason is structural: the model reads instructions and untrusted data through the same channel. A filter tuned on known patterns still misses a novel phrasing. Every mitigation available today reduces the odds of a successful attack; none removes them.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It is the first thing a security reviewer probes on any AI feature that reads outside content. That means a webpage, an uploaded file, an email, or a customer's own message history. The concern is not academic. A model that can also send an email, issue a refund or query a database turns a successful injection into something already done. It is no longer just an embarrassing reply. ## Prompt injection examples: ten cases and what each one does Prompt injection examples fall into two groups: direct cases, where the attacker is the system's primary user, and indirect cases, where a third party plants the text in content the system reads. That is the split [NIST AI 100-2 E2025](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-2e2025.pdf) uses. [Greshake et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.12173) demonstrated the indirect kind in 2023 against real systems, including Bing's GPT-4 powered Chat. | Example and source | How the text reaches the model | What it does | | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Support chatbot told to ignore its guidelines ([OWASP 2026](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-genai-llm-top-10-2026/), scenario 1) | Direct: the attacker's own message | Queries private data stores and sends emails, giving unauthorised access and privilege escalation | | EmailGPT, [CVE-2024-5184](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-5184) ([OWASP 2025](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/), scenario 5) | Direct: a malicious prompt from anyone with access to the service | Takes over the service logic, leaking hard-coded system prompts or running unwanted prompts | | Web page summary (OWASP 2026, scenario 2) | Indirect: hidden instructions in a page the user asks the model to summarise | Inserts a markdown image whose URL carries the private conversation to the attacker | | Job-description PDF (OWASP 2026, scenario 3) | Indirect: an AI-detection instruction embedded in the PDF | The applicant's model surfaces it and the recruiting system flags them, with neither party acting maliciously | | Poisoned document in a [RAG](/glossary/retrieval-augmented-generation) corpus (OWASP 2026, scenario 4) | Indirect: a document the attacker added to the store the application retrieves from | A matching query returns it, and its instructions alter the output | | Instructions split across resume fields (OWASP 2026, scenario 5) | Indirect: fragments in a resume's header, body and attachment | Evades a per-field classifier, and the recombined parts manipulate the model's recommendation | | Instruction hidden in an image (OWASP 2026, scenario 6) | Indirect: an image a multimodal model processes | The vision encoder extracts it, and the model gives harmful output or makes an unauthorised tool call | | [EchoLeak](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.10540) in Microsoft 365 Copilot, [CVE-2025-32711](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-32711) (OWASP 2026, scenario 7) | Indirect: one crafted email the assistant reads | Leaks organisational data with no user interaction, past a prompt-injection classifier | | Poisoned GitHub issue, from [Invariant Labs](https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-github-vulnerability) (OWASP 2026, scenario 9) | Indirect: the user's agent reads it through the GitHub [MCP](/glossary/mcp) server | Pulls private repository data into context and leaks it in a pull request on the public repository | | Encoded or low-resource-language payload (OWASP 2026, common example 8) | Either route, with the payload in Base64, ROT13, emoji or a low-resource language | Evades classifiers and filters that never saw the encoding | OWASP's 2026 edition files EmailGPT under indirect injection, though the National Vulnerability Database record and its [Black Duck advisory](https://www.blackduck.com/blog/cyrc-advisory-prompt-injection-emailgpt.html) describe a direct prompt. It labels the resume case direct input, though the applicant is the person screened, not the system's user. The table follows NIST's definitions in both. The same edition calls prompt injection intrinsic to current generative AI, since models make no architectural distinction between instructions and data. It says no reliable prevention mechanism exists today and no single control is sufficient. Here is one example mapping of its controls to the cases, using the 2026 numbering: - Direct cases: constrain the model's role in the system prompt (control 1), though an attacker who infers the prompt can bypass it - Cases that end in an action: keep credentials and state changes in code under least privilege as [guardrails](/glossary/guardrails) (control 4), check response formats there (control 2), and require [human-in-the-loop](/glossary/human-in-the-loop) confirmation before privileged or irreversible steps (control 7) - Indirect cases: pass external content through a separate, labelled channel (control 6), which OWASP says reduces attack success in non-adaptive tests only - Cases built to evade filters: filter at every modality boundary, for example in an [LLM gateway](/glossary/llm-gateway) (control 3), though rephrasing or encoding evades semantic filters - Every case: baseline with attack cases in [evals](/glossary/evals), then run [red teaming](/glossary/red-teaming) with the defence disclosed to the testers (control 11) ## What to do about it Never let a model's output directly trigger a sensitive action without a check enforced in code. Keep the model's own permissions to the smallest set it needs. Treat anything the model reads from outside the conversation as untrusted input, the way a web application treats a user-supplied string. Evals for exactly this kind of attack belong in the same pipeline that gates every other change. That is how I structure the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint).

rows.text: Article 3 defines a provider by two acts done together. The first is developing the system, or having someone else develop it. The second is placing it on the market or putting it into service, under the provider's own name or trademark. Payment is irrelevant. Giving the system away under your own brand still makes you the provider. A deployer is defined by use, not branding: using the system under the deployer's own authority. The only carve-out is personal, non-professional activity. A company using a tool internally is a deployer even if it never touches a customer. That test has a sharp edge. A company that fine-tunes a vendor's model and ships the result under its own product name has made itself the provider of that product. It does not matter that it built none of the underlying model. Owning the brand is what matters, not how much of the system the company actually wrote.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It surfaces in a contract negotiation once both sides realise the label matters more than expected. A provider owes technical documentation and a conformity assessment, while a deployer mainly owes human oversight and monitoring. A board hears about it when a vendor's contract quietly assigns the company duties it assumed the vendor carried. Getting the role wrong can leave a company holding an obligation nobody budgeted for. ## What to do about it Run the provider-or-deployer test per system, not per company. Rebranding one vendor's model can make a company a provider for that product while it stays a deployer for everything else it merely uses. Write the answer into the AI register alongside the risk tier, since a security questionnaire will eventually ask for both. The [Fractional CAIO Retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) is where I answer this kind of question inside a live negotiation. ## Deployer obligations checklist Article 26 of the EU AI Act sets these duties for a deployer of a [high-risk AI system](/glossary/high-risk-ai-system). They apply to high-risk systems only. The provider carries a separate set of duties, and public authorities and some biometric uses carry further duties in the same Article. - Use the system as the provider's instructions for use say. - Assign [human oversight](/glossary/human-oversight) to people who have the competence, training, authority and support to do it. - Make sure the input data you control is relevant and representative for the system's purpose. - Monitor the system against those instructions. If you have reason to think it presents a risk, tell the provider, importer or distributor and the market surveillance authority without undue delay, and suspend its use. - Report a [serious incident](/glossary/serious-incident-reporting) at once, to the provider first. - Keep the logs the system generates, as far as you control them, for at least six months unless other law says otherwise. - If you are an employer, tell the workers' representatives and the affected workers before you use a high-risk system at work. - Tell people when a high-risk system listed in Annex III makes or helps make a decision about them. - Use the provider's information for your [data protection impact assessment](/glossary/dpia) where one is required. - Cooperate with the competent authorities.

rows.text: A red team engagement produces a different kind of output than a test run. It is a list of the specific techniques that worked, detailed enough for someone else to reproduce the failure. It also carries a judgement on what an attacker could actually do with it. That reproducibility is what separates a report from an anecdote about something that broke once. NIST's generative AI profile recommends red teaming as a check against specific categories of harm, including information leakage and harmful content generation. Those failures depend on someone actively trying to cause them; they rarely show up in ordinary use. The finding that matters is the one nobody predicted going in.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up Boards and security reviewers increasingly ask for it by name, rather than accepting "we ran evals" as a full answer. An eval suite built by the same team that built the system tends to test what that team already expected to go wrong. It matters more, not less, once a system can take actions or read outside content. A missed failure then moves from a bad reply to a completed action. ## What to do about it Budget real time, not an afternoon, for someone to actively try prompt injection, data extraction and off-limits requests. Do it against the actual live system, not a sanitised demo. Write down exactly what broke, and fix the underlying guardrail, not just the one example that happened to get tried. I treat this as part of shipping in the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint), folding findings back into the eval suite before launch.

rows.text: The document store is usually a vector index. The system converts passages into embeddings, numerical representations of meaning, and matches a query against them by similarity, not exact keyword. Matching on meaning lets the system find a relevant passage even when the question shares none of the same words as the document. OWASP, the group that publishes widely used security-risk lists, tracks this as its own risk category. In a shared vector database, one customer's data can leak into another customer's results. Embeddings carry a second risk: someone can sometimes invert them to recover the source text they came from. Both risks sit inside the retrieval layer, invisible to anyone reviewing only the model or the prompts it receives.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up Procurement asks "is this RAG, or did you train on our data," because the two have different data-handling implications. RAG typically sends only retrieved snippets to the model at query time, rather than baking a customer's content into the model's own weights. It also comes up once someone questions accuracy. A wrong answer usually traces to a retrieval problem, not a flaw in the model itself. ## What to do about it Control access at the document-store level, not only at the chat interface. RAG will surface anything in the index to anyone who can ask the right question, regardless of who is meant to see it. Treat the document store itself as a data-classification boundary. Check what happens when a document containing hidden instructions ends up inside it. That exact scenario is one of the checks in the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint).

rows.text: The duty applies once a malfunction leads to death, serious harm, or a serious breach of someone's fundamental rights. Article 73 sets the default deadline at fifteen days from when the provider becomes aware of the incident. A widespread infringement or a serious disruption to critical infrastructure tightens that to two days. A death tightens it further, to ten days. Every deadline runs from awareness, not from the incident itself. Once the provider files the report, it has to investigate: assess the risk, take corrective action, and cooperate with the authority. It cannot alter the system in a way that would affect the investigation's findings without telling the authority first. The duty also covers serious harm to property or the environment, not only harm to people, though that case still runs on the fifteen-day default.

rows.text: The hardest form to spot is a model downloaded and run locally on a laptop. It never crosses the network as a request to a known AI vendor. The same problem shows up wherever an employee reaches for a tool without asking. A developer might call a model's API directly from a side project. A browser extension might quietly send page content to a third party to generate its summary. None of it sits inside a contract governing how that vendor handles company or customer data, because no one negotiated one. None of it appears in the AI register either. A security review or an incident response then starts from a blind spot, not a known list. The tool itself is rarely the real risk. The missing record of its use is.

rows.text: A sub-processor is a vendor an AI provider hands a company's data to behind the scenes. The model provider behind a SaaS tool is a common example. GDPR Article 28 requires the provider to get the customer's permission, and to bind the sub-processor to the same data protections by contract.

rows.text: GDPR Article 28 calls the AI vendor the processor and your company the controller. It gives the processor two ways to add a sub-processor. Specific authorisation names the sub-processor up front, so the controller signs off by name. General authorisation lets the processor add sub-processors as needed, but it has to tell the controller first and give a real chance to object. Either way, the processor must pass down the same data-protection obligations it owes directly, in the contract itself, not just a notice. The chain does not stop at one level either. The processor often runs its own infrastructure through a further sub-processor, such as a cloud host or a fine-tuning partner. That passes the same flow-down obligation another level down. Asking for the sub-processor list is really asking how many hops sit between a company's data and the last party that can actually see it.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It is a routine line on a security questionnaire: "list your sub-processors." It is also a revealing one. Teams build most AI features on someone else's model, which makes a sub-processor almost guaranteed rather than an edge case. A buyer who skips the question is signing a contract blind. They will not know where their data actually goes once it leaves the vendor's own systems. ## What to do about it Ask every AI vendor for its sub-processor list, and how it notifies customers of a change. Then check honestly: does the notice give a real chance to object, or just a record that it happened? Add the answer to the AI register entry for that vendor, next to the data classification of what reaches them. The [Fractional CAIO Retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) is where I check vendor contracts for this gap before a renewal.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It is different from a marketing spec sheet or an engineering wiki page. A regulator or notified body wants the specific content the Act lists, not a general description of the product. It also comes up in procurement due diligence, where a buyer of a high-risk system sometimes asks to see excerpts before signing. A vendor who can produce none of it has told you something. ## Technical documentation template: the nine Annex IV headings and their fields The template is [Annex IV](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27/eng) of the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act), which lists the minimum content of the technical documentation of a [high-risk AI system](/glossary/high-risk-ai-system). Article 11(1) requires it before the system goes on the market or into service, and requires it to stay up to date. The duty falls on the [provider](/glossary/provider-vs-deployer) (Article 16, point (a)). Copy these nine headings and fill the fields under each. 1. General description - Intended purpose, provider name, system version and its relation to earlier versions - Interactions with outside hardware, software or other AI systems, where applicable - Versions of relevant software or firmware, and any update requirements - All forms in which the system is placed on the market or put into service, such as embedded software, downloads or APIs - Hardware the system is meant to run on - For a product component: photographs or illustrations of external features, markings and internal layout - Basic description of the deployer's user interface - Instructions for use for the deployer 2. Elements and development process - Development methods and steps, including pre-trained systems or third-party tools and how you used, integrated or changed them - Design specification: logic and algorithms, key choices with rationale and assumptions about the people it is intended for, classification choices, optimisation target and parameter relevance, expected output and output quality, trade-offs made to meet Articles 8 to 15 - Architecture: how software components build on or feed into each other, plus the computing resources used to develop, train, test and validate - Where relevant, datasheets on training methods and training data: provenance, scope, main characteristics, how it was obtained and selected, labelling, cleaning - Assessment of the [human oversight](/glossary/human-oversight) measures needed, including technical measures that help deployers interpret outputs - Where applicable, pre-determined changes to the system and its performance, with the technical solutions that keep it compliant - Validation and testing: procedures, test data, metrics for accuracy, robustness and the other requirements, potentially discriminatory impacts, test logs and reports dated and signed by the responsible people - Cybersecurity measures 3. Monitoring, functioning and control - Capabilities and limits, with accuracy for specific persons or groups and overall expected accuracy - Foreseeable unintended outcomes and sources of risk to health and safety, fundamental rights and discrimination - Human oversight measures needed under Article 14, with the technical measures that help deployers interpret outputs - Specifications for input data, as appropriate 4. Performance metrics: why they suit this specific system 5. Risk management system: a detailed description under Article 9 6. Lifecycle changes: relevant changes you made to the system 7. Standards: harmonised standards from the Official Journal applied in full or in part or, where none, the solutions used to meet Articles 8 to 15 and the other standards and specifications applied 8. EU declaration of conformity: a copy 9. Post-market evaluation: the system that evaluates performance after release, including the [post-market monitoring](/glossary/post-market-monitoring) plan Add your own document control line above point 1: document version, date, system version covered. Annex IV does not list it. Article 11(1), as [Regulation (EU) 2026/1744](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng) amended it, lets SMEs, including start-ups, and small mid-cap enterprises provide these elements in a simplified manner.
