rows.text: In my reading of the sources cited here, adoption telemetry for AI tools needs six measures: - Coverage of approved tools. - Paid versus active use, with retention by team. - One agreed outcome per use case. - Delivery health, for engineering use cases. - Cost per outcome. - A short repeated survey, read as opinion. That set is a synthesis, not a finding any source states. The evidence for it starts with a randomised trial. In July 2025, METR published a randomised trial. Sixteen experienced open-source developers worked on 246 issues. Before the trial they expected AI to make them 24% faster. Afterwards they believed it had made them 20% faster. Their tasks took 19% longer with AI allowed. METR now marks that result as out of date. That gap between what the developers believed and what the trial found is why the list above treats a survey as opinion. In my reading, a dashboard built on self-report inherits it, and no cited source shows usage counts predicting a result. Because METR marks the result as out of date, take the lesson as one about method. It is not a lesson about the size of any one effect. Executives report little effect, and that is also self-report. An NBER working paper issued in February 2026 surveyed nearly 6,000 senior executives in the US, UK, Germany and Australia. It found that 69% of firms use AI. Nine in ten executives reported no impact on employment or productivity over three years. ## How far apart can belief and evidence be? The table sorts six sources by how each one got its result: a trial or study, work-system data, or what people said. | Source and date | Kind | Result | How far to trust it | | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | METR randomised trial, 10 July 2025 | Randomised trial | Tasks took 19% longer with AI allowed. Developers had expected a 24% speed-up and afterwards believed 20%. 16 developers, 246 issues. | Small, with early-2025 tools. METR now marks the result out of date. | | METR follow-up, 24 February 2026 | Follow-up study | Raw estimates: returning developers 18% faster, new developers 4% faster. Both intervals include a slowdown. 57 developers, 800 or more tasks. | METR calls it "an unreliable signal". Many developers declined to include tasks they did not want to do without AI, which likely biases the estimate downward. METR calls its data "only very weak evidence" of the size of the gain. | | Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2025 | Measured from work-system data | Issues resolved per hour rose 15% on average across 5,172 support agents. Less experienced agents improved on speed and quality. Gains for the most experienced agents were small. | Journal article with a staggered rollout. One setting, customer support. Figures are from the abstract. | | METR survey, 11 May 2026 | Reported by people | 349 technical workers. Median self-reported speed-up of three times, and 1.4 to 2 times in the value of their work. | Convenience sample, with a response rate near 2% for emailed invitations. METR says survey estimates tend to be larger than field-experiment estimates. | | NBER working paper 34836, February 2026 (revised March) | Reported by executives | Nearly 6,000 senior executives in the US, UK, Germany and Australia. 69% of firms use AI. Nine in ten report no impact on employment or productivity over three years. | Executive self-report. Figures are from the abstract. | | DORA report, September 2025 | Reported by people | Survey of nearly 5,000 people. More than 80% say AI raised their productivity. | A snapshot. DORA describes comparisons, not effects. Published by a vendor (Google Cloud). | Reported figures disagree. Executives report little impact, while technical workers report large gains. They were asked different questions. Technical workers were asked about their own speed and the value of their work. Executives were asked about employment and productivity over three years. The first three rows disagree in size and sign, and METR flags both of its own results as limited. In February 2026 METR said it believes developers are likely more sped up in early 2026. It called its own data "only very weak evidence" of the size of the gain. Any sentence that says AI makes people faster or slower ages quickly. A survey of your own staff belongs in the reported group. METR says survey estimates tend to be larger than field-experiment estimates. ## What do the usual adoption panels count? The panels below are the usual ones in the sources cited here. That is an inference, not a count. Each tool defines an active user its own way. Figures from two tools do not compare. | Source | What counts as active | | ------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | GitHub Copilot usage metrics | At least two active days in the trailing 28 to be placed in a usage phase. GitHub says "Passive" is not a measure of inactivity. | | Microsoft 365 Copilot Dashboard | Usage levels over a rolling 12 weeks. A returning user has at least one action in both the current and the previous period. | | DORA 2025 report | No log rule. Adoption is a survey factor made of reliance, trust and reflexive use. | Each panel below has a reason it misleads. | Measure | What it counts | Why it misleads | | -------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Seats or licences | Money spent. | In GitHub's reports, seat data is not included. It sits in a separate user-management API. | | Daily or weekly active users | One event in a window. | The window and the event differ by vendor, as the table above shows. | | Usage frequency, prompt counts | How often. | DORA's 2024 report, also published by Google Cloud, said measuring usage frequency is "likely not as meaningful as measuring reliance". | | Lines of code accepted, pull requests merged | Output volume. | GitHub calls its lines figure directional. A preprint on Cursor, covering open-source projects, found a short jump in lines added and lasting rises in static-analysis warnings and complexity. Faros, a vendor, found that teams with high adoption completed 21% more tasks and merged 98% more pull requests, with 91% longer review time and no significant link to company-level improvement. Its data is observational. | | Acceptance rate | Suggestions taken. | In a 2022 preprint on Copilot users, it tracked how productive users said they felt, rather than how long the accepted code lasted. | | Vendor hours saved and ROI | Action counts times fixed minutes times a wage. | Microsoft builds assisted hours from action counts, fixed minutes per action, and meeting recaps counted by meeting length. A default hourly rate then values them. GitHub says its ROI figures are estimates rather than exact financial results. | | Self-reported speed-up | Opinion. | METR says that in its 2025 trial people overestimated the effect on their task time by 40 percentage points. METR now marks that result out of date. | | Vendor resolution or deflection | Conversations that ended. | Intercom counts a customer who leaves without asking again as resolved, and charges for it, even if the customer is unhappy, unless its agent escalates. | | Adoption multiplier | Engaged users against passive users. | GitHub divides the average merged pull requests of engaged users by that of passive users. That compares people who chose the tool with people who did not, so it cannot isolate the tool's effect. That is an inference, not a GitHub statement. | DORA's 2025 report says: "The conversation must shift from adoption to effective use." DORA's page on measurement frameworks calls it a "common misconception that logs-based metrics are objective". None of the sources cited here shows a usage count predicting a business result. The research behind this article found no independent study that tests whether a usage-based adoption metric predicts outcomes. ## What should adoption telemetry measure instead? This set is a synthesis of the evidence above. No source states it in these words. Sort every number by where it came from. Logs show what people did. Surveys show what people said. The system where the work is recorded shows what happened there, and a randomised trial compares like against like. No one of these is the whole truth on its own. Six measures hold up better, and each has a limit. | Measure | Question it answers | What it cannot tell you | | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | | Coverage | How much AI use at work runs through approved tools? | Whether those tools help. | | Paid versus active, and retention by team | Which seats sit unused, and do people who tried a tool keep using it? | Whether the tool works. | | One outcome per use case | Did the outcome agreed before rollout move, against a baseline or a comparison group? | Why it moved, if there is no comparison. | | Delivery health (engineering use cases) | Did throughput or instability get worse as use grew? | Whether the use case pays off. | | Cost per outcome | What does one unit of the outcome cost? | Whether it is the right outcome. | | A short repeated survey | Do people trust the output, rely on it, and say where it gets in the way? | Whether work got faster. Read it as opinion. | The first two rows are diagnostics. Coverage is a governance question about where AI is used. Paid versus active use and retention show where a tool sits unused, which wastes money and points to a workflow problem. In this set, only the third row can show value. Put the weight on the outcome, delivery health, cost and survey rows, and read the survey as opinion. The [approach page](/approach) says I check who is still using the system a month after launch. The rule is people active in week four over people active in week one, per team, from gateway logs. Active means two different active days within four weeks. I count people, not accounts. When a team stops using a tool, I treat it as a workflow question, not a people question. Delivery health is on the list because DORA's 2025 report, published by Google Cloud, found AI adoption going with higher delivery throughput and still with higher instability. DORA describes that as a comparison in a snapshot, not an effect. For the survey, I reuse the items DORA publishes on trust, reliance and AI stance. I use them word for word and credit DORA. I ask once a quarter, and it takes five minutes to answer. This agrees with the [approach page](/approach). There, [evals](/glossary/evals) in CI, [tracing](/glossary/observability), [cost per outcome](/faq/how-is-cost-per-outcome-measured) and a rollback path come before a workflow touches a customer. The measures here add one line. Telemetry shows whether use lasted. An outcome measure shows whether it worked. These are different jobs. The [evals in CI article](/blog/evals-in-ci-for-llm-agents) covers testing a change before it ships. Adoption telemetry asks whether people keep using the system. ## How do you tell whether it worked? Agree the outcome before rollout. Read it from the system that already records it, such as ticketing, CI or your CRM, and not from the AI tool's own logs. The [pilot article](/blog/why-your-ai-pilot-never-reached-production) covers how to pick an outcome you can measure. Each use case gets one outcome metric. The client's owner chooses it and signs it before the start. The support-agent study in the table read its outcome, issues resolved per hour, from work-system data and not from tool logs. It used a staggered rollout. Then compare against something. A clean comparison is hard, even for researchers. METR's 2026 follow-up produced what it called an unreliable signal. METR's stated reasons include developers choosing not to participate rather than work without AI. It also lists developers becoming more selective about which tasks they submitted. I roll a tool out in waves by team. The teams still waiting are the comparison group. ## What should you check before collecting data about people? The rules below are general rules for monitoring staff, applied here by analogy. The sources cited here include no regulator text or court decision on AI usage logs. Start with the risk that is easy to miss. A team count built to plan training can turn into a person-level view used to judge performance. The ICO, the UK regulator, gives a clear example. Data collected to manage workspace capacity should not be re-used for performance management without a new lawful basis and a test of necessity and proportionality. That is UK law, not EU law. Treat a log that names a person as personal data about staff. The GDPR asks for a stated purpose, no more data than needed and no longer retention than needed (Article 5). Screen the plan for a DPIA first, and read the [DPIA entry](/glossary/dpia) for when monitoring staff triggers one. A client's data protection officer or counsel runs the DPIA screening. I hand them the question set. Do not rely on staff consent. The Article 29 Working Party's 2017 opinion said consent is highly unlikely to be a legal basis for data processing at work. The exception is where employees can refuse without adverse consequence. That opinion was written under the old Data Protection Directive, so treat it as persuasive guidance, not current law. Where a works council or staff body exists, check its rights before you switch anything on. | Country | What the text says | How far to trust it | | ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Germany | Works Constitution Act, section 87(1) no. 6: the works council has a say over technical devices meant to monitor behaviour or performance. The Federal Labour Court (1 ABR 20/21, 8 March 2022) reads this as objective suitability: a device counts if it can collect such data, whatever the employer intends. That case concerned Microsoft Office 365, where the parties did not dispute that the data could be used to check behaviour or performance. Applying it to AI usage logs is an inference. | Statute and court decision, both read in the original. | | Netherlands | Works Councils Act, article 27(1): the works council must consent to rules on the processing and protection of staff personal data. It must also consent to provisions aimed at or suitable for checking presence, behaviour or performance, where they cover all or a group of staff. | Secondary copy of the statute. The official text was not read. | | France | CNIL: a monitoring device must pass tests of justification and proportionality, go to staff representatives (the CSE, at employers with 50 or more staff) and be announced to staff beforehand. | Regulator guidance, dated 9 July 2026, read in the original French and paraphrased here. | I take clients with works councils. Engaging the council before switch-on is a standard step. Keep three things off any dashboard: rankings of named people, prompt content and re-use for performance reviews. The reasons are the ICO example above, the GDPR rule on data minimisation and a warning from DX, a vendor of measurement software. DX warns against using these metrics to judge individuals and says code volume is "particularly susceptible to gaming". Claude Code's documentation says prompt text is off by default. It includes the signed-in user's email, and the documentation tells operators to filter it at their own backend if that is a concern. That is an inference, not something the documentation says: the choice between named and team data sits at your own collector. Set a smallest group you will show, so that a count cannot point at one person. Microsoft's Viva Insights asks administrators to set a minimum group size of at least five. That is a product setting, not a legal figure, and the sources cited here give no legal threshold. The same page says the end-user opt-out does not apply to Copilot usage data, which stays available at the row level. That suggests a group-size floor limits what a report shows, not what is stored. That is an inference. Tell staff before the first log is collected. The CNIL says staff must be told beforehand. The ICO says to seek and document workers' views unless there is a good reason not to. The [acceptable use policy article](/blog/ai-acceptable-use-policy-for-a-50-person-company) covers the policy itself, not the telemetry behind it. I show breakdowns by team only, and a group needs at least five people. I collect no prompt content. I tell staff before telemetry starts. A named-person view is never the default. It exists only for a narrow stated purpose, recorded, approved by two people and kept 30 days. ## Where does the dashboard template fit? The [Adoption Telemetry Dashboard Template](/resources/adoption-telemetry-dashboard-template) turns these measures into eight panels. Paid versus active and retention become two panels, and the survey splits into trust and policy clarity. Each panel names the question it answers, the data source and the decision it supports. It is a page to copy into your own tool, not a live dashboard. Version 0.1 covers coding assistants and chat assistants. The coverage panel reads gateway logs, sign-in app lists, expense lines, API bills and the [AI register](/glossary/ai-register). The [register article](/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-system-register-in-a-week) shows how to build one. The [unapproved tools answer](/faq/what-do-we-do-about-tools-staff-are-already-using-without-approval) covers what to do about tools staff already use without approval. The [gateway config](/resources/llm-gateway-governance-config) already sets rate limits per team, not per user. The [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint) builds a dashboard that shows tracing and cost per outcome side by side. Its page promises no other panels. The [fractional CAIO retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) includes a review of every AI initiative, shadow tools included. ## What does this article leave out? It reports no client results and no numbers from my own telemetry. The evidence it cites comes from public studies and vendor documents. Most of the experimental evidence predates agentic tools, so treat each figure as a dated finding. It does not say which baseline method suits your company or which person-level views to allow. Those depend on your company, your country and your staff representatives. It does not say whether a plain count dashboard is an AI system under the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act), and no source cited here settles that. It is a summary of public texts, not legal advice. Take the legal questions to your data protection officer or counsel.

rows.text: An AI acceptable use policy only earns its place once it decides who approves a new AI tool and which data tier may reach which category of vendor. Beyond that, it decides whether a person checks AI output before it reaches a customer or a contract. It also decides when the company must tell a customer they are dealing with an AI system. Most templates answer the first two questions and stay quiet on the rest. That is exactly why staff read them once and then ignore them. A policy this size needs one named owner, not a committee. It also needs a review interval short enough to catch the tool people started using without asking. ISO/IEC 42001 treats a policy like this as one part of a management system, not a standalone document. The EU AI Act already requires disclosure once an AI system talks to a customer directly. Skip the enforcement clause and none of the rest holds.

rows.text: Most companies between 30 and 300 people already have staff using AI tools, whether or not a policy says so. The policy that works is not the longest one. It states which data may go where, who approves a new tool, and what happens when someone gets it wrong. It does this in language a new hire reads in one sitting. ## What does a working AI acceptable use policy actually need to say? A policy that survives contact with real staff decides a short list of things, not a long one. Nine sections make up a working one. Each row here names the section, the decision it forces, and the specific failure it exists to prevent. | Section | What it decides | Failure it prevents | | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Scope | Which staff, contractors and AI tools the policy covers. | A contractor or a new hire assuming the rules do not apply to them. | | Data classification | Which data tier may reach which category of AI vendor. | Client or personal data pasted into a public chatbot with no data agreement. | | Approved tools and requests | Which AI systems are pre-approved, and how staff add another one. | Staff picking an unapproved tool because asking takes too long. | | Human review | Whether a person checks AI output before it reaches a customer, a contract or a filing. | An unreviewed AI draft going out under someone's name. | | Customer disclosure | When the company must tell a customer they are talking to an AI system or seeing AI-made content. | A hidden AI interaction reaching a customer where disclosure is a legal duty. | | Vendor training use | Whether a vendor may use company or client input to train its own models. | Confidential input quietly improving a vendor's public model. | | Ownership and review | Who owns the policy, and how often it is checked against what staff actually use. | A policy that describes a tool nobody uses, and stays silent about the one everyone does. | | Incident reporting | What staff do the moment an AI system produces something wrong or exposes data. | A bad output or a leak going unreported because nobody knew who to tell. | | Enforcement | What happens after a breach, and who decides. | A rule everyone knows the company never actually enforces. | The customer disclosure row is not optional once a system talks to people outside the company. Article 50 of the EU AI Act already requires a provider or a deployer to tell a person they are interacting with an AI system. It also requires labelling content the system generated, whether or not that system counts as high-risk. A staff-facing policy has to name who checks that duty before a customer-facing AI feature ships. The policy must not leave that to whoever built the feature to remember. ## What should the policy refuse to try to do? A policy that tries to be the technical control fails twice. It fails once because a paragraph of text cannot stop a paste into a browser. It fails again because staff read that overreach as proof the whole document is for show. Access limits, contract terms and vendor settings do the technical work. The policy states the rule those controls exist to support. Listing every approved tool by name reads as complete on the day you publish it. It is wrong within weeks, because a new model or a new vendor account always arrives faster than a document gets updated. A policy built around named tools also implies that anything missing from the list is quietly fine, and a reviewer wants to see the opposite. An outright ban is the easiest policy to write and the least effective one to run. It does not remove the reason someone went looking for an AI tool in the first place. It just moves that search out of sight, where it is much harder to see or govern. ## What do you do about the tools staff are already using? By the time you draft a policy, some staff are already using AI without asking anyone first. That means drafting client emails in a personal chatbot account or running a browser extension nobody vetted. It also means building a habit around a coding assistant they picked themselves. That is [shadow AI](/glossary/shadow-ai), and treating it as rare is the first mistake a policy can make. Two moves fix more of it than a warning email does. First, make the approved path faster than the workaround: a fast yes for a low-risk tool beats a slow review nobody wants to wait for. Second, check instead of asking. Checking browser extensions, expense claims and what the company actually pays AI vendors shows what people are really running. That beats trusting a self-reported survey. ## What happens when someone breaks the policy? Most breaches are not sabotage. Someone pastes a client's contract into a personal chatbot account to move faster, not to leak it. That is different from someone who was told a tool was blocked and used it anyway, or who hid AI involvement in work they signed off as their own. A policy that cannot tell the two apart will punish the wrong case or excuse the real one. One named role decides what happens next. That is the same person who owns the AI register and the policy itself, not a group chat and not a vote. They classify what happened and decide whether legal or an affected client needs to hear about it. They also choose the response, from a conversation to removal of access to company systems. That decision runs through the disciplinary process HR already has for any other policy breach. The AI policy needs a clear point where that existing process starts, not a punishment system of its own. Silence is its own answer too. If a policy never states what happens after a breach, staff test it once and learn from the result whether any of it is real. ## Who should own it, and how does it stay current? The same person who is already accountable for AI risk overall should hold this document. A shared inbox cannot hold it, because someone has to be answerable when a customer or an auditor asks a direct question. [ISO/IEC 42001](/glossary/iso-iec-42001) treats a policy like this as one part of a management system, reviewed on a schedule and checked against a live inventory. A review interval only works if you tie it to something that actually changes. That can be a new hire, a new vendor account, or a client contract that names a data rule of its own. Quarterly is a reasonable default for a company this size. The exact interval matters less than the fact that one exists and someone is accountable for keeping it. The version I run for my own practice is public at [my AI policy](/ai-policy). It is one page, a worked example of the same shape at a much smaller scale. The [Starter Kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit) lists the documents a security review asks for and who signs each. It suits a company with more than one person to coordinate. ## What doesn't a policy like this solve? A written policy does not tell you whether anyone inside the company actually owns AI risk today. If nobody does, there is no obvious person to hand the draft to. So the gap usually surfaces during an [AI readiness and risk assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment), before it ever reaches the policy stage. Someone determined to break the rule will do it regardless; no policy stops that. A policy removes the excuse of not knowing, and it gives the company a fair, defensible reason to act when someone crosses the line anyway. Nobody enforces it without an owner, a review date and a stated consequence. Skip those and it is a page people skim once and never open again.

rows.text: ## What should the assessment cover? An AI readiness assessment template for SMB teams works best when it starts with a specific piece of work. Pick a task with a clear owner, a known input, and an output someone can inspect. Writing a draft reply for staff to review is easier to assess than a goal to automate customer service. Open the [AI readiness scorecard](/resources/ai-readiness-scorecard) and use its strategy, data, delivery, people, and governance axes to structure the review. The scorecard is the artifact. The notes you gather around it explain why you chose each answer and what needs to happen next. Write down where the task starts and ends, who uses the result, and what happens when the result is wrong. Name the business outcome separately from the proposed tool. That distinction lets the team compare a different approach if the first tool cannot meet the need. Keep the assessment scoped to the proposed use. A result for an internal draft does not settle whether the same tool should send replies to customers. ## Who should fill in the scorecard? Ask the person accountable for the outcome to sponsor the review. That person should be able to decide whether the proposed work is worth pursuing and who can make time for it. The sponsor need not supply every technical answer. Bring in the person who does the work, the owner of the data, and someone who can assess the proposed tools. Ask whoever handles security or privacy to review the parts within their remit. In a small company, one person may hold several of these roles. Ask each participant for evidence rather than a general opinion. A staff member can show the current workflow and where exceptions occur. A data owner can identify the source and access rules. An engineering lead can show how the proposed tool would connect to existing systems. Name a decision owner before the review ends. If nobody can accept the remaining risk or fund the fixes, record that as a gap rather than assuming approval will follow. ## How do we assess strategy and the work itself? Describe the result the business wants in terms the workflow owner can check. For a draft reply, that might be less staff time spent composing routine answers while keeping the review step. Record how staff would judge whether a draft is usable, and keep examples of both usable and poor drafts. Set a boundary around the proposed test. Note which requests belong in scope and which must go straight to a person. For example, a team might test routine account questions while excluding complaints and requests involving sensitive records. Check whether the work occurs often enough to justify the setup and review effort. Ask what staff do today when a request falls outside the usual path. The answers may point to a simpler change in the workflow instead of a model. Choose a comparison before testing. The team can compare reviewed drafts with its current process for the same kind of request. Record what counts as useful, what counts as an error, and who will judge disputed cases. ## What should we check about data? List the inputs the proposed workflow needs, where they come from, and who is allowed to see them. Include material that staff may paste into a tool, as well as data passed through a system connection. Ask the data owner whether each input is needed for the task. Review the quality of the source material with the people who use it. Old guidance, conflicting records, and missing fields can make a draft hard to trust. Record who can correct the source and how the team will know which version to use. Use the site's [data classification](/glossary/data-classification) guidance to discuss the sensitivity of each input. Check the proposed vendor terms and settings for storage, access, deletion, and any use of submitted data. If an answer is unclear, ask the vendor and retain the response with the assessment. For personal data, use the [privacy framework](https://www.nist.gov/privacy-framework) to help structure the review of data handling. Do not put live records into a test until the relevant owner has agreed on the scope and safeguards. ## How do we judge delivery readiness? Trace the proposed path from input to reviewed output. Identify where the tool runs, who can access it, and what connects it to business systems. A sketch can expose a missing owner or an unexpected route for data before anyone builds the workflow. Decide how the team will test outputs against the task. The [evals](/glossary/evals) page explains the site's term for that work. For the assessment, ask who will supply representative cases, review failures, and decide whether a change can proceed. Plan for the ordinary failure path as well as the happy path. A reviewer needs a way to reject a draft, correct it, and complete the work without relying on the tool. If the tool cannot be reached, staff should know where the task goes instead. Check access and security before connecting live systems. The [application security guidance](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/) can help the technical owner frame a review of model-based applications. Record which checks apply to the proposed design and who will perform them. ## How do we assess people and governance? Ask the staff who will use the tool where they need discretion. A reviewer should know what to check, when to reject an output, and whom to contact when the task falls outside the test scope. Include the work of reviewing and correcting outputs in the plan. Record the person who owns the proposed use and the person who can stop it. They may be the same person, but the decision should be explicit. Agree how staff report a bad output or a data concern and where that report goes. The [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) can provide a place to connect the use to its owner and review record. If staff are already using similar tools, ask how they use them and what information they enter. The answer may change the scope of the assessment. The NIST AI RMF is intended for voluntary use. It can help the team frame its risk discussion, but an assessment using it does not by itself prove compliance or make a use safe. ## How should we record evidence and gaps? Keep the scorecard answers tied to a working record. The table below is a suggested companion, not a description of fields in the downloadable scorecard. Copy its headings into a document or sheet and add a row for each issue that affects the proposed use. | Review area | Evidence to seek | Gap and next action | | ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | Strategy | A named outcome, task boundary, and decision owner | Define the outcome with the workflow owner | | Data | Sources, access rules, and vendor data settings | Confirm an unclear setting before using live data | | Delivery | A test plan, system path, and fallback | Prepare test cases and agree who reviews them | | People | Review instructions and a route for reporting errors | Walk staff through the proposed review step | | Governance | A use owner, stop decision, and risk record | Assign the owner and record the open decision | Use plain status labels in the companion record: ready, partial, blocked, or unknown. Agree what evidence is needed to move an item to ready. Unknown means the team has not checked, while blocked means it knows of a problem that prevents the planned test. Link to the evidence where the team can find it. A policy title alone may be too broad. Point to the relevant section, decision, test result, or vendor response, and note who checked it. ## When is a pilot ready to start? Review the open items with the decision owner and the people who will run the test. A pilot can start within its agreed scope when the necessary access, data handling, review process, and fallback are in place. Record any remaining limits and the person responsible for watching them. Do not average away a blocker with strong answers elsewhere. A clear business goal cannot fix an unapproved data flow. If a control is missing, either close the gap or change the test so the gap no longer applies. Write the decision in terms staff can use. For example, approve a draft-only test with named reviewers and specified inputs, rather than approving the tool for general use. State what would cause the owner to pause the test and how staff should report a problem. If the team lacks the capacity to assess a material risk, seek a review before proceeding. The [AI readiness and risk assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment) is an option when the business needs help turning open questions into a scoped decision. ## What happens after the assessment? Assign each open action to a person who can complete it, and agree when the decision owner will check progress. Keep the evidence and decision record with the scorecard so a later reviewer can see what was known when the test was approved. Revisit the assessment when the proposed use changes. Moving from staff-reviewed drafts to messages sent without review changes the decision, even if the same tool remains in place. New data sources, users, or system connections can also change what needs to be checked. During a pilot, collect the examples that challenged the original assumptions. A rejected draft may reveal a weak source, an unclear instruction, or a task that should remain with staff. Route the finding to the person who can change that part of the work. Use the [AI readiness scorecard](/resources/ai-readiness-scorecard) as the starting record, then update the companion notes as decisions and evidence change. Close an action only when its owner can show the agreed result.

rows.text: ## How do you use the scorecard for a real decision? The AI readiness scorecard five drivers framework covers strategy, data, delivery, people, and governance. Begin with the [AI readiness scorecard](/resources/ai-readiness-scorecard) and choose a workflow your team can describe in plain terms. Name its intended users, the output they need, and the decision that follows from it. A narrow scope makes the answers easier to check. For example, a team might review a proposed tool that drafts replies for staff to inspect. The review should cover the material used to draft replies, the review step, and what happens when the draft is wrong. It should not assume that a score for this task applies to every use of the same tool. Use the scorecard's own instructions for scoring. Beside each answer, keep a link to the evidence, the name of its owner, and any unresolved question. A policy draft, a working test, and a promise to do the work later carry different weight. Mark missing evidence clearly rather than filling the gap with an optimistic score. | Driver | Evidence to look for | | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | | Strategy | A named problem, owner, and decision about scope | | Data | Permission to use the inputs and a way to check their quality | | Delivery | A test method, release owner, and support plan | | People | Time, training, and a clear route to report trouble | | Governance | A record of risks, approvals, and response duties | The table is a starting point for discussion, not a replacement for the scorecard. Ask each owner to show what exists today, then record what still needs a decision. ## What should strategy prove before work starts? Strategy connects the proposed workflow to a problem worth solving. Ask the sponsor to describe the current task, who performs it, and what would change if the new workflow worked. The answer should name a business owner who can make trade-offs, not just a team that wants to try a tool. Agree on an outcome that can be checked against the current process. That might be less time spent drafting a reply, provided the review work does not erase the saving. It might be a better way to find a relevant document, provided staff can check that the result is current. Record how the team will judge the outcome before choosing a vendor or building a demo. Scope matters as much as the intended benefit. Write down what the workflow will handle, what stays outside it, and when a person must take over. If the sponsor cannot accept those limits, the team has a strategy gap even if the technology looks promising. The [assessment service](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment) is a possible next step when the sponsor needs a deeper review of those choices. Bring the proposed scope and the decisions that remain open. This gives the discussion a concrete subject instead of a broad request to become ready for AI. ## Which data questions change the score? Start with the actual inputs and outputs of the chosen task. List where the source material lives, who controls access, and whether the team has permission to use it for the proposed purpose. Include the text staff enter into the tool as well as the records the tool retrieves or produces. Then inspect whether the material fits the task. A folder may be easy to reach but contain old instructions, repeated files, or records with no clear owner. Ask who can correct those problems and how the workflow will avoid relying on material that has been withdrawn. A sample review can expose questions that an access request alone will miss. Sensitive material needs a clear handling decision before it enters a test. The team should know what can be shared with a vendor, where outputs will be stored, and who can see them. Use the site's [data classification](/glossary/data-classification) entry when deciding how to discuss different kinds of material with the people who own them. Keep access and quality as separate notes. A team may have permission to use a source while lacking confidence in its content. It may also have useful records that cannot yet be shared for the proposed use. Each case calls for a different owner and a different next action. ## Can the team deliver and support the workflow? A working demonstration gives the team something to inspect, but delivery needs a path for testing, release, and support. Ask who will build or configure the workflow, who can change it, and who will decide whether a change is ready for users. Those duties should survive the end of a pilot. Prepare examples that represent the work staff expect to do. Include difficult cases and cases where the tool should decline or hand the task back. Agree on how reviewers will judge the results, then keep the examples available when the workflow changes. The [evals entry](/glossary/evals) gives the site definition for this kind of testing. The team also needs a way to notice trouble after release. Decide where users report a bad result, who checks the report, and how the workflow can be paused or rolled back. Record who pays for support work and where that work sits among other team duties. For a wider view of production practices, the [machine learning delivery guidance](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/mlops-continuous-delivery-and-automation-pipelines-in-machine-learning) offers material to consider. Apply its ideas to the proposed workflow rather than assuming that every practice fits a small internal tool. ## Are the people doing the work ready to use it? Talk to the staff who will use the output, not just the sponsor who requested it. Ask what they need to inspect, where errors would be costly, and whether the proposed handoff fits their working day. A process that depends on careful review needs enough time for that review to happen. Training should follow the task. Show users what the tool is meant to do, what material they may enter, and how to reject or correct an output. Give reviewers a route to a person who can answer questions. Keep the instructions close to the work rather than relying on a single launch session. Check the effect on roles and workload. If staff must review every draft, their manager needs to account for that work. If a specialist must approve exceptions, the specialist needs time and a way to see the relevant record. An owner named on paper may not have the authority or capacity to carry out the role. Ask for a small trial with the people who would use the workflow. Governance starts with clear ownership of the risks and decisions tied to the workflow. Identify who can approve the use, who can accept an open risk, and who must be told when something goes wrong. The site's [AI governance entry](/glossary/ai-governance) provides the definition used across these pages. Put the decision in a record that the delivery team can find. Describe the intended use, the data involved, the main failure cases, and the controls the team plans to use. Note any open issue, its owner, and the decision needed to close it. A record with no route to approval leaves the team guessing at release time. Vendor use deserves the same attention as an internal build. Ask what the supplier can access, what the contract permits, and how the team would stop using the service. The [vendor assessment questionnaire](/blog/ai-vendor-assessment-questionnaire-template) provides questions to take into that conversation. Have the relevant contract and security owners check the answers. The named owner must make that decision against the evidence at hand. ## What should happen after the scores are recorded? Read across the drivers before discussing any overall result. Look for a gap that could block the specific workflow, even if other areas appear ready. A team might have a clear business case and willing users, yet lack permission to use the source records. In that case, a delivery plan should wait for a data decision. Turn each material gap into a task with an owner and a decision point. State what evidence would change the assessment, where that evidence will be kept, and who will review it. If the team cannot name those things, the next action may be to narrow the workflow rather than continue building it. Keep disagreements in the record. A delivery lead may judge a test set adequate while a user sees missing cases. Ask both people to identify the examples behind their views, then agree on who can accept the remaining uncertainty. Do not erase the disagreement merely to produce a tidy score. Revisit the scorecard when the workflow changes in a way that affects the answers. New users, new source material, or a different vendor can alter the evidence the team relied on. If the open questions span several owners or call for an independent view, take the completed scorecard into an [AI readiness and risk assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment).

rows.text: ## Where can I get an AI vendor assessment questionnaire template? The [AI governance starter kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit) contains a vendor questionnaire alongside the other documents used in a procurement review. Start there if you need the artifact. The questions in this article help you adapt a review to the service you want to buy. Write down the product name, the proposed workflow and the business owner before sending questions. Describe what people will submit, what the service will return and who will use the output. Include any planned links to internal systems or customer records. Give the vendor enough context to answer for the right product and settings. A response about a different service or a feature you will not buy may leave the actual use unchecked. Ask the supplier to identify any answers that depend on a contract, configuration or optional feature. Keep the completed questionnaire with the review record, rather than treating the returned file as approval. The buyer still needs to compare the answers with the intended use and decide who will resolve gaps. ## What questions should we send the vendor? Copy the prompts into your review record and leave space for an answer, evidence and a follow-up. Ask for the product and contract scope beside each response. The prompts below are a starting point, not a scorecard with automatic pass marks. | Topic | Prompt for the vendor | Evidence to request | | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | | Data use | Describe how inputs, outputs and uploaded files are used, including any model training. | Product terms and settings that govern the proposed use. | | Storage and deletion | State where data is stored, how long it is kept and how deletion works. | Retention terms and a description of the deletion process. | | Access and suppliers | Identify who can access customer data and which other suppliers handle it. | Access controls and the applicable supplier list. | | Security | Describe how access, encryption and security testing apply to the service. | A recent security report or a written control summary. | | Model behavior | Explain how the service is tested, changed and monitored for the intended task. | Test scope, known limits and change notices. | | Incidents | Explain how the vendor detects, reports and handles incidents affecting customer data or service use. | Incident terms, contact route and response process. | Ask for a named contact who can clarify technical answers. If a response applies only under particular settings, have the vendor state those settings. Record who will check them before the service goes live. ## How much detail should the review ask for? Match the review to what the service can see and do. A tool used with public text presents a different buying decision from a tool that can read customer records or change them. The reviewer should understand the proposed access before deciding how much evidence to request. Map the path of the data from the user or source system to the vendor and back. Include files, prompts, outputs and any logs that may contain copies. Note who can view each part and whether the service can call another tool or take an action. Use the site's [data classification](/glossary/data-classification) page when deciding what information may enter the service. If the intended data is not yet known, ask the business owner to settle that question before approval. A broad claim that the tool is safe for all data does not resolve the gap. Document the boundary of the purchase as well. A pilot with restricted data and users may need different conditions from a service connected to live operations. The decision should say which use has been reviewed and which uses need another check. ## What should we ask about data and training? Ask the vendor to distinguish service delivery from model training and other uses of customer content. Cover prompts, uploaded files, outputs and any data kept in logs. A reply that addresses only uploaded files may leave other copies outside the answer. Request the default setting, the setting available under the proposed contract and the steps needed to change it. If an administrator must turn a control on, assign someone to verify it. Keep the written terms with the setting record so the team can see what was agreed. Ask where the service stores and processes the data, including any suppliers involved. The [sub-processor](/glossary/sub-processor) page provides context for reviewing those relationships. Request notice of changes that would affect the agreed handling of the data. For a processor handling personal data, GDPR Article 28 calls for a contract or other legal act that sets out the subject matter and duration of processing. Read the [regulation](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj) alongside the proposed terms, and involve the person responsible for privacy review. The questionnaire should surface issues for that review rather than claim to settle them. ## How do we check security and access controls? Ask how the vendor restricts access to the service and to customer data. Cover user accounts, administrator access and the process for removing access when a person leaves. If the product can connect to internal systems, ask which permissions it needs and how those permissions can be limited. Request evidence that applies to the service being purchased. A security report for a parent company or a different product may still provide context, but it should not be treated as proof for the whole service. Ask what the report covers and whether any exclusions affect the planned use. For a language model service, include questions about untrusted material reaching the model and the actions the model can trigger. Use the [language model security project](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/) as a starting point for that discussion. Ask the vendor what protections apply in the proposed configuration and how customers can test them. Where evidence is confidential, agree on a review method rather than asking for a public copy. Record who saw the material, what it covered and any questions left open. Do not record a control as verified merely because a document exists. ## How should we assess model quality and changes? Describe the task the model will perform and the mistakes that matter to the business. Ask the vendor for test results that relate to that task, the language used and the conditions in which staff will rely on the output. General product demonstrations are useful context, but they do not establish fitness for your workflow. Agree on a sample of cases your team can check before release. Include ordinary requests, difficult inputs and cases where the correct response is to decline or ask for help. The [evals](/glossary/evals) page covers the site's terminology for this work. Ask how the supplier announces model or product changes and whether customers can test a change before relying on it. Record who will review a notice and decide whether the existing checks still apply. If the vendor cannot offer advance testing, agree on another way to detect a change that affects the workflow. Use the [risk management framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) as a reference when deciding how the checks connect to ownership and ongoing review. Keep test results and known limits with the purchase record. Give users a route to report errors that the test cases missed. ## What evidence is enough for a buying decision? Evidence should answer the question it is meant to support and cover the product in scope. For example, a retention policy can support a discussion about stored data, while contract terms can establish what the vendor agrees to provide. Neither should be treated as proof of an unrelated control. Check the date, author and scope of each document the vendor supplies. Ask whether it reflects the current service and proposed hosting arrangement. When a claim rests on a product setting, request a description or demonstration of that setting and assign a buyer to check it. Record exceptions without smoothing them into a pass. A vendor may have a planned control that is not yet available, or a control that applies only to a different plan. Note the effect on the proposed use and ask for a written commitment if the purchase depends on a change. The reviewer can request a restricted document review when the vendor cannot send a report. If that is not possible, document the evidence gap and offer the decision owner clear choices. Those choices may include limiting the data, delaying the connection or choosing another supplier. ## Who signs off on the questionnaire? The business owner should state why the service is needed and which workflow is in scope. Security, privacy and technical reviewers should assess the answers that fall within their remit. A named decision owner should then accept the remaining risk or send the purchase back for more work. Use the site's guide to [AI risk ownership in vendor procurement](/blog/named-person-responsible-for-ai-risk-in-vendor-procurement) when assigning those roles. The person coordinating the questionnaire does not have to make every specialist decision. Each open issue should still have an owner and a clear route to a final decision. Record the result as approved, approved with conditions, deferred or declined. For a conditional approval, specify the restricted use, the action required and who will check completion. Attach the relevant contract terms and evidence references so the team can find the basis for the decision later. Share the decision with the people who will configure and use the service. An approval that assumes restricted access is hard to enforce if the administrator never receives that condition. Add the service to the [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) with a link to the review record. ## When should we ask the vendor again? Set a review trigger when approving the service, and name the person who will watch for it. A change in data type, user access or connected systems can alter the basis of the original decision. A vendor change to its model, suppliers or data terms can also call for another look. Start the follow-up with the original scope and the changed condition. Ask the vendor only for answers and evidence needed to assess that change, unless the earlier record is no longer reliable. This keeps the review tied to the decision rather than sending the whole form by habit. Check whether open conditions were completed and whether the people who own the service have changed. Review error reports and incidents against the use that was approved. If the service now performs a different task, ask the business owner to describe that task before extending access. Keep the old decision and add the new result to the record. That gives the next reviewer a way to see what changed, what was accepted and which conditions remain in force.

rows.text: ## What belongs in a one-page board memo for AI strategy? The board memo AI strategy one page format puts a decision, its evidence and its limits in front of directors. It should be short enough to scan, but complete enough to support a vote or a request for changes. Start with the choice management wants the board to make. Then explain the business need, the proposed scope and the conditions attached to it. The memo also needs an owner with the authority to act. A group can contribute to the work, but the board should know who will answer for delivery and report setbacks. Put the spending request beside the decision, including any limit management is asking the board to approve. Reserve space for the most consequential risks and the next review point. Supporting papers can hold the details without making directors search for the basic case. The [AI readiness and risk assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment) is a route to a board memo when management needs a clearer view of its starting position. ## What decision should the board be asked to make? Choose a decision that matches the evidence available. If the business has a defined problem but little test evidence, ask for permission to investigate within a spending limit. If a test has produced credible results, ask for a specific next step and explain what must remain under review. Avoid a broad request to approve AI across the company. That wording leaves open which work may start, who can commit funds and when the board will see results. A narrower request gives management room to act while preserving a clear point for further approval. The following example is illustrative. Its wording is a model for a decision, not a claim about an actual company or project. | Memo element | Illustrative wording | | ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Decision | Approve a bounded test of an internal support workflow. | | Purpose | Find out whether staff can resolve routine requests with less manual work. | | Limit | Keep the test within the approved budget and named team. | | Condition | Review quality, data access and staff feedback before any wider use. | | Owner | Assign an accountable business executive to report the result. | If the board wants a different limit or a stronger review condition, record that change with the decision. The owner can then plan against an agreed mandate rather than infer one from the discussion. ## How should the memo make the business case? Describe the problem in terms the board can judge without knowing the tools. Name the work affected, who does it today and why management wants to change it. A useful case explains the cost of the current approach or the service problem it creates. It also says what evidence would show that the proposed work is worth continuing. Choose a measure that follows the work through to an outcome. For a support workflow, speed alone may hide poor answers or extra checking by staff. Pair any speed measure with a way to judge quality and the effort required to correct mistakes. Record the starting point before the test if management wants to make a fair comparison. Keep estimates separate from observed results. If staff have identified a possible saving but have not tested it, say so. Explain the main assumption behind the estimate and who will check it. The [readiness scorecard](/resources/ai-readiness-scorecard) can help structure the questions management asks before committing to a direction. ## Which risks deserve space on the page? Select risks that could change the board's decision, the scope of the work or the conditions for release. These may include access to sensitive information, unreliable output, a weak route for staff to correct errors, or a supplier dependency that is hard to replace. The right list depends on the proposed use, not on a generic ranking. For each material risk, state the response and the person responsible for it. A promise to manage risk gives directors little to assess. A stronger statement says what access will be restricted, who will review the result and what happens if the review fails. Put the full record in a supporting paper, where reviewers can see the basis for each judgement. The [US risk management guidance](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) offers a way to structure that wider review. For work involving personal data, the [UK data protection regulator's guidance](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/artificial-intelligence/guidance-on-ai-and-data-protection/) is a useful source for questions about data use. The memo should identify the relevant concern and point to the assessment rather than claim that a short review settles every legal question. ## How much spending should management request? Ask for the amount needed to reach the next decision, not an open commitment to an eventual rollout. Include the expected cost of staff time, supplier fees, review work and any changes needed to existing systems. Where the amount is uncertain, show the estimate as a range in the supporting paper and say what could move it. The board needs to know which costs are included in the request and which would require another approval. A test may appear inexpensive if it excludes the work needed to connect data, check results or train staff. Make those boundaries explicit even when another team will carry the cost. Set a limit that the accountable owner can monitor. Describe what happens if the work is likely to exceed it, including who may approve a change and when the matter returns to the board. For a choice between building and buying, the [cost comparison guide](/blog/build-vs-buy-ai-3-year-tco) offers a way to examine costs beyond the initial purchase. ## Who owns delivery and when does the board hear back? Name a business owner for the outcome and give that person a clear route to the teams doing the work. The owner should be able to explain progress, risks and spending in the same terms used in the memo. Technical, security and legal staff may each own parts of the review, but the board still needs a single point of accountability. Agree on a return point tied to a decision rather than a routine status report. For example, management might return when the test results are ready and ask whether to stop, revise the scope or fund a wider release. The report should include the evidence behind the recommendation and any material change in risk or cost. Make the stop conditions visible before work starts. These might include an inability to protect the data used in the test, results that do not meet the agreed quality bar, or a forecast that exceeds the spending limit. The [operating model guide](/blog/how-to-choose-an-ai-operating-model-for-a-mid-size-company) can help management assign work across teams without obscuring the board's named owner. ## What evidence should sit behind the memo? A short memo works best when directors can inspect the records behind its claims. Keep a record of the proposed use, the people affected, the data involved and the result of any tests. Link the memo to the relevant documents and identify who maintains them. If a record does not yet exist, say what management will produce before the next decision. Separate evidence from judgement in those papers. A test result can show what happened under the conditions tested. Management must still judge whether those conditions reflect the work the business intends to do. Note gaps in coverage and explain how the next review will address them. The [AI system register](/glossary/ai-register) can provide a place to track systems and their owners. The [OECD AI principles](https://oecd.ai/en/ai-principles) can also inform questions about transparency and accountability. Use those questions to test the proposal, then keep the memo focused on the choices directors must make. ## How should the memo handle uncertainty and dissent? Put a material disagreement in the memo rather than waiting for it to surface in the meeting. If the business owner wants a wider test and the security team recommends a narrower one, state the difference and the reason for management's proposal. Directors can then decide whether the proposed conditions are sufficient for the next step. Use plain labels for what is known, estimated and still to be checked. Avoid giving a forecast the visual weight of a measured result. If the decision rests on an assumption about staff adoption or supplier performance, name it and explain how the team will test it. The board can approve a bounded test while keeping that assumption open. Before sending the paper, ask someone outside the project team to read the decision and spending request without an oral briefing. If that reader cannot tell what approval would permit, revise the wording. Send the memo with its supporting papers and record any conditions the board adds to its approval.

rows.text: ## How should you compare build vs buy AI 3-year TCO? Start with a single workflow and write down the outcome it must produce. Specify who uses it, what data it handles and what happens when an answer needs review. Give both options the same expected workload and the same service expectations. A comparison becomes misleading when the build covers a narrow task but the purchase includes a wider service. Use the [build vs buy AI kit](/resources/build-vs-buy-ai-kit) to set out the decision and capture costs for each path. The worksheet gives the cost discussion a place alongside the other criteria. Keep the estimate separate from the decision itself: a low total does not settle whether a team can deliver or operate the workflow. Set the start and end of the estimate before collecting prices. Include work before launch and costs that continue after launch. If either option leaves a contract or an asset at the end, record the remaining obligation or value. Finance can then decide how to treat it consistently. Keep a note of the date and source of each assumption so the model can be updated when a quote or plan changes. ## Which costs belong on both sides? Put equivalent work in equivalent rows, even when different teams do it. A supplier may include monitoring in a fee while the build team plans to provide it themselves. Show both costs, then note what the supplier's service actually covers. This avoids treating a missing invoice as proof that no work exists. | Cost area | Build estimate | Buy estimate | | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Setup | Design, development, data preparation and testing | Selection, setup, configuration and acceptance testing | | Use | Hosting, model calls, storage and network use | Subscription, usage charges and any hosting outside the contract | | Operations | Support, review, fixes and model changes | Internal support, vendor management and changes to connected systems | | Risk and exit | Security work, records, export and replacement | Security review, data export, termination and replacement | Add a row when a material cost does not fit cleanly. Record the quantity, rate, timing and source behind each amount. If a cost is shared with another system, state the share assigned to this workflow and why. Do not allocate the whole shared bill to both options. Give credits or savings their own lines so reviewers can see whether they depend on work that has yet to happen. ## How do you price the work your team will do? Ask the people who will do the work to estimate time by role and phase. Include product decisions, engineering, security, legal review and support where they apply. Multiply each estimate by a consistent internal rate chosen with finance. Show the hours as well as the money, since scarce capacity can matter even when the budget is available. For a build, include time to connect data, handle failed requests and test changes. For a purchase, include selection, access setup, workflow changes and checks against the supplier's releases. Both paths may need staff to review output or resolve cases the system cannot complete. Estimate that effort from the expected case volume and review rate, rather than assuming it disappears after launch. Separate work that adds spending from work absorbed by the current team. The latter still has an opportunity cost: people doing this work cannot spend the same time elsewhere. Ask the team lead which planned work would move. That answer can expose a delivery constraint that a total expressed only in money would hide. ## How should usage and vendor charges enter the model? Translate expected activity into the units used by each supplier or platform. A business task may produce several model requests, and each request may vary in size. Retries, long documents and human review can change the cost of a completed task. Keep those drivers visible instead of using one unexplained average rate. Read the quote alongside the supplier's pricing terms. Check what is included, what is metered and whether the price changes with volume or service level. The [Amazon Bedrock pricing page](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/) is an example of a public source to consult when estimating model use. Use the terms for the actual services under consideration, rather than borrowing a rate from an unrelated product. Include any minimum commitment, support charge and cost of connected services. Ask the vendor how usage is measured and how the bill can be inspected. For the build path, obtain the same detail from the platform team. A small sample of real tasks can help estimate request sizes and retry rates, but label the result as a sample rather than a forecast. ## What does it cost to keep the workflow reliable? Set an acceptance threshold before comparing the options. The threshold should reflect the work: an error in a draft for internal review may need a different response from an error sent to a customer. Agree who checks the output and who can pause the workflow when results fall short. Budget for the tests and people needed to maintain that threshold. The site's [evals page](/glossary/evals) provides a place to start when planning checks for changes. Include test data upkeep, review of failed cases and time to investigate shifts in results. If the vendor supplies test results, ask whether they cover your data and intended use. Your team may still need its own acceptance checks. Support costs should reflect the service users expect. Name the team that receives reports, fixes permissions and communicates with the supplier. Include cover for absences and a route for urgent cases. The [risk management framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) offers a source for thinking about risk across the life of a system. Use it to inform the work plan, then price the specific tasks your team selects. ## How do data rights and exit affect the estimate? Ask what data enters each option, where it goes and who can access it. Check whether the supplier can use submitted data for purposes beyond the service. Record the answer and the contract provision that supports it. The site's [customer data FAQ](/faq/are-models-trained-on-our-customer-data) sets out the question to raise when reviewing a supplier. An exit estimate starts with the assets needed to continue the work. These may include source data, configurations, test cases, logs and records of decisions. For each asset, identify the owner, export method and format. Ask whether the replacement team can use the exported material without depending on the original provider. Price the work to extract, check and move those assets. Add any notice period, termination charge or overlap between old and new services when the contract calls for it. A build has an exit cost too: the team may need to document custom code or replace a component it no longer supports. Where the terms are unknown, leave a range and assign someone to obtain an answer before signing. ## How should finance compare costs that occur at different times? Lay out costs by the period in which the business expects to pay or perform the work. Keep launch spending separate from recurring charges and later replacement work. This view shows cash needs as well as the total. It also makes a delayed launch visible, because both spending and expected use may move. If finance uses discounted cash flow, apply the same method and rate to both options. Discounting expresses future cash flows in present terms using an agreed rate. Keep an undiscounted view beside it so the timing and actual budget requirements remain clear. Do not mix a discounted total for one path with an undiscounted total for the other. Treat past spending as context rather than a cost that the new decision can undo. Include future commitments only when they differ between the options or matter to the budget view. Record any assumed resale value or contract credit separately from certain costs. The [cloud cost optimization guidance](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/cost-optimization) is useful when setting up ongoing cost ownership and review, especially where usage changes after launch. ## What happens when adoption or quality changes? Build a base case from the best evidence available, then vary the inputs most likely to change the result. Lower adoption can leave a minimum supplier commitment underused. Higher demand can increase model calls, support work and review time. A quality shortfall can add manual work or require a change in model or provider. Change linked inputs together when the scenario calls for it. If more tasks need review, update both reviewer hours and the number of tasks completed without help. If usage rises, check whether the supplier's rate or service tier also changes. Keep the base assumptions intact so a reviewer can trace why each scenario differs. Find the point at which the preferred option changes. That point identifies the assumption worth testing before a commitment. For example, a quote with a firm usage allowance may matter more than a small change in the internal labor rate. Use the [cost-per-outcome FAQ](/faq/how-is-cost-per-outcome-measured) to frame what counts as a completed outcome. Avoid counting requests as successful work when users still need to correct or repeat it. ## Who should make and revisit the decision? Give one person responsibility for assembling the estimate and resolving gaps. The business owner should confirm the workflow and expected outcomes. Engineering should review delivery and support effort, while finance checks rates, timing and treatment of shared costs. Security and legal should review the data and contract assumptions that apply to the proposed service. Write down the chosen path, the alternatives considered and the assumptions that could reverse the choice. Keep the supplier quote, internal estimates and test evidence with that record. If an important input is still unknown, name its owner and the point at which the team must resolve it. A conditional decision is useful when the condition is explicit and someone can check it. Set a review date tied to a meaningful event, such as contract renewal or a change in workload. Compare actual use and support effort with the estimate, then adjust the forecast. If results diverge enough to change the decision, the owner can reopen it with current evidence. The [AI risk ownership FAQ](/faq/how-does-ai-risk-get-recorded-and-who-signs-it-off) offers a related starting point for assigning risk decisions.
