rows.text: An eval suite that only runs on a laptop protects nobody. The same regression a developer catches by eye on a good day slips through on a bad one. A model provider's silent update slips through every time. Putting [an eval suite](/glossary/evals) in CI turns a habit into a gate. The pull request cannot merge until the numbers clear, whoever is watching. ## How do you build an eval set from production traffic? Pull the first cases from what the agent has actually handled, not from what a spec said it should handle. Real traces carry the phrasing, the edge cases, and the odd multi-step requests. A person writing test data from imagination never thinks to include them. A support agent's eval set should read like a week of its own transcripts, because that is exactly what it is. Sample across a period long enough that one good or bad week does not decide the result. A month of traffic spans weekdays, weekends, and spikes the business already expects, which is a sturdier base than one convenient week. Mix the set on purpose. Include three kinds of case: routine ones that should always pass, a handful known to be hard, and a few with no single acceptable answer. Most agent tasks in production fall into that last kind. Store the set next to the code it tests, in a format a reviewer can read in a pull request. Change it through the same review a code change gets. Revisit the set on a fixed schedule rather than whenever someone remembers. Retire a case once the product has genuinely outgrown it. Add one the day a new failure reaches production. That keeps the set tracking how people actually use the agent. ## How do you score an agent when there is no golden answer? Most agent tasks do not reduce to one correct string, so do not force them into that shape. A support reply, a summary, or a multi-step tool sequence can be right in more than one way. A scorer built for exact match will reject good answers as often as it catches bad ones. Score in layers instead, cheapest and most reliable checks first. Start with deterministic checks on anything mechanical. Check whether the agent called the right tool, with a valid argument set, in a shape that downstream code can actually parse. These checks are cheap, and they never disagree with themselves. In most agentic systems, they catch a large share of regressions before a judge ever runs. OWASP's list of risks in large language model applications names excessive agency as one of the standard failure modes worth testing for. Excessive agency means an agent taking an action its task never asked for. Write a case for every tool the agent can call. Each case should check that the tool stays quiet when not needed, and that it fires correctly when needed. For the answer's content, add a reference-free judge. Look at the question and whatever the agent actually retrieved. Then check whether every claim in the answer traces back to a document it had in hand. This catches a fluent, confident answer that is not supported by anything the system looked at. A plain accuracy score misses that failure mode entirely. Where no rubric fits cleanly, fall back to a comparison against the last known-good version. Show a judge both outputs, blind to which one is new, and ask it to pick a winner. A judge finds picking a winner easier than defending an absolute score out of some invented scale. A win rate against a fixed baseline is also a steadier number to watch than a score with no anchor. NIST's AI RMF frames this as a selection problem under its Measure function. Which method fits depends on what is actually being measured. A team documents why it chose a metric, and which ones it rejected. That team ends up with a sturdier suite than one that picked whatever was easiest to compute. ## What happens when the judge itself is flaky? A judge model can score the same input differently on two runs, especially at a higher temperature. That alone will make a pipeline look unstable, even when the agent under test has not changed. Set the judge's own temperature as low as the provider allows. Treat any remaining run-to-run disagreement as a property of the judge to manage. Calibrate the judge on a fixed schedule against a small set of cases a human has already scored. The number that matters is agreement between the judge and the human reviewers. A judge that is consistent but consistently wrong is worse than one that is honestly uncertain. Consistent wrongness hides the problem instead of showing it. Let the judge decline a case it cannot confidently assess. A skipped case should fall out of the pass-rate calculation, rather than count as either a pass or a fail. A case the judge skips often is telling you the rubric does not cover that situation yet. When one specific case flips between pass and fail on identical re-runs, treat that case as broken, not the whole gate. Quarantine it. Keep it running so you can see it, stop it from blocking a merge, and put a name against fixing its rubric or its sampling. Only then should it rejoin the set that actually gates a build. ## What should the pipeline check, and what does a failing check do to the build? Not every check should carry the same weight. A wrong tool call and a slow response are both real problems, but only one of them should stop a release. The table below is the shape of a working gate. It shows what each row measures, how it gets a number, and what that number does to the build when it fails. | What to score | How to score it | What a failing score does to the build | | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Task success on labelled cases | Exact match or a deterministic rule against a known-good answer. | Blocks the merge immediately, with no override. | | Task success with no golden answer | A rubric-based judge scores the answer against stated criteria, not against a reference. | Blocks the merge once the pass rate drops below the floor set for that task. | | Faithfulness to retrieved context | A reference-free judge checks whether each claim traces back to a document the agent actually retrieved. | Blocks the merge; an unsupported claim counts as a defect, not a style note. | | Preference against the last good version | Pairwise comparison: the judge sees both outputs, blind to which is new, and picks a winner. | Blocks the merge if the new version loses on more cases than the agreed margin allows. | | Tool-call correctness | Deterministic check that the agent called the right tool with a valid, schema-checked argument set. | Blocks the merge; a malformed call fails loudly instead of degrading quietly. | | Judge-human agreement | Re-run the rubric against a human-labelled sample on a fixed schedule and compare agreement. | Does not block a single pull request; a drop pages the eval owner to fix the rubric. | | Cost per completed run | Sum of model and tool cost across the eval set, divided by cases completed. | Blocks the merge once the run exceeds the ceiling set in the pipeline config. | | Response time under load | Wall-clock time per case, measured in the same job as the scores. | Warns on the pull request; blocks only if it breaches the budget agreed with the product owner. | ## Where does the cost ceiling sit? Put a cost ceiling in the same job as the quality score. Do not put it on a separate dashboard someone checks once a week. Agent systems fail commercially long before they fail technically. Consider a tool call that retries a few times on a bad response: harmless in a demo, ruinous once real traffic hits it. Measure cost per completed run, across the whole eval set, the way you measure the pass rate. A change that makes the agent slower or more expensive without a real gain is a regression, even if every other score stays green. A [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint) puts this gate in place before a workflow takes its first real user. That is a cheaper time to find the problem than after the first invoice. ## What does the pipeline do when a check fails? A failing check blocks the merge by default. The pull request gets a summary next to the diff that caused it. That summary lists which cases failed, what the agent returned, and what the check expected. Nobody reconstructs the failure from a log. Not every failure deserves the same response. A wrong tool call or an unsupported claim should stop the release outright. A latency or cost warning close to its budget, or a drop in judge-human agreement, can page an owner instead, without stopping every other change in the queue. Keep that distinction explicit in the pipeline config, not in someone's memory of which checks are actually load-bearing. Only a named reviewer, not the author of the change, can override a hard block. That override has to write itself into the same log the eval results live in. An override that leaves no trace is indistinguishable from no gate at all. It gets used that way the next time someone is in a hurry.

rows.text: ## How does fractional CAIO pricing work at Meshin? Meshin uses a fixed structure for each offer rather than an hourly rate. The amount reaches you in writing before work starts. The [pricing page](/pricing) is the starting point for the offer structure, and the [charging FAQ](/faq/how-do-you-charge-for-the-work) covers how the work is charged. A fixed structure still needs a clear scope. The written proposal should say what work is covered, who takes part and what the buyer will receive. It should also explain any conditions that could change the agreed work. Without those details, a fixed fee can leave the buyer unsure what has actually been bought. Before accepting a proposal, ask the person doing the work to walk through it. Take a current decision or task and ask whether it falls inside the agreement. If the answer depends on access, input from your staff or a supplier decision, have that dependency recorded. This makes it easier to spot gaps before they become a dispute about scope. The amount is only one part of the commitment. Time from your own staff, access to systems and outside supplier charges can all affect the cost of getting work done. Ask for those commitments to be visible alongside the fee. ## Which type of work should the fee cover? Start with the result your team needs, then choose the shape of the engagement. A review of the current position has a different end point from getting a workflow ready for use. Ongoing leadership calls for another kind of agreement, with a way to set priorities as needs change. | Work needed | Question to settle before agreeing a fee | | ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- | | Assessment | What will be reviewed, and what will the team receive? | | Delivery work | Which workflow is in scope, and who can approve its use? | | Ongoing leadership | Which decisions and meetings need continuing attention? | | Handover | Who takes over each task, and what material will they receive? | The [readiness and risk assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment), [production sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint) and [fractional CAIO retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) describe different ways to arrange the work. Read the relevant offer before asking for a proposal. A buyer can also use the [readiness scorecard](/resources/ai-readiness-scorecard) to identify gaps worth discussing. The scorecard can frame the conversation, but it cannot settle the scope on its own. Name the business problem, the people affected and the decision you need to make. Those details give a proposed engagement a boundary that both sides can test. ## What should a written proposal include? A proposal should connect the fee to work that a buyer can recognise. Ask for a description of the outcome, the work products and the people who must take part. A useful proposal also names the person who can accept the work for the client. For delivery work, ask how the team will decide whether a workflow is ready for use. The answer might include a test set, a review by the people who use the result and a clear route for recording defects. Ask who prepares the test material and who decides whether an unresolved issue blocks use. For ongoing work, ask how priorities will be set and revisited. The agreement should distinguish time spent advising from decisions that remain with your company. It should also explain how the buyer raises a new request when existing work is already in progress. A work product can be a decision record, a plan or a piece of working software. The name alone is not enough to judge its value. Ask what it will contain, who will use it and whether your team can maintain it. Where the answer depends on access to an existing system, confirm who can grant that access. ## Which costs should I ask about separately? The proposal should say whether the fee includes outside services or whether your company pays them directly. Ask about model access, hosting, software subscriptions and any specialist work brought in for the engagement. The answer may differ by project, so record it rather than relying on an assumption. Where a supplier charges for use, ask which account will hold the service and who can see the bills. A spending limit can help, but someone must also decide what happens when the limit is reached. Agree whether work pauses, switches to a different service or needs a fresh approval. Cloud costs deserve the same care as the leadership fee. The [AWS cost guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/cost-optimization-pillar/welcome.html) gives buyers a framework for thinking about cloud spending. Use it to prepare questions about who monitors use and who has authority to change a service. Your team's time is another commitment to make visible. An internal engineer may need to grant access, review changes or own the system after handover. A legal or security colleague may need to review a supplier. Ask the proposed lead to identify these needs before your team commits to a schedule. ## Who makes decisions during the engagement? Price is hard to compare if proposals assign different amounts of decision work to the buyer. Ask which decisions the fractional lead can make and which need approval from your company. Name a person for each approval, including a substitute if that person is away. For example, the lead may recommend a supplier while the buyer keeps the authority to sign its contract. A delivery team may prepare a workflow while a business owner decides whether its output is fit for use. Record those boundaries in the proposal or in a work plan linked to it. Also agree how to handle a decision that cannot wait for the next planned meeting. Name the route for raising it, the person who responds and what the team should do while waiting. This matters when a supplier changes access or a test finds a serious defect. The [AI operating model page](/glossary/ai-operating-model) provides a starting point for discussing how responsibilities fit together. Use the proposal to apply those responsibilities to the people who will actually do the work. A title alone does not establish who can approve a purchase, accept risk or stop a release. ## How should we agree changes to the work? Set a process for changes before the first request arrives. A new workflow, an extra supplier review or a change in access can alter the work. Ask who can request a change and who must approve it for each side. The change record should describe the request, its effect on the current plan and any proposed change to the fee. It should also say what happens to work already agreed. The buyer can then choose to accept the change, defer it or keep the current scope. Do not rely on a meeting note that leaves the fee open. Ask for the revised terms in writing before the extra work begins. If the change needs a quick decision, agree how the written record will be confirmed and stored. It is useful to distinguish a defect in an agreed work product from a new request. If a report omits something the proposal promised, the parties should address that under the existing agreement. If the buyer wants a new analysis, discuss it as a scope change. The proposal should explain how questions about that boundary will be resolved. ## How do I compare proposals from different providers? Give each provider the same description of the problem and ask them to state their assumptions. Compare the work they propose, not just the amount at the bottom. A lower fee may cover less delivery work or leave more review and coordination with your staff. Look at the proposed access to the person doing the work. Ask who attends key meetings, who reviews work products and who stands in if that person is unavailable. The answer helps you judge whether the proposed arrangement fits the decisions your company needs to make. For work involving a live service, ask how the provider will discuss reliability and service expectations. The [Google Site Reliability Engineering book](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/) explains how service objectives can focus that discussion. Your agreement should say who chooses the measures and who acts when the service falls short. Check the proposed approach to company data as well. The [FTC guide to protecting personal information](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/protecting-personal-information-guide-business) gives businesses questions to consider about handling data. Ask each provider what access they need, where information will be stored and how access will be removed. These answers can expose work that a fee comparison alone misses. ## What should happen when the engagement ends? Agree the end terms while both sides are planning the work. Ask how notice works, what happens to work in progress and whether any charges remain after the end date. The [retainer exit FAQ](/faq/how-does-the-retainer-end) is a starting point for that conversation. Name the internal owner who will receive each active task. That person needs access to the work products, open decisions and supplier contacts, not just a final meeting. Ask for a list of unresolved issues with their next action and owner. Where software or data is involved, settle access and ownership in the written agreement. Ask which accounts belong to your company, who holds the code and how any temporary access will be removed. The [ownership FAQ](/faq/who-owns-the-code-and-the-data) addresses code and data, while the [handover playbook](/resources/handover-playbook) can help your team plan the transfer. A handover needs an acceptance check. Have the receiving owner find a document, open the relevant system and explain the next decision in their own words. If they cannot do that, record what is missing and agree who will supply it. The work should remain usable after the outside lead leaves.

rows.text: An outside AI lead sets up governance or ships a first system. Sooner or later the role has to sit with someone on the payroll. Four questions run through a handover: what moves, who takes the role, who signs what, and how the company knows it worked. ## Is there a standard way to hand over AI leadership? None turned up. In October 2026, searches of standards bodies, regulators and journals found no standard, law or study on this exact move. What exists sits next door. Interim and fractional executives have exit practices. Engineering teams have ways to transfer ownership of a service. A UK financial regulator has rules for handing over a senior role. The [NIST AI RMF](/glossary/nist-ai-rmf) and the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act) texts checked in October 2026 never mention a change of person. The evidence is thin. [One academic model of interim assignments](https://doi.org/10.1108/JOEPP-10-2019-0094) says the evidence base on interim effectiveness lacks empirical studies. A company linked to two of its authors funded its literature search. Most checklists come from firms that sell interim or fractional staff. Read what follows as practice that others found sensible, plus some points that have no outside source. None of it is proven. ## What has to move in a handover? Documents alone can fall short. [Esya](https://esya.studio/notes/ai-evals-runbook-handover), a UK studio that builds AI inside client companies, writes that a folder of documents can be complete while the handover is not. It says the receiving team also needs the route to deploy and controlled access to systems. It needs monitoring data, the [evals](/glossary/evals) and the runbook. It needs authority over incidents and practised knowledge. Esya sells related work, so read that as a peer's view. The table shows what each source asks for, and how much weight it can bear. Six rows come from sources about handovers, exits or onboarding. The three NIST rows are marked. The NIST text checked in October 2026 never mentions a change of person, so applying it to a handover is this page's reading. | What moves | What a source asks for | The source and its weight | | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Decisions and reasons. | Handover material should include judgement and opinion, not just facts and figures. | [UK Financial Conduct Authority handbook](https://handbook.fca.org.uk/handbook/sysc25/sysc25s9). Regulator guidance for UK financial firms, so an analogy only. | | Work in progress. | A status report on the goals set at the start: what got done, what remains and what new issues emerged. | [CompassPoint](https://www.compasspoint.org/sites/default/files/documents/Interim%20EDs%20-%20final.pdf). A practitioner's guide to interim directors of US nonprofits. | | The list of AI systems. | Mechanisms to inventory AI systems. | [NIST AI RMF](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/5-sec-core/), Govern 1.6. A voluntary framework that NIST says it is revising. Not about handovers: this row is the page's reading. | | Roles and authority. | Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication for mapping, measuring and managing AI risks are documented and clear to individuals and teams throughout the organisation. | NIST AI RMF, Govern 2.1. Voluntary. Not about handovers: this row is the page's reading. | | How to run and change the system. | The route to deploy, monitoring data, the evals, a runbook and authority over incidents. | Esya. A studio that sells related work. | | Access. | Revoke access in one coordinated step on or before the last day, and confirm it in writing. | [Fractionus](https://fractionus.com/blog/fractional-executive-offboarding). A marketplace that sells fractional executives, so one vendor's opinion. | | Monitoring and incident duty. | Monitoring plans that cover incident response, recovery and change management. | NIST AI RMF, Manage 4.1. Voluntary. Not about handovers: this row is the page's reading. | | Someone to ask. | The development team must be available to back up and advise the receiving team while it settles. | [Google's SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/evolving-sre-engagement-model/). The operator's own account of its engineering teams. | | A report on how it went. | An exit review that names the issues the client needs to address. | [Institute of Interim Management code](https://iim.org.uk/resources/code-of-conduct/). A professional body's code for UK interim managers. | Nine rows are a lot to move on one day. Google's book describes a progressive transfer of responsibilities and ownership, including parts of operations, the change management process and access rights. This page reads that as support for moving a handover in steps. My access list has six categories: the [AI register](/glossary/ai-register), the [LLM gateway](/glossary/llm-gateway), CI/CD, the cloud consoles, the vendor panels and the SSO admin. The client's internal owner or IT lead revokes each one. Revocation is confirmed in writing the same day. A revoke-all line sits on the last-day checklist. ## Who should take the role? The company side needs one named person with the authority to pause the system. The [pilot article](/blog/why-your-ai-pilot-never-reached-production) says the same. It adds that the person should have written at least one eval case and watched a rollback rehearsal. Someone who was not part of the build inherits a document, not an understanding. The usual successor is the tech lead or the head of data. A COO takes the role when AI sits deep in company processes. One person holds the role. This site's own pages point to two jobs inside the role. One is answering for risk, including the authority to stop a launch. The other is keeping the system working, including the eval case and the rollback rehearsal. One person holds both jobs. [NIST's playbook](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/playbook/govern/) suggests managing development apart from testing, so that someone can correct a system independently of its builders. That is about testing, not owners, but it shows why a company might split the jobs. A US federal memo from April 2025 makes a different choice. The [memo from the Office of Management and Budget](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/M-25-21-Accelerating-Federal-Use-of-AI-through-Innovation-Governance-and-Public-Trust.pdf) lets an agency head name an existing officer as chief AI officer. The chief information officer is one example, if that person has significant expertise in AI. The memo binds US federal agencies only, so for a private company it is an analogy. It also requires agencies to tell the Office of Management and Budget within thirty days when the officer changes or the post is vacant. Later revisions were not checked. Sometimes nobody inside can take the role yet. The academic paper cited earlier notes that recruiting a senior executive can take six months or more. That figure is not specific to AI roles. No competence framework for a chief AI officer or head of AI from a standards body or regulator turned up in the search. The test the new owner must pass has to be written locally. ## How do you know the handover worked? Test behaviour, not paperwork. [Google's SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/evolving-sre-engagement-model/) says a production readiness review is considered a prerequisite for a site reliability team to accept responsibility for the production side of a service. So the receiving side sets a bar before it takes ownership. That is a reading of the text. A specialist team can refuse a service that fails the review. A single internal owner may lack that power, so agree the check with the outside lead in advance. Esya's test is short: the receiving team has practised the response and can make the next change without waiting for the builders to return. Some checks already appear on this site. The pilot article says the new owner should have written at least one eval case and watched a rollback rehearsal. The [approach page](/approach) lists a related measure under engineering capability. It tests whether your engineers can already roll back a bad model without waiting on the outside lead. Three checks close my handover, and I judge each one. The new owner writes an eval case. The new owner runs a rollback rehearsal. The new owner handles one incident without me in the room. Write the full list of checks with the outside lead before the handover starts. For each check, name who judges it and what counts as a pass. [CE Interim](https://ceinterim.com/interim-manager-exit-strategy-and-handover-explained/), which supplies interim managers, lists three causes of failed handovers. The first is making changes without enough involvement of the internal team. The second is treating knowledge transfer as a final step. The third is relying too heavily on the interim as the central decision maker. It adds that a handover is a confirmation, not a critical moment, when the organisation already runs on its own before the interim leaves. Read it as a provider's marketing page. Esya also lists promises that are not enough on their own, such as "contact the builder", "documentation has been shared" and "support remains available". One more check comes later. [Fractionus](https://fractionus.com/blog/fractional-executive-offboarding) suggests asking the successor at the thirty-day mark what they wish they had known on day one. It is one vendor's suggestion. ## Who signs what after the handover date? Every decision that carries a signature needs a name on the handover date. Examples are risk acceptances, policy exceptions, vendor approvals, changes to eval thresholds, rollback calls and answers to customer security questionnaires. Write the old signer and the new signer next to each one, with the date the change takes effect. Customer paperwork that names the outside lead needs a new name, and someone has to tell the customer. None of the sources in the table above lists who may sign what, so this part is the page's own advice. Until the handover date, I sign risk acceptances and the customer security questionnaires that carry my name. From that date, the internal owner signs. The client tells its own customers, and I provide the letter template. The [FAQ on how AI risk is recorded and signed off](/faq/how-does-ai-risk-get-recorded-and-who-signs-it-off) explains how AI risk is recorded and how the Retainer signs each entry while it is running. Accountability stays with the company. The NIST AI RMF says executive leadership takes responsibility for decisions about AI risk. The EU AI Act puts the duties of a deployer on the body that uses an AI system under its authority. On that reading, an adviser's departure moves no deployer duty, because the duty never sat with the adviser. It is a reading of the text and not legal advice, so ask counsel before relying on it. ## Do the AI rules say who must take over? None of the AI rules checked names a successor. The Commission was asked whether an AI officer is necessary. For the AI literacy duty, its [guidance](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/ai-literacy-questions-answers) says no specific governance structure is mandated and no certificate is needed. That guidance is not binding law. [Article 26](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-26) covers [high-risk systems](/glossary/high-risk-ai-system). It asks deployers to give [human oversight](/glossary/human-oversight) to people who have the competence, training and authority for it, and the support they need. None of the articles checked asks for an AI officer. The duties in Article 26 start on 2 December 2027 for systems that are high-risk under Annex III and on 2 August 2028 for those under Annex I. [Regulation (EU) 2026/1744](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj) set those dates in July 2026. Most high-risk systems already on the market before those dates come under the duties only if their design changes significantly. Those intended for use by public authorities must comply by 2 August 2030 in any case. Whether a system counts as high-risk is a question for counsel. The NIST AI RMF is voluntary. Its Govern function asks for clear, documented roles and for training for the people in them. It also says executive leadership takes responsibility for risk decisions. NIST says it is revising the framework, so check the current text. The contents of [ISO/IEC 42001](/glossary/iso-iec-42001) list roles, responsibilities and authorities, and competence. Its full text is paid, so nothing from it is quoted here. None of the NIST or EU texts checked says what to do when the person changes, and the ISO text was not read in full. A handover is where role clauses like these get tested. That is a reading, not a rule. ## How long does a handover take? The sources that say how long a handover takes disagree, and none is about AI. Lengths run from a few weeks to a few quarters, depending on the setting. CompassPoint's guide for nonprofits describes a short overlap, then a few weeks of drop-in help. Fractionus suggests starting weeks before the last day. Google describes quarters for engineering teams taking over a service. My handover takes three months, in three phases. In months one and two, the new owner and I work side by side. In month three, the new owner leads and I review. At the end of month three come the final test and the signatures. The end date is fixed in the month-one plan, not the contract. A fixed date and a ready receiver can pull against each other. Write down both, and agree who may move the date. The [Institute of Interim Management](https://iim.org.uk/resources/code-of-conduct/) code of conduct asks members to agree formal termination terms with the client. These include a handover period and a period of notice. Sources agree that some reachable help after the last day is useful, and differ on how much. Google's book says the development team must stay available to advise the receiving team while it settles. CompassPoint's guide suggests drop-in days, then availability by phone as needed. Fractionus suggests optional advisory time after the exit, though its own page gives two different windows. Whatever is agreed, write down the length, the scope and who may call. For thirty days after the last day, I answer questions by email within one working day. I hold one review call on day 30. Anything beyond that is a separate agreement. ## What this does not solve The sources are neighbouring fields, vendor advice and voluntary frameworks. No outcome study of AI-leadership handovers turned up, so nothing here shows that a practice leads to better results later. No engagement has yet ended in a full handover by this method. It is not legal advice. The readings of the EU AI Act here are plain-language summaries and need counsel before anyone relies on them. It does not cover the case where nobody inside can take the role. That calls for a hiring or reassignment decision, and no handover method replaces it. The [Fractional CAIO Retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) is built to end with a named internal owner and written decisions. [The FAQ on how the Retainer ends](/faq/how-does-the-retainer-end) and the [approach page](/approach) say more. The [Handover Playbook](/resources/handover-playbook) turns these questions into six tables to fill in.

rows.text: A security review of an AI system usually starts with one question: what is actually running. If the honest answer takes a week of digging through chat logs and old tickets, the review stalls before it reaches architecture or data flows. An [AI system register](/glossary/ai-register), also called an AI register, is the fix. You can build one in a week with a spreadsheet and four interviews. ## Why does a security reviewer ask for it before anything else? A security or procurement reviewer asks one version of the same question first: what touches our data. Without a register, answering that means paging engineering, marketing, finance and support one by one, and hoping nobody forgot a tool. The [NIST AI RMF](/glossary/nist-ai-rmf) treats this as a named control, not a nice extra. Its Govern function includes a specific requirement: a mechanism to inventory AI systems, resourced according to how much risk the organisation is willing to carry. Everything a reviewer asks next, a data flow diagram, a vendor contract clause, an incident plan, gets scoped against rows already on this list. Skip the register, and the reviewer either stalls the process or signs off on a system nobody can fully describe. ## What should the register record? A register only earns its keep if a reviewer can answer their own questions from it, without a follow-up meeting. What follows is close to the version I hand a client. It has enough fields to answer a first review, and no field that exists only to look thorough. | What to record | Why a reviewer wants it | Who fills it in | | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Name the system and what it does. | A reviewer cannot scope a check against a system they cannot picture. | The system's product or engineering owner. | | Note whether the company built it in-house or bought it, and which vendor or model sits behind it. | A vendor's own controls become part of the risk the moment its API touches your data. | Whoever set up the account or the integration. | | List the data the system can see. | This sets the risk tier and decides which contract terms and legal duties actually apply. | The team that owns the data source, with legal signing off. | | Record who relies on the system's output. | Blast radius matters as much as data sensitivity when a reviewer decides how much scrutiny to apply. | The system owner, from usage or team headcount. | | Mark its deployment status: pilot, production or retired. | A pilot running on sample data is a different conversation from a live system holding real customer records. | The system owner, kept current as status changes. | | Name one internal owner. | A reviewer wants a person who can answer for the system, not a distribution list nobody reads. | Whoever runs the team that operates the system. | | Assign a risk tier. | This decides how much documentation, testing and sign-off the reviewer expects before anything ships. | Whoever runs the security or risk review, not the system's own owner. | | Log the date it was last checked. | A register that has not moved in a year gets treated the same as no register at all. | Whoever owns the register process, on a fixed schedule. | ## How do you build one in a week without buying a tool? None of this needs procurement. A spreadsheet, a shared document and four short conversations get a usable first version out the door. Most systems never started as a formal AI project, so the list has to go looking for them. - **Monday.** Create the spreadsheet with those three columns. Seed it with every system already in use: the model inside the product, the support tool, the analytics dashboard that quietly added an AI summary. - **Tuesday and Wednesday.** Interview engineering, marketing, finance and support directly, not by survey. Ask each team what they actually use day to day, since a spreadsheet plug-in with a model behind it belongs on the list too. - **Thursday.** Fill in the vendor, data and risk-tier columns from what you heard. Flag anything nobody could describe clearly for a follow-up conversation rather than a guess. - **Friday.** Assign an owner to every row, pick a reviewer for the risk tiers, and put a recheck date on the calendar before anyone calls the list finished. ## What a register does not do Building the register is the easy part of this, and several harder parts of AI governance sit outside it. It does not replace a lawyer's read of a vendor contract. The register tells legal which vendor to check and what data reaches them. It says nothing about whether that vendor's specific contract terms are safe to sign. Those terms change often enough that last year's answer will not do. The registration duty in the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act) is a separate, public step for certain high-risk systems. It means registering under Article 49, in the database the Commission set up under Article 71, before the system goes live. An internal register is how you find out fast which systems might owe that separate duty; it is not a substitute for filing it. It does not stay accurate on its own, either. A register nobody owns drifts out of date within a quarter, and a stale register reads to a reviewer as no register at all. If you would rather someone else run the discovery and the first risk pass, an [AI Readiness & Risk Assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment) does the same work in two weeks. It also hands you a finished register. The [starter kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit) lists the register with the other documents a security review asks for.

rows.text: This page starts from what is required, then asks what the evidence supports. The [AI operating model](/glossary/ai-operating-model) here is the one the glossary defines. What the law requires about structure is narrow, and the dates are still moving. What the evidence supports is long and weak. ## Does any law require an AI committee or a Chief AI Officer? For a private company, no source reviewed for this page requires any of four things. They are a committee, a centre of excellence, a hub-and-spoke model and a Chief AI Officer. The European Commission's [AI literacy Q&A](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/ai-literacy-questions-answers) asks whether an AI officer is necessary, as under the GDPR. It also asks whether an organisation must set up an [AI governance](/glossary/ai-governance) board. The answer is "No, no specific governance structure is mandated to comply with article 4 of the AI Act." That answer covers Article 4 only. The one binding rule found for this page that does require such structures is American. [OMB's memo on federal AI use](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/M-25-21-Accelerating-Federal-Use-of-AI-through-Innovation-Governance-and-Public-Trust.pdf), dated 3 April 2025, tells each federal agency to name a Chief AI Officer. Each agency covered by the CFO Act must also convene an AI governance board. Even there, agencies "are permitted to rely on existing governance bodies." The memo binds US federal agencies and nobody else. The standards read the same way. The [NIST AI RMF](/glossary/nist-ai-rmf) is voluntary. Its [published text](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/nist.ai.100-1.pdf) calls it "use-case agnostic, providing flexibility to organizations of all sizes." It prescribes no committee or team shape. [ISO/IEC 42001](/glossary/iso-iec-42001) applies to "any organization, regardless of size." Its contents list roles, responsibilities and authorities. The standard is sold, not published, so its clause text was not read for this page. ## What does the law require instead? In the Articles reviewed here, the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act) asks for duties, not structures. Which duties apply depends on what a company does with AI. It also depends on whether the company is the [provider or the deployer](/glossary/provider-vs-deployer) of each system. The table lists the duties of the Articles reviewed, by trigger, using the [consolidated text](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27/eng). The [Digital Omnibus](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng), Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, rewrote some of the wording and moved the dates in July 2026. The last column is a reading of what each duty needs in practice. It is not law text. | If your company… | The duty | Applies from | What it needs in practice | | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Provides or deploys any AI system | Article 4: take measures to support the AI literacy of staff and others who use AI for you. No specific level is required. | In application since 2 February 2025. National authorities enforce from 2 August 2026. | Someone to run the measures. The Commission says there is no need for a certificate and that organisations can keep an internal record of trainings. | | Runs a chatbot or generates synthetic content | Article 50: transparency duties for providers and deployers of chatbots, generative systems and deepfake content. Providers of generative systems must mark outputs in a machine-readable format. | 2 August 2026. Generative systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 have until 2 December 2026 to mark. | An owner for disclosure wording, and for marking if you provide the system. | | Provides a [high-risk AI system](/glossary/high-risk-ai-system) | Article 17: a documented quality management system with an accountability framework. It sets out the responsibilities of management and other staff. It must fit the size of the provider. | 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems. 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. | A written accountability framework. | | Deploys a high-risk AI system | Article 26: give [human oversight](/glossary/human-oversight) to people with "the necessary competence, training and authority". Also monitor the system, keep logs for six months or more, and report risks. | The same two dates. | Named overseers. The Act leaves the deployer "freedom to organise its own resources and activities". | | Changes a system someone else built | Article 25: a deployer becomes the provider if it puts its own name on a high-risk system or changes it substantially. The same happens if it changes a system's purpose so that it becomes high-risk. | No start date for Article 25 in the sources reviewed. | A change-control step that decides when the role flips. | Look at what these duties name. They name an accountability framework (Article 17) and people with the competence, training and authority for human oversight (Article 26). None names a committee, a centre of excellence or a Chief AI Officer. In practice, Article 4 needs someone to run the literacy measures and Article 50 needs an owner for disclosure wording; that is a reading, not law text. The Commission adds that, for deployers of high-risk systems, the duty to train staff for human oversight "remains in place" alongside Article 4. I deliver the Article 4 literacy measures for clients. Each role gets a short session built for that role and a one-page list of dos and don'ts. The client signs the internal record. ### How firm are the EU dates? The omnibus was signed on 8 July 2026 and is in force from 27 July. It moved the high-risk dates to 2 December 2027 (Annex III systems) and 2 August 2028 (Annex I systems). Its preamble gives the reason: "the delayed availability of standards, common specifications, and alternative guidance and the delayed establishment of national competent authorities." It also rewrote Article 4 and Article 17(2). Treat the new dates with care. The omnibus dates from July 2026, and several Commission guidelines are still pending, so the practical detail is still to come. I plan client work against the dates recorded on this page: Annex III from 2 December 2027 and Annex I from 2 August 2028. I do not put dates in contracts. Company size also changes the exposure to fines. Small and medium-sized companies pay the lower of the two fine limits. The omnibus extends that rule to small mid-cap companies, a new size class just above them, for all but the highest tier. ## Who decides, and who answers? This page treats five decisions as ones that need a named owner; that is the writer's reading, not a finding of any source. The table sets what law and standards say about each against what surveys report. The last table in the next section gives the sample behind each survey. | Decision | What law and standards say | What organisations report | | ------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Approve a system for production | NIST asks executive leadership to take responsibility for decisions about AI risk (GOVERN 2.3). It prescribes no committee or team shape. | The Bank of England and FCA surveyed 118 firms in 2024. 72% give accountability for AI use cases to executive leadership. Most name three or more accountable people or bodies. | | Own the evaluation | NIST MEASURE 1.3: internal experts who did not build the system, or independent assessors, join regular assessments. | No source reviewed says who should own an evaluation set after handover at a company of this size. | | Sign risk acceptance | NIST asks for residual risk to be documented. It names no signer, and neither do the AI Act articles reviewed. | The US federal memo names one: a waiver of its requirements for high-impact AI needs a written determination by the agency's Chief AI Officer. | | Keep the inventory | NIST GOVERN 1.6 asks for mechanisms to inventory AI systems. | ASIC found some licensees with no AI inventory and others with several dispersed model registers. | | Run it after launch | AI Act Article 26: deployers of high-risk systems monitor them, keep logs for six months or more and report risks. | A 2025 survey sponsored by Pacific AI found that 48% of organisations monitor production AI systems. It gives no clear figure for companies of this size. | In the table, NIST speaks to four of these decisions and AI Act Article 26 to the fifth. Of the texts reviewed, no NIST subcategory names an approver, NIST names no risk-acceptance signer and the AI Act articles reviewed name none. Practice varies too. The IAPP and Credo AI report says: "There is no clear best practice for how to build and organize an AI governance team." ASIC describes better and poorer practice for a committee where one exists. It describes better practice as a cross-functional, executive-level committee with clear responsibility and decision-making authority. Poorer practice was a committee that met infrequently and had a poorly defined mandate. Fewer than a third of the licensees it reviewed had a committee, or were setting one up. The [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) is where the owner and risk tier of each system live, and a short review checklist can be attached to each entry. The [register post](/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-system-register-in-a-week) shows how to keep one. ## Which structures do companies use, and how good is the evidence? Each structure in this table carries a grade in plain words. Required means a law or binding rule says it. Observed means a regulator or a survey reports what organisations do, with the sample named. Recommended means a research centre, a consultancy or a vendor says organisations should. Popular means many vendors repeat it and no data was found behind it. Described, not evaluated means an arrangement is described and no effect is reported. | Structure | What it means | What the evidence is | Grade | | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Centralised | One team or centre of excellence decides, and often builds. | [Gartner](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-06-30-gartner-survey-finds-forty-five-percent-of-organizations-with-high-artificial-intelligence-maturity-keep-artificial-intelligence-projects-operational-for-at-least-three-years) reports that almost 60% of high-maturity organisations centralise AI strategy, governance, data and infrastructure. | Observed. Gartner scores maturity from a seven-question survey; its press release does not list the questions. | | Hub-and-spoke or federated | A central group sets standards. Units run the work. | [McKinsey's guide](https://www.hkdca.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/data-leaders-operating-guide-scaling-ai-mckinsey.pdf) describes three archetypes: centralised, federated and decentralised, with a trade-off for each, and says the decentralised one needs very high domain maturity and sufficient scale. [IBM](https://www.ibm.com/thought-leadership/institute-business-value/en-us/report/chief-ai-officer) surveyed Chief AI Officers. Those leading hub-and-spoke or centralised models report twice as many pilots moved into production and 36% higher ROI. Every respondent was a Chief AI Officer, so each already had a central AI leader. IBM adds that organisations generally move from decentralised models to centralised or hub-and-spoke models as they scale. rows.text: An AI agent can send the same action again when a tool call times out, even if the first call already changed something. Give each intended action a stable operation key, and store that key with the request before the action leaves your system. A retry must reuse the key rather than create a fresh one. The receiving service also needs to honor the key, or the caller needs a safe way to check whether the action took effect. Keep a durable record of the request, its state, and any receipt so a restarted worker can continue without guessing. If the outcome remains uncertain, stop automatic retries and send the case for review. This design reduces duplicate effects, but it cannot promise that every outside service will prevent them. The safe choice depends on what the receiving service can guarantee and how long its protection lasts.

rows.text: ## Where can a retry cause a duplicate action? To decide how to prevent duplicate AI agent actions on retries, start where an effect becomes real. A customer message may be sent, a refund issued, or a record changed. The agent can lose the reply after the receiving service has already done the work. A timeout tells the caller that it lacks an answer, not that the action failed. The same problem can occur when a worker crashes after sending a request. A queue may deliver the task again, or a person may restart a failed workflow. Another agent run might reach the same business decision and submit it as fresh work. Each path needs a way to identify the intended action across attempts. Draw the boundary around the actual effect, not just the model response. A repeated draft may be harmless, while a repeated payment may cost money. List each tool that can change data or contact someone. For each tool, write down who receives the request and how to find proof of the result. ## What should an operation key identify? Assign a stable key when the system accepts an intended business action. Keep it through queue delivery, worker restarts, and calls to the receiving service. The key should identify the action the user approved, rather than the process that happens to execute it. Generating a new key inside each retry defeats the protection. A refund request, for example, needs a key tied to that particular approved refund. A later, separately approved refund needs a different key, even if the customer and amount match. Avoid deriving the key from the customer alone, since that could suppress a valid later action. A unique key created at approval can distinguish those cases. Store the approved request beside the key, including the target and the material details. When a retry arrives, compare those details with the stored request. Reject a mismatch and ask for a new approval if the action has changed. Scope keys to the right account or tenant so one customer's request cannot collide with another's. The [AWS guidance on safe retries](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/) discusses caller-provided request identifiers and the risk of treating similar requests as the same intent. Use that distinction when choosing where the key is created. ## What record should survive a worker restart? Keep a durable action record outside the agent's memory. It should hold the operation key, approved request, current state, attempt history, and any receipt from the receiving service. Record who approved the action when approval is part of the workflow. A worker that restarts can then read the record before deciding what to do. The state should distinguish work that has not been sent from work whose outcome is unknown. It should also distinguish a confirmed result from a request that was rejected. The table gives a practical starting point for those states. | State | What the worker should do | | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | | Ready | Claim the action before attempting the call. | | Sending | Keep other workers from sending the same action concurrently. | | Outcome unknown | Check the receiving service or use a protected retry. | | Confirmed | Return the stored result without sending again. | | Rejected | Record the reason and require a deliberate next step. | A lock or claim needs an expiry so abandoned work can be recovered. Expiry alone must not authorize another external call. The new worker still has to resolve any earlier call that may have reached the receiver. ## How do concurrent workers avoid sending twice? Make the claim on an action an atomic change in the durable store. That means the store accepts the claim as a single change, rather than letting workers separately read and update the same record. Enforce uniqueness for the operation key within its intended scope. Only the worker that wins the claim may start the send path. A worker can pause after claiming the action while another takes over an expired claim. The first worker might then resume and send a request anyway. Use a claim version to stop stale workers from updating local state, and check ownership immediately before sending. That check narrows the race but cannot by itself prevent a stale worker from reaching an outside service. For the external effect, send the same operation key to a receiver that supports duplicate protection. If the receiver lacks that protection, a local lock cannot close the gap between checking the claim and making the call. Hold uncertain cases for a check instead of treating claim expiry as proof of failure. ## What if the service accepts the request but the reply is lost? Treat a lost reply as an unknown outcome, not as a rejection. First look for a receipt or a status record using the operation key or a receiver-issued reference. Make sure the lookup covers the account and action being checked. A result that matches the approved request can move the local record to confirmed. A missing result is harder to interpret. The receiver may take time to make a new action visible, or its search may not cover every action. Only treat absence as proof of failure when the service's documented lookup makes that conclusion safe. Otherwise, retain the unknown state and ask an owner to resolve it. Some services accept an operation key and use it to recognize a repeated request. Check the service's rules for matching request details, returned errors, and the period when the key remains valid. [Stripe's documentation on idempotent requests](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests) describes these rules for its API. Do not assume another provider behaves the same way. Once a provider's protection has expired, reusing the old key may create a fresh effect. Reconcile the earlier attempt before any new send, including a send initiated by a person. ## Can a queue or local transaction solve the whole problem? A queue helps carry work between parts of a system, but delivery alone does not prove an action happened once. The worker must handle a message that arrives again after a crash or a lost acknowledgement. The [Amazon SQS guide on repeated delivery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues-at-least-once-delivery.html) gives an example of a queue where consumers need to account for that case. Use a local database transaction to save the approved action and a pending delivery record together. A transaction is a group of local changes that commit together or do not commit at all. A separate worker can then send the pending record and update its state. This avoids losing the intent when the process stops between saving the action and scheduling the work. The local transaction does not include a remote provider unless both systems share a suitable transaction mechanism. A crash after the provider acts can still leave the local record uncertain. The worker therefore needs the same key, receiver protection, or outcome check described for a direct call. ## What should happen when a retry stays uncertain? Give each action a clear owner and a path for review. Show that person the approved request, prior attempts, last known state, and any receipt or lookup result. The reviewer needs enough context to distinguish a missing effect from an effect that is merely hard to find. Restrict who can send again or approve a replacement action. A review screen should not offer a generic retry button without explaining the risk. If a receiver has no reliable lookup and no duplicate protection, a fresh send may cause another effect. The owner may need to contact the recipient or check a separate business record. Record the decision and its evidence alongside the action. For reversible changes, define a separate recovery action and approve it on its own terms. Reversing a record does not necessarily undo an email or recover a payment. The [agent rollback guide](/blog/how-to-roll-back-an-ai-agent-deployment) covers the wider deployment response, while this record tracks the fate of each affected action. ## How should teams test the retry path? Test with a controllable receiver that can accept a request and then drop the reply. Restart the worker before it records the result, and verify that the next attempt keeps the same key. Check the receiver's effect count as well as the local state. A successful response in the application does not prove that the recipient saw only the intended effect. Run competing workers against the same action and pause one after it claims the work. Let the claim expire, resume the paused worker, and inspect what each worker sends. Test a changed request with an existing key and confirm that the system rejects it. Also test a valid new action that resembles an earlier one. Exercise a receiver whose duplicate protection has expired and a lookup that returns no conclusive result. Both cases should reach review rather than a blind send. Add these cases to the checks described in [agent evals in CI](/blog/evals-in-ci-for-llm-agents), and keep the fake receiver's behavior distinct from the real provider's documented guarantees. ## What evidence should operators keep? Record the operation key and state changes in traces without placing sensitive request details in every log. Keep the approved payload and receipts in a protected store with access limited to people who need them. Link attempts to the same action so an operator can follow the path across worker restarts. The [tool-call tracing guide](/blog/how-to-trace-ai-agent-tool-calls-in-production) covers how to connect those events. Set retention for action records around the period when retries, disputes, and manual checks can occur. Compare that period with the receiver's key retention before enabling automatic retries. If the local record expires too early, a later delivery can look like new work. If the receiver forgets first, a retained local key alone cannot prevent a second external effect. Review unknown outcomes and repeated delivery as operational signals. A rising backlog can point to provider failures, missing receipts, or a lookup that cannot settle cases. Assign someone to inspect the backlog and resolve individual actions before clearing their records.

rows.text: ## What should you stop first? To decide how to roll back an AI agent deployment, stop its ability to take risky actions before changing versions. Pause admission of new tasks at the entry point. Then block tool calls that can send messages, change records or spend money. Keep a safe read path open only if the incident lead needs it and can verify its scope. Check that the pause covers scheduled jobs, retries and direct callers as well as the main interface. A banner in the user interface does not stop a worker that already has a task. Ask the service owner to confirm the actual block at the tool boundary. If the pause does not take effect, isolate the affected worker or revoke its access through the normal emergency process. Keep the containment change separate from the release switch. A shared credential may serve other workloads, so identify its users before revoking it. If access must be cut at once, record the wider effect and alert those owners. Do not wait for a complete diagnosis while the agent can still cause harm. ## How do you choose a safe release to restore? Find the last release that passed the checks needed for this workflow. The target must include the agent code, prompt versions, model selection, tool configuration and routing rules. Capture the identifiers from the release record rather than relying on a person’s memory. Link the target to the checks that supported its release. Check whether that bundle still works with current data and external services. An older worker may read a newer task state incorrectly, or its model endpoint may no longer be available. An earlier permission set may also restore access that the team has since removed for safety. Review those changes before granting the old agent any authority to act. Keep the current release record and relevant logs for investigation, subject to the team’s data handling rules. Save enough detail to compare the failing and chosen bundles. Avoid copying sensitive task content into an incident chat when a protected link will do. If no known release is safe, leave the agent paused and send urgent work to a manual queue. ## How do you switch the deployment back? Use the normal deployment control to select the chosen release while the action block remains in place. Restore its matching configuration from versioned records. Confirm the model endpoint, prompt, tool allowlist and routing rules that each worker actually receives. A release label alone is not proof that every setting changed. If the agent runs on Kubernetes, the [Deployment documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/) describes its revision and rollback controls. Those controls cover the deployment resource, so check separately for settings or services managed outside it. Apply any needed configuration change through its own controlled path. Record what was restored and what was deliberately left unchanged. Watch for old and new workers running at the same time during the switch. Keep the queue paused until the team knows which version can claim work. If the restored worker fails to start or cannot read current state, stop the rollout rather than repeatedly restarting it. The incident lead should choose a repair or manual path before more traffic enters. ## What happens to tasks already in flight? List tasks accepted before the pause and group them by their last confirmed state. The table gives the team a starting point for deciding what to inspect. Record the evidence for each task before moving it to a new state. | Last confirmed state | Check before proceeding | | ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- | | No tool call made | Check that the restored release can read the saved task safely. | | Tool call sent, result unknown | Check the destination before any retry. | | External action confirmed | Ask the destination owner whether a correction is needed. | Stop automatic retries while the team inspects those records. A retry can repeat a payment, send another message or overwrite a change. Where the tool supports a stable request key, check the result against that key before deciding whether to retry. If the result remains unknown, ask the system owner to verify it at the destination. Treat saved conversations and task state with care when moving between releases. The restored agent may have different expectations about fields, tool results or pending approvals. Test a copy of representative state in a restricted environment before resuming those tasks. Quarantine records that cannot be read safely, and give their owners a clear route for manual completion. ## How do you handle actions that already happened? Build a record of actions that may have reached systems outside the agent. Use task history, tool logs and the destination system to establish what actually happened. Include the affected account or record, the action, its status and the person responsible for the next decision. Protect that record as you would the underlying data. Do not assume every action has an automatic inverse. A sent message may need a correction, while a changed record may need its prior value restored. A purchase or payment may need a separate cancellation or refund. Ask the owner of the destination system to approve the remedy and confirm the result. Keep uncertain cases open until someone checks them at the destination. If a correction could overwrite a later human change, compare the current record with the expected state first. Tell affected users what they need to do when a remedy changes their work. Record the outcome beside the original task so a later retry does not repeat it. ## How do you check the restored agent safely? Start with a restricted test account and tools that cannot make live changes. Run representative tasks through the restored path, including a case that exposed the fault. Check the selected model, prompt, tool calls and final result. Inspect the worker logs as well as the output shown to the user. Next, test the action boundary with an approved destination that can tolerate a controlled change. Confirm that blocked actions stay blocked and that allowed actions reach only their intended target. Check that a failed call does not create an uncontrolled retry. Have the service owner inspect the destination record rather than relying only on the agent’s report. Use the team’s existing [evals in continuous integration](/blog/evals-in-ci-for-llm-agents) to select repeatable checks, and add the incident case when its data can be handled safely. Compare results with the release criteria agreed before the test. A fluent answer does not show whether a tool call was safe. If any required check fails, keep the action block in place and repair the release. ## When can traffic return? The incident lead should ask the service and risk owners to review the test results and open issues. Agree who can approve the return, which users or tasks enter first, and what signs require another pause. Record that decision where the on-call team can find it. The [agentic architecture articles](/blog/category/agentic-architecture) provide context for the wider system around that decision. Release a small, controlled share of work only after the tool boundary and queue are ready. Watch task outcomes, tool calls, retries and reports from the destination systems. Compare the restored path with its expected behaviour, including whether human approvals are being reached. Keep the team available to stop work again if the fault returns. Expand access only when the agreed checks remain satisfactory. Do not clear a quarantine queue merely because new tasks are working. Each held task still needs a decision about its state and any external effect. If the team cannot observe a critical action, keep that action blocked until it can be checked. ## How do you prepare for the next rollback? Write a runbook with the actual controls, owners and links for the deployed system. It should say how to pause each entry point, block each tool and locate a release bundle. Include the manual route for urgent work and the authority needed to reopen traffic. Store the runbook where the on-call team can reach it during an outage. Practice with a test agent and a queue that cannot affect live users. Change a prompt or routing setting, then restore the recorded bundle and verify what each worker receives. Include a task with an uncertain tool result so the team must check the destination before retrying. Note any step that depends on a single person or an undocumented credential. The [safe deployment practices described by Amazon](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/automating-safe-hands-off-deployments/) and the [release checks in Google’s canarying guidance](https://sre.google/workbook/canarying-releases/) can inform that exercise. Fit the checks to the agent’s actual tools and failure modes. Update the runbook after the exercise, and assign an owner to test any change that affects the recovery path.

The result should let an engineer reconstruct the path without giving every reader access to customer data.
