rows.text: ## Where should the trace start? Trace AI agent tool calls in production by linking every tool attempt to the request that caused it. Begin at the service that accepts the user request or scheduled job. Create a request span there, and carry its context into the agent runtime. Give each tool attempt its own span beneath the relevant agent step. A span needs a clear start and end. For a tool call, start before the runtime sends the request and finish after it receives the outcome. Record the tool name, the attempt outcome and a safe identifier for the operation. Include the error class when the call fails, without copying the full error message by default. A trace should show calls the runtime refused as well as calls it sent. A policy denial can otherwise look like an agent that stopped without explanation. Record the decision and its reason code at the boundary where the denial happens. Link the decision to the intended operation without storing the rejected payload. The [OpenTelemetry trace documentation](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/traces/) describes how spans form a trace. For the wider service design, see the site's [agent architecture article](/blog/multi-agent-reference-architecture-in-production). ## Which fields make a tool call useful to investigate? Choose fields that let an engineer follow the path and identify the result. The table is a starting point for a tool span, not a demand to capture every field from the tool payload. | Field | Investigation use | | --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | | Tool name and operation | Shows which action the agent tried to run. | | Outcome and error class | Separates success, failure, denial and timeout. | | Attempt and operation identifiers | Connects retries to the same intended action. | | Trace and service identifiers | Helps find related spans and service logs. | | Policy decision and reason code | Shows why a call was allowed or stopped. | Add the version of the tool interface or agent release when it helps compare behavior after a change. Use a stable name for each operation so a dashboard does not split the same action across several labels. Keep free text out of labels used for grouping, since user input can create too many distinct values. The operation identifier should be distinct from the trace identifier. A retry may belong to the same operation while producing a separate attempt span. Treat identifiers as potentially sensitive if they can be joined to a person or account. Apply the same access rules to related logs. ## How does context cross service and queue boundaries? Pass trace context from the agent runtime to the service that executes the tool. Use the tracing library's propagation support at both ends, and check that any gateway preserves the context. The [OpenTelemetry context propagation guide](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/context-propagation/) covers propagation across process boundaries. Queues need an explicit design because the worker may run after the request handler finishes. Put trace context in message metadata where the queue and its access rules allow it. At the worker, extract that context before recording the execution. Use a span link when a direct parent relationship would misrepresent the work, such as a batch that combines messages from different requests. Record a safe job identifier on both sides of the queue. That identifier gives the team another way to investigate if context is missing. Do not silently attach unrelated work to a guessed parent. Mark the context gap and keep the worker's own trace so the execution remains visible. External tools may not accept or return trace context. In that case, trace the outbound call locally and record a safe provider request identifier if one is available. Confirm that sharing any correlation field with the provider fits the data agreement. ## How should retries and side effects appear? Give every attempt its own span, even when the runtime retries the same tool operation. Record the reason for the retry and link each attempt to the same operation identifier. A single span for the whole sequence can hide a timeout followed by a successful response. For calls that change data or send messages, track whether the effect is known to have happened. A timeout can leave the outcome uncertain: the remote service may have acted before the response was lost. The trace should show that uncertainty rather than label the action as a clean failure. Agree on an idempotency method with the tool owner before enabling automatic retries for a write. An idempotency key lets a receiving service recognize repeated requests for the same intended action. Record a safe reference to that key, not a secret or a customer payload. Check the tool's actual behavior before relying on the key to prevent duplicate effects. When a human approves a proposed action, record the approval decision and link it to the operation. If execution happens later, preserve the link through the queue or job record. The trace should distinguish approval from completion of the action. ## What should stay out of a production trace? Start with metadata and add content only for a documented investigation need. Raw prompts, retrieved passages, tool arguments and responses can contain customer data or secrets. A trace store may have a wider audience than the system that holds the original content. Classify each proposed field before adding it to instrumentation. Decide who needs access, how long the field must remain available and whether it can be removed at collection. The site's [data classification glossary](/glossary/data-classification) is a starting point for that review. The [OpenTelemetry sensitive data guidance](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/security/handling-sensitive-data/) describes ways to reduce sensitive data in telemetry. Filtering at the source reduces the chance that unwanted content reaches a collector or vendor. Review error paths too, because exception messages can contain request bodies or credentials. Test the filters with representative synthetic data, then inspect the trace store and linked logs. A hash or masked value still needs review if it can be linked back to a person. Restrict access to traces by role and record who can change collection settings. Set a deletion path that covers copies sent to external systems as well as the primary store. ## How can a team find missing traces? Make trace coverage a visible part of the service checks. Send a known test request through the agent and confirm that the expected tool attempt appears under the request. Run the same check through the deployed gateway and worker path, not just a local test. Compare counts of tool attempts from the runtime with counts reaching the trace backend. A gap can point to dropped context, exporter trouble or a collection rule. Account for deliberate sampling before treating the difference as a fault. Keep the underlying counts free of customer content. Sampling can reduce storage, but it means a particular request may have no complete trace. Decide which failures or high-risk actions need stronger capture, and verify that the chosen setup can keep them. Do not promise a complete investigation record from a sampled trace stream. When the trace backend is unavailable, the tool boundary still needs a defined response. Choose whether the action can proceed, must wait or must be denied. Base that choice on the effect of the action and the separate evidence available. Alert the service owner when the chosen path is used. ## Which records need to survive beyond a trace? Keep a separate audit record when an action needs durable evidence of a decision or change. A trace can point to that record, while the record keeps its own access and retention rules. This matters when traces are sampled, deleted on a shorter schedule or stored with a third party. For a consequential tool action, the record can identify the actor or service, the intended operation, the decision and the known result. Include a safe link back to the trace when one exists. Record corrections as later events so an uncertain result can be resolved without erasing the earlier state. Assign an owner for the tool and another contact for the trace pipeline if those duties sit with different teams. Agree who investigates a missing action record and who can approve changes to captured fields. The [system register guide](/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-system-register-in-a-week) can help place those responsibilities alongside the system record. Review access to the audit record separately from access to traces. An engineer may need timing and error details without needing the full business record. A reviewer may need the decision history without access to runtime diagnostics. ## How do you test the tracing setup before release? Build a test path that calls a harmless tool with synthetic inputs. Check the request span, tool span, outcome and service link in the trace backend. Then force a timeout and a retry, and confirm that each attempt has a distinct span tied to the same operation. Test a denied call and a delayed queue job as well. Inspect the result when propagation metadata is removed, and confirm that the gap is visible without inventing a parent. For a write-capable tool, test an uncertain response and verify how the service records the final state. Add checks for secret leakage in error messages and tool fields. Inspect both trace data and the logs reached through its identifiers. Repeat the checks after changes to the agent runtime, gateway or tool client, since any of those can break the chain. The [agent evaluation starter](/resources/agent-evals-ci-starter) provides a place to connect these checks to release work. Keep a short runbook with the trace query, the service owner and the fallback record to inspect. Use it during a practice incident before relying on it for a live failure.

rows.text: There is no standard multi-agent reference architecture in the sources reviewed here. What exists is vendor guidance from Microsoft, Google Cloud, AWS and Anthropic. In my reading, it repeats four ideas: a coordinating agent routes work, tools sit behind one controlled boundary, state lives outside the model, and every call is logged against a named identity. On whether several agents beat one, the disagreement is between Anthropic and Cognition, not among the clouds. Anthropic reports gains from its own multi-agent research system on breadth-first queries. Cognition argued in 2025 against agents working together, and in April 2026 said its observations still hold for parallel writers. A Google Research study found results from large gains to large losses, depending on the task. Production work needs limits on every run, state that survives a crash, and a trace of every call. It needs approval for high-impact actions, versioned changes with a way back, and one accountable person. The sources back these unevenly, and the table grades the points that matter most.

rows.text: Microsoft, Google Cloud and AWS each publish guidance on multi-agent systems. The guidance is useful, and it agrees on more than you might expect. It is also vendor guidance with little measured evidence behind it. In my reading it says least about limits, rollback and ownership. This page grades the main claims and says plainly where the research found nothing. A multi-agent system, in these sources, puts several agents on one task. Each agent is a model with its own instructions and tools. One agent usually coordinates the rest. The sources call it an orchestrator, a supervisor, a coordinator, a manager agent or a lead agent. This page says orchestrator. The [agentic workflow](/glossary/agentic-workflow) entry in the glossary covers the wider idea. Outside claims name their source, and a date where the page has one. I read each page on 2 October 2026, except the Gartner release. Gartner blocks scripted reads, so I checked its sentences on a reproduction. Several of the pages change often. Where I write that I found no source, I mean none among the sources I read. A miss does not prove nobody says it elsewhere. ## How far can each claim be trusted? Treat most of it as advice. Almost none of it was measured in a production workload. The table grades the points that matter most, and the sections after it give the detail. | Point | What the sources show | How far to trust it | | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | One agent or several | Anthropic (13 June 2025) reports gains from its multi-agent research system. Cognition (12 June 2025) argued against agents working together. On 22 April 2026 it said its observations still hold for parallel writers. | Each is one vendor's own work. I found no source that compares both in a production workload. | | Test failure rates | A NeurIPS 2025 paper (revised 26 October 2025) found failure rates from 41% to 86.7% across seven open-source frameworks. | Peer reviewed. It tested open-source frameworks, not production systems with an eval gate. | | Cancelled projects | Gartner (25 June 2025) forecasts that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027. | A forecast. The release leans on a poll of 3,412 webinar attendees. | | Runaway loops | Anthropic says early versions spawned 50 subagents for simple queries. A preprint (2 July 2026) found loop-prone code in 47 projects. | Not found: a dated, checkable post-mortem from production. The only accounts found repeat one set of figures with no primary record. | | Human approval | Anthropic (25 May 2026) says users approved roughly 93% of permission prompts. Microsoft (4 June 2026) calls bypass of the human step the most consistently exploited failure mode. | Each is the vendor's own finding. Anthropic's post gives no method for its figure. | | Evals in CI | Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework (3 December 2025) and Anthropic's evals post (9 January 2026) say to run evaluations in CI/CD pipelines. | Two primary sources among the pages searched. A practice, not a standard. | | Rollback speed | Microsoft says "immediate". Temporal says "instant". | Not found: a target time in any source reviewed. | ## Do the big vendors agree on a shape? My reading is mostly yes, on four ideas. A coordinating agent routes work to others. Tool access goes through one controlled boundary. State lives outside the model. Every call is logged against a named identity. The guides do not all say all four, but each idea recurs. Microsoft's [reference architecture](https://microsoft.github.io/multi-agent-reference-architecture/docs/reference-architecture/Reference-Architecture.html), last updated on 18 August 2025, has an orchestrator. It consults a classifier to route a request and a registry to find agents. It connects tools through a [Model Context Protocol](/glossary/mcp) server and keeps state in persistent storage. The [multi-agent guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/multiagent-ai-system) from Google Cloud, last reviewed on 16 September 2025, also centres on a coordinator agent. Microsoft, Google Cloud and Anthropic each advise starting small. Microsoft (12 February 2026) says to use the lowest level of complexity that reliably meets your requirements. Google Cloud (reviewed 28 May 2026) recommends starting with a single agent if you are early in agent development. Anthropic (19 December 2024, updated 10 August 2026) advises finding the simplest solution possible and adding complexity only when needed. AWS (10 June 2026) warns of coordination overhead, handoff complexity and distributed failure modes. An undated AWS Marketplace learning module, written in the first person, also recommends the simplest pattern that fits your workflow. These are companies that sell the platforms. The Microsoft and Google Cloud pages quoted above report no measured data. Their agreement tells you what the vendors advise. ## Should the default be one agent or several? Start with one. Microsoft, Google Cloud and Anthropic each advise starting small, and the sources still disagree about what comes next. Two of the sources landed a day apart, and my reading is that they disagree on where the line sits. Cognition, which makes the Devin coding agent, published ["Don't Build Multi-Agents"](https://cognition.com/blog/dont-build-multi-agents) on 12 June 2025. Anthropic described its [multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system) on 13 June 2025. Cognition wrote that "in 2025, running multiple agents in collaboration only results in fragile systems." One of its principles was to share context. Anthropic says its research system "uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern". A lead agent coordinates specialised subagents that run in parallel. Anthropic's own evaluations show that such systems "excel especially for breadth-first queries". I read that as a read-heavy task, graded by the vendor itself. Cognition came back to the question on 22 April 2026. Its original observations, it wrote, "still hold today for parallel-writer swarms". It also described a narrower pattern that works, in which several agents add intelligence to a task while "writes stay single-threaded". The same post gives two rules that pull apart. One says to "share as much context as possible between the agents". For review agents, it says the technique works best when the coding and review agents "do not share any context beforehand". My default puts the line between reading and writing. Many independent reads suit several agents. Writes that must agree suit one. I found no source that tested this in a production workload. The closest measurement found is a Google Research study of agent designs on benchmark tasks. Its [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08296), posted on 9 December 2025 and revised on 8 April 2026, compared several designs with a single agent. Results ran from a gain of 80.8% to a loss of 70.0%, depending on the task. The Google Research blog post about the paper, of 28 January 2026, reports that independent agents amplified errors 17.2 times, and centralised ones 4.4 times. The blog counts fewer test configurations than the paper's latest abstract, so the paper changed after the blog. I cannot say the multipliers hold for the paper. Anthropic's own post says multi-agent systems "work mainly because they help spend enough tokens to solve the problem". One reading is that more tokens help, however they are spent. I found no source that separates the gain from structure from the gain from extra tokens. ## What do the failure studies show? Multi-agent systems fail often in tests, and the studies below do not show how often they fail in production. One is MAST, from Cemri and colleagues, accepted to the NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks track. It read the traces of seven open-source multi-agent frameworks and found [failure rates from 41% to 86.7%](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.13657). Repeated steps and agents that miss a finished task were among the common failures. The paper is peer reviewed. It tested open-source frameworks, not production systems with an eval gate in front of them. A runaway loop is a different case, because it costs money. The research found no dated, checkable post-mortem of one in production. The only accounts I found were blog posts that repeat one set of figures with no primary record. What I found is weaker. Anthropic says early versions of its research system made errors such as spawning 50 subagents for simple queries. A [preprint of 2 July 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01641), "When Agents Do Not Stop", scanned public agent repositories for code that can start an infinite loop. It counts code patterns and does not show a loop that ran in production. My own case is the one first-hand example here: a runaway loop in client work, with no client named. An automatic stop ended it: a step limit and a cost ceiling. The account is anonymised. Hijacking is another documented failure. NIST's CAISI tested agent hijacking on a public benchmark. The strongest new attack succeeded 81% of the time, against 11% for the strongest baseline attack. [NIST published the result](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2025/01/technical-blog-strengthening-ai-agent-hijacking-evaluations) on 17 January 2025 and updated it on 19 December 2025. That is a benchmark, so it shows what is possible. It gives no rate for real systems. NIST's wording is that many agents that read untrusted text are open to [prompt injection](/glossary/prompt-injection). ## Where do limits and cost controls belong? On every run, set by a person, with a defined result when the limit is reached. The defaults in popular frameworks differ, and they count different things. The table shows five frameworks as read on 2 October 2026. The OpenAI default comes from its source code on GitHub, and the other rows from documentation pages. | Framework | Default loop limit | What it counts | | ---------------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | | OpenAI Agents SDK | 10 | Turns of the agent loop in one run. Setting none removes the limit. | | LangGraph | 1,000 | Steps, since version 1.0.6. | | Microsoft Agent Framework | 100 | Iterations of a workflow run toward convergence. | | Google Agent Development Kit | None stated | A loop agent ends on a stop signal or on a maximum you set. | | Claude Agent SDK | No limit unless set | The docs advise setting a budget for production agents. | A turn, a step and an iteration are different units, so in my reading the three numbers cannot be compared. Step limits and cost limits are also separate controls. I give every run a step limit. A run that reaches it stops, an alert goes out, and a person decides whether it resumes. I print no numbers. The Claude Agent SDK documentation says the loop runs until Claude finishes if you set no limits. It calls a budget a good default for production agents. The [FAQ on cost per outcome](/faq/how-is-cost-per-outcome-measured) gives this site's definition of the measure, and I would set a ceiling from your own traces. ## Does an agent need durable state and traces? Yes, the sources say both. State has to survive a crash, and every call needs a trace. Anthropic's [managed agents post](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/managed-agents) of 8 April 2026 keeps the session log outside the process that runs the agent. Nothing in that process has to survive a crash. Temporal, which sells durable execution, says its service hands the work to another process after a crash and rebuilds the state. LangGraph's documentation says in-memory checkpoints are lost when the process restarts, and it recommends a durable checkpointer. The principle is well supported. I found no source that says every production agent needs a separate engine, and none that measures the benefit. Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework (3 December 2025) says to attribute every action to a specific agent instance and conversation ID. The OpenTelemetry conventions for agent spans were still marked as in development in the repository file read on 2 October 2026. Whether the core traces signal is stable is unconfirmed, so this page makes no claim about it. OpenAI's Agents SDK turns tracing on by default, warns that traces may capture sensitive data, and does not offer tracing under zero data retention. A full trace is kept for 30 days, then only metrics are kept. Personal data is masked before it enters the trace. Anthropic (9 January 2026, updated 18 March 2026) says an eval suite makes problems visible before they reach users, and that it needs clear ownership. Running [evals](/glossary/evals) in the pipeline that ships changes is a narrower claim. Two primary sources say it: Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework and Anthropic's evals post, which calls automated evals especially useful pre-launch and in CI/CD. The Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework says to integrate evaluations into CI/CD pipelines before production. The [post on evals in CI](/blog/evals-in-ci-for-llm-agents) is about running them without a golden answer. In my work, a failing eval blocks the merge. I set the threshold on the first run against historical data, and it only rises, never falls. The owner can override a block, in writing in the pull request. ## Who approves what, and who owns the system? A person should approve high-impact actions, and one named person should own the system. The sources agree on the first and say less about the second. The Model Context Protocol specification (revision 28 July 2026) says there should always be a [human in the loop](/glossary/human-in-the-loop) who can deny tool invocations. The word is "should", and the specification says the protocol cannot enforce its own security principles. AWS sorts actions into three tiers, autonomous, notify and approve, by impact and reversibility, so that not every action waits for a person. Approval is also a control that can fail. Anthropic reports that its telemetry showed users approved roughly 93% of permission prompts (25 May 2026). It adds that the more approvals a user sees, the less attention each one gets. Microsoft's [AI Red Team](/glossary/red-teaming) calls bypass of the human step the most consistently exploited failure mode (4 June 2026). Both are the vendors' own findings. Anthropic's post gives no method for its figure. This page cannot say how many prompts is too many. In my work, two things always need a person: money, and anything that goes outside the company. Everything else runs within limits. Access follows the same logic. Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework (page updated 26 June 2026) says agent actions must be attributable and enforceable to a unique identity. The MCP authorization specification says authorization is optional for implementations. I read that as follows: a claim of least privilege through MCP describes how someone configured it, and the protocol does not guarantee it. On ownership, Microsoft's framework says to give agent governance to the leaders who already own cloud governance, security and compliance. It also says to designate a human role accountable for approving deployments and monitoring compliance. Microsoft's reference architecture site describes a cross-functional governance committee. In my reading these fit together if the committee advises and one person decides. This site's [approach page](/approach) asks for one named person who can refuse a launch and is accountable for AI risk. In my work, one named owner holds the budget, the access rights and the stop button. That owner cannot change the risk policy or switch off the eval gate alone. Both need a second person. The [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act) names people with competence and authority too. Its [human oversight](/glossary/human-oversight) duties apply to [high-risk systems](/glossary/high-risk-ai-system) only. The Commission's AI Act service desk still shows the 2024 text of those articles. ## Can you roll back a multi-agent change? Microsoft's guidance says yes, if you version everything that shapes behaviour. I found no target time in the sources I read, so they cannot say how fast. My target is that the last deploy rolls back in minutes with one command. I publish no measured case until one happens and is written up. Microsoft's security page for its reference architecture (updated 12 May 2025) says to version every agent's logic, prompt configuration and communication contract. It also says to enable immediate rollback to a previous version when anomalies are detected. Temporal's "Why Temporal?" page promises instant rollback, with no measurement behind the word. I pin models by exact ID. A model changes only through a commit in version control, and a rollback reverts that commit. Pinning a model does not always pin behaviour. Anthropic's documentation says infrastructure updates occasionally produce minor differences in observable behaviour even when the model ID and weights have not changed. I read that as follows: rolling back the model ID does not always roll back behaviour. Evals run after a rollback are how you would see the difference. Providers also retire models on published schedules, so a pinned model has an end date. Anthropic and OpenAI each publish a deprecations page, and someone has to read it. ## Which claims did the research not find a source for? The research looked for each of these and did not find it. - A dated, checkable post-mortem of a production agent loop that ran away and cost real money. - Any multi-agent reference architecture from a standards body. NIST announced an AI agent standards initiative on 17 February 2026. Its page, updated on 14 August 2026, describes convenings and gap analyses, and the research found no finished NIST guidance for agents. The ISO, IEC and IEEE catalogues were not browsed, so the honest wording is "not found". - Measured results that compare one agent with several inside one company's production workload. - A target time for rollback in any source reviewed. - Support for the "four planes" model of control, execution, state and capability beyond one undated AWS Marketplace learning module, written in the first person. One figure rests on a weak source. A LangChain blog of 16 June 2025 says to start small with evals and that even about twenty examples is enough. LangChain sells agent tooling and the post is commentary, so this page does not adopt the figure. Retrieval and memory design were outside this research. The [retrieval-augmented generation](/glossary/retrieval-augmented-generation) entry covers the basics. ## Does this site commit to any of it? Yes, to five controls. The [approach page](/approach) names evals in CI, tracing, cost per outcome, a rollback path and a named owner. The [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint) delivers all five on one workflow. In my reading, the sources above back them unevenly. Tracing recurs across the guides, and a named owner is clearest in Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework. Rollback appears as a practice in three of the 14 pages I searched. Evals in CI appears in the two primary sources named above. The outside sources cover spend limits and spend per reasoning cycle or per agent, which is a different measure from cost per outcome. I found no target time for rollback in the sources I read. The FAQ on [what counts as in production](/faq/what-counts-as-in-production-for-the-90-day-sprint) gives the bar this site uses.

rows.text: ## Who should own AI risk in a vendor review? The named AI risk owner coordinates vendor review, records unresolved risks, and routes each decision to the person with authority to approve it. Choose someone who can follow the purchase from the first request through the final decision. A job title alone does not give that person access to evidence or the authority to resolve a dispute. Start with the intended use. A writing tool used for public copy raises different questions from a service handling customer records. The owner needs the business request, the proposed data, the expected users, and a description of where the vendor's output will go. Ask the requester to name the decision or workflow that depends on the output. The owner then finds the specialists needed for that use. Security can assess access and technical controls. Legal can examine contract terms and data commitments. The business owner can judge whether the remaining risk is acceptable for the intended work, within the company's approval rules. Record a deputy or a handover contact for absences. Without one, a review can stall when a customer or vendor asks a question after the purchase. The [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) can link the service to its owner and review record without turning the register into a substitute for the underlying evidence. ## What authority does the named person need? The owner needs permission to request documents, convene reviewers, challenge an incomplete answer, and return a purchase for more work. They also need a route to someone who can decide when the evidence remains incomplete. These rights should be agreed before a difficult review reaches a deadline. Use the following split as a starting point, then adapt it to the company's actual approval rules. | Role | Decision or contribution | | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | | AI risk owner | Coordinates the review, records gaps, and recommends a path. | | Business owner | Confirms the use case and seeks approval for residual risk. | | Security and legal reviewers | Assess evidence and terms within their respective remits. | | Authorized approver | Accepts risk or signs the purchase within delegated authority. | One person may hold more than one role. The record should still show which decision they made and under what authority. If the AI risk owner is external, the engagement should say whether that person can make decisions or only recommend them. A recommendation to proceed is not a contract signature. Equally, a security review does not establish that the business has accepted every remaining risk. Link each open issue to the person who can close it, accept it, or stop the purchase. ## What should the owner ask the vendor for? Ask for evidence that matches the proposed use, rather than sending a questionnaire without context. Give the vendor a short description of the workflow and the kinds of data involved. Ask which parts of the service receive that data and which other providers take part in delivering it. Request the terms and technical material that explain access, retention, deletion, incident handling, and changes to the service. Where model training is relevant, ask whether the vendor uses customer data for that purpose and what choices are available. Check the answer against the contract and the settings the team will actually use. The site's [answer about model training and customer data](/faq/are-models-trained-on-our-customer-data) offers a related starting point for that discussion. Evidence needs a clear scope. A document about a vendor's general security program may not describe a particular model, product feature, or deployment. Ask the vendor to identify the service and configuration covered by each answer. If the vendor cannot provide a document, record the gap and ask what alternative evidence it can share. The [cyber supply chain guidance](https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/cyber-supply-chain-risk-management) is useful background for examining supplier relationships. Apply its ideas to the actual purchase rather than treating a vendor's completed form as the decision itself. ## How should the owner test claims against the intended use? A vendor answer is useful only if the team can connect it to the proposed workflow. Compare the response with the planned data flows, user access, and output handling. If the purchase request says customer records will be entered, a promise about public test data does not answer the question. Ask engineering to show where data enters the service and where results return. Find out whether staff can change the model, add connected tools, or send output to another system. Those choices can change the risk even when the supplier and contract stay the same. For a service that generates an answer used in a decision, agree how people will check the result. Define who may rely on it and what happens when the output is wrong or unsupported. The [human oversight](/glossary/human-oversight) page provides a related route for examining that part of the workflow. The [risk framework guidance](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) provides a broader structure for assessing AI risks. The owner can use that structure to frame questions, while the technical and business teams supply evidence from their own use. Keep the distinction clear between a vendor's description of a control and proof that the chosen setup uses it. ## How are gaps and risk acceptance recorded? Keep a decision record with the purchase, not just a copy of the vendor's answers. Describe the intended use, the evidence reviewed, the open gaps, and the person responsible for each follow-up. State whether the business can proceed, must change the proposed use, or needs a further decision. For each gap, write down its practical consequence. An unclear deletion term, for example, matters because the business may not know what happens to submitted data when the service ends. Record the vendor's response, any internal check, and the conditions attached to approval. Avoid marking a gap closed merely because someone has agreed to revisit it. If a decision-maker accepts a risk, record the scope of that acceptance. Approval for a limited internal trial should not silently become approval for customer-facing use. The record should identify the approver, the reason for the decision, and the event that prompts another review. The [risk sign-off answer](/faq/how-does-ai-risk-get-recorded-and-who-signs-it-off) connects this step to the site's wider approach. Link the decision from the register so a later reviewer can find the source documents and see what was actually approved. ## Who answers a customer's procurement questionnaire? When your company is the supplier, the question comes from the other direction. The customer wants to know who can explain your AI controls and stand behind the answers. The named owner gathers the response, checks its scope, and brings in the people who operate the service. The site's [customer questionnaire answer](/faq/who-answers-customer-security-questionnaires) states: “I do, as the named officer on record.” For the retainer, confirm the named contact, the work covered, and the decision rights in the engagement. The [fractional chief AI officer service](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) is the relevant route for that discussion. Before sending a response, compare it with the product the customer will receive. Ask engineering to check the deployment and data flows. Ask security and legal to review statements in their areas. If a control is planned or applies only to a different service, say so rather than presenting it as universal. Keep a record of the submitted answers and the evidence behind them. A customer may return with a contract clause or an audit request that refers to the response. The owner should be able to find the source, identify who checked it, and route a challenge to the right team. ## When should a vendor review be reopened? Reopen the review when the proposed use changes enough to affect an earlier decision. Examples include a new category of data, a wider group of users, or a connection that lets the service send results elsewhere. A vendor change can matter too, especially when it affects the service or evidence the company relied on. The owner should agree how teams will report such changes. Procurement may hear about contract changes first, while engineering may see a new feature in use. A short route back to the owner helps both teams flag changes before an old approval gets reused in a different setting. Check whether the original decision still covers the new use. If it does not, ask the relevant reviewers to examine the change and record a fresh decision. Keep the earlier record so the team can see what changed and why. Do not erase an accepted gap just because the vendor has supplied an updated document. For questions about personal data, the [data protection guidance for AI](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/artificial-intelligence/guidance-on-ai-and-data-protection/) offers material to discuss with the person responsible for privacy. Set the boundary of the work before naming an external person in a procurement response. Identify the services and vendor reviews they will cover, the internal contacts they can call on, and the records they can access. Agree who answers when the named person is unavailable. The company should retain a clear route for decisions it has not delegated. Give the external owner a way to raise an urgent gap and identify the internal person who can pause a purchase or accept a risk. If the officer will speak directly to customers, agree who checks the response and who may make contractual commitments. Also decide where review records will live. The company needs access to vendor evidence, decision notes, and customer responses after the engagement ends. A handover should identify open actions and the next contact for each one. The [handover playbook](/resources/handover-playbook) provides a place to start that discussion. Before sending the next questionnaire, test the arrangement with an actual request. Ask the proposed owner to trace an answer from the customer's question to the supporting evidence and its internal reviewer. Any missing access or unclear approval right is then visible before the answer becomes a commitment.

rows.text: An AI pilot never reached production because of an organisational gap, not a technical one. A demo only has to impress the person running it. Production has to survive a change of prompt, a change of model and a change of the person who built it. It has to do that without anyone noticing except a number on a dashboard. Six conditions decide whether that gap closes. One named owner still answers for the system a year after launch. A data classification signed off by someone with authority says what a vendor may see. An outcome number moves when the system works, matched by an eval that runs in the build pipeline before every release. Tracing shows which step produced a bad answer, and a rollback fires on a threshold, not an argument. Most stalled pilots are missing the first two, and a team cannot build the rest until those exist.

rows.text: A pilot stalls in the space between working once and working every time. Most proof-of-concepts skip four things production always needs. Two of them are a named owner who still answers a year after launch and a decision about which data may leave the building. The other two are a number that says whether the system is working, and an automatic check that catches a regression before a customer does. ## Where do pilots actually stop? ### Nobody owns the risk Pilots are usually built by whoever was curious enough to try. That person is rarely still around, or still in charge, once the project needs a decision about risk. Nobody has the standing to say the system is ready, and nobody has to explain a bad output to a customer or a regulator. Ownership means one name attached to the outcome, with the budget and the authority to pause the system if it misbehaves. A shared inbox or a Slack channel does not count. Without that name, every stall becomes permanent, because nobody is accountable for unsticking it. ### Legal has not said which data may leave Most pilots reach a vendor's API before anyone has classified the data going into the prompt. That is fine for a demo running on sample records. It stops a rollout the moment a security review asks what customer data the system touches and where it goes. The NIST AI RMF treats this as a governance decision under its Govern function, not a technical detail to settle after launch. Without a data classification written down in advance, every new use case reopens the same argument with legal. The pilot waits on a decision nobody has been asked to make yet. ### There is no measurable outcome A pilot that nobody can prove is working also cannot be proven to be failing, which is worse. Teams show accuracy on a curated test set, or a handful of good transcripts. Nobody has picked the business number the system is meant to move. Examples are tickets resolved, hours saved or the error rate on a defined task. Without that number, a debate about whether to invest further has no evidence on either side. The safest move for everyone involved is to let the pilot run quietly forever, rather than kill it or fund it properly. ### Nobody would notice a regression Prompts change, the underlying model changes on a provider's own schedule, and traffic drifts. Pilots rarely have a way to detect when any of that makes the output worse. There is no test suite running against real examples before a change ships. So a regression appears first as a customer complaint or a bad downstream decision, not as a failed build. That is the opposite of how the rest of the engineering organisation ships software. This gap is usually the reason a platform or security review declines to sign off. ## What has to be true to ship? Six conditions turn a pilot into something a platform team will actually run. None of them are exotic. Most engineering teams already do the equivalent for every other production system they own. | Condition | What it means in practice | What its absence looks like | | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | An owner. | One named person, on the team that runs the system, with authority to pause it. | No one can explain a bad output, so the stall becomes permanent. | | A data classification. | A written answer, agreed with whoever owns data risk, on what a vendor may store. | Every new use case reopens the same argument with legal. | | A measurable outcome. | One number the business already tracks, with a floor the system must clear. | Nobody can prove the pilot works, so it runs quietly forever instead of shipping or dying. | | Evals in CI. | Real test cases run on every prompt or model change; OWASP treats this as baseline hygiene. | A regression reaches a customer before anyone on the team sees it. | | Tracing and cost per outcome. | Every run logged well enough to reconstruct, with a cost a finance team can read. | Nobody can say what a run costs, or which step produced a bad answer. | | Rollback. | A rehearsed way to revert to the last prompt, model or version within minutes. | The team improvises during the first real incident instead of using a tested path. | For a system that touches decisions about people, the EU AI Act sets a similar bar for higher-risk uses. It requires a documented risk-management process, records that make a decision traceable and a human who can step in. Meeting the six conditions above gets most of the way there even for teams the Act does not yet cover. ## How would I sequence it? I run this as one pass, not six parallel workstreams, because the six conditions above depend on each other. You cannot set a rollback threshold before you have a measured outcome, and you cannot classify data before someone owns the decision to do it. ### Pick one process Choose a single workflow with enough volume to matter and an outcome you can measure without a survey, not five pilots running at once. An [AI readiness and risk assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment) is the fastest way to get that choice onto paper. Two weeks of reading the existing systems and vendor list end in a memo. The memo names an owner candidate, a first data classification and the number the process should move. For a rougher first pass, the [AI readiness scorecard](/resources/ai-readiness-scorecard) takes an afternoon. ### Build it in ninety days A [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint) turns that memo into a running system. Evals get written alongside the first working version, rather than bolted on at the end. Tracing and cost per outcome go live on a dashboard from week one. The rollback path gets rehearsed before real traffic arrives, not during the first incident. ### Hand it to someone who was in the room The internal owner should have written at least one eval case and watched the rollback rehearsal, so the runbook describes a system they already understand. A handover document given to someone who was not part of the build is a liability with a due date, not a transfer of knowledge. ## What this does not solve This sequence gets one process into production with the six conditions in place. Several harder governance questions stay outside it. Your risk appetite is still your call, not this sequence's. Two companies with the same pilot and the same data can reasonably choose different answers about what a vendor may see. That decision belongs to whoever owns risk at your company, not something a framework or an outside advisor can make for you. It does not replace a legal review of your contracts with model vendors. Classifying data tells your lawyers what question to ask. It does not answer whether a specific vendor's terms are acceptable, and that answer changes as vendors change their terms. The underlying model is exactly as reliable as it was before this sequence started. Evals catch regressions against the cases you thought to test. They do not catch every way a general-purpose model can fail on a case nobody wrote down. That is why the rollback path matters as much as the evals do. It does not scale to five processes at once. The sequence above is built for one workflow with one owner. Running it for a second or third process repeats the same ninety days. It does not shortcut them.

rows.text: ## What this is A panel specification for tracking how AI tools are used at work. It has eight panels. Each names the question it answers, the data source and the decision it supports. It is a page, not a dashboard file. You copy the panels into whatever tool you already run. Version 0.1 covers coding assistants and chat assistants. Version 0.2 will cover SaaS tools with AI built in and internal agents. I will write it when clients who run them appear. The panels fall into three kinds. The coverage, seat and retention panels count what people did. The two survey panels count what people said. The outcome, delivery health and cost panels read what the work produced. The outcome, delivery health, cost and trust panels carry the weight, and the trust survey is read as opinion. That order is a synthesis of the sources, not a finding any of them states. The [adoption telemetry article](/blog/adoption-telemetry-measuring-if-ai-is-actually-used) gives the evidence behind it. ## The eight panels | # | Panel | Question it answers | Data source | Decision it supports | | --- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 1 | Coverage | What share of AI use at work runs through approved tools? | [LLM gateway](/glossary/llm-gateway) request logs, the sign-in app list, expense lines, API bills and the [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) | Which tools to approve, replace or block, and where the approved path is hard | | 2 | Paid versus active | Which paid seats see no use? | Vendor admin APIs, such as GitHub's user-management `last_activity_at` | Reclaim or reassign seats, and aim training | | 3 | Retention by team | Do people who tried a tool keep using it at 4, 8 and 12 weeks? | Gateway or vendor logs, with one written definition of active | Change the workflow or retire the tool | | 4 | Outcome per use case | Did the outcome agreed before rollout move, against a baseline or a comparison group? | The system of record for that outcome, such as ticketing, CI or your CRM, not the AI tool's own logs | Scale, fix or retire the use case | | 5 | Delivery health (engineering use cases) | Did throughput or instability get worse as use grew? | CI/CD and version control: DORA's lead time for changes, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate and rework rate, plus review time | Slow or pause a rollout when instability rises | | 6 | Cost per outcome | What does one unit of the outcome cost? | Spend and the outcome count from the outcome panel, as set out in [how cost per outcome is measured](/faq/how-is-cost-per-outcome-measured) | Budget, build versus buy, and model choice | | 7 | Trust and friction pulse | Do people trust the output, rely on it, and say where it gets in the way? | A five-minute survey once a quarter, using the trust and reliance items DORA publishes, word for word and with credit. The smallest-group rule applies | Training and verification effort, and tool choice | | 8 | Policy clarity | Do staff know what is expected, what is allowed and what applies to them? | The same survey, using the four AI-stance items in DORA's 2025 report, word for word and with credit | Fix how the acceptable use policy is explained | The delivery health and cost panels apply to engineering and workflow use cases. Write the outcome panel for each use case. ## Fix these definitions before you build - What counts as active. GitHub needs two active days in the trailing 28 to place a user in a usage phase. Microsoft counts a returning user as one with an action in both the current and the previous period. Choose one rule, write it on the panel and keep it. Mine is two different active days within four weeks, and I count people, not accounts. - When you check retention. The retention panel uses 4, 8 and 12 weeks. Week 4 is the first check. I read it as people active in week 4 over people active in week 1, per team, from gateway logs. - The smallest group you show. Mine is five people. Microsoft's Viva Insights needs its minimum group size set to at least five. That is a product setting. The sources read here give no legal figure for a minimum group size. Write down your own. ## What stays off the dashboard - Seat count as adoption. A seat shows money spent, and GitHub keeps seat data apart from its usage reports. - Daily or weekly active users with no written definition. GitHub, Microsoft and DORA each define active differently. - Prompt counts. DORA's 2024 report, published by Google Cloud, said measuring usage frequency is "likely not as meaningful as measuring reliance". - Lines of code accepted as a success measure. GitHub calls its own lines figure directional. - Acceptance rate as a success measure. In a 2022 preprint on Copilot users it tracked how productive users said they felt. - Vendor hours saved or ROI as value. Microsoft builds assisted hours from action counts, fixed minutes per action, and meeting recaps counted by meeting length. A default hourly rate then values them. - Rankings of named people. DX, a vendor of measurement software, warns against using these metrics to judge individuals. - Prompt content. The GDPR asks for no more data than needed, and Claude Code's documentation says prompt text is off by default. I collect none. ## Who sees what Show team-level figures by default, for teams of five or more. Where you control the collector, filter or redact the person field before data reaches the dashboard. Claude Code includes the signed-in user's email by default, and its documentation says to filter it at your own backend if that is a concern. The paid versus active panel shows idle seats by team. Reclaiming a seat needs a name, and a name is person-level data. Show named views only for a narrow stated purpose, recorded, approved by two people and kept 30 days. Write down who sees the list. Then run the screening in the [adoption telemetry article](/blog/adoption-telemetry-measuring-if-ai-is-actually-used) before the list exists. ## What it is not It is not a live dashboard, and it is not an export for one tool. It does not show that an AI tool works. Only the outcome panel can do that, against a baseline or a comparison group, and that is a synthesis, not a finding any source states. It is a summary of public documents, not legal advice.

rows.text: ## What this is A CI workflow and an eval case format for one [agentic workflow](/glossary/agentic-workflow). The same discipline sits inside the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint). A prompt or model change should not merge without passing a test set first. ## The eval case format | Field | Purpose | Example | | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | id | A stable name, so a failure is traceable across runs | refund-double-charge | | input | The exact prompt or tool call the agent receives | Customer says they were charged twice | | expected | A pass rule: an exact match, a check, or a second model acting as a grader | Refund issued, ticket closed, no invented apology | | tags | The failure mode a case guards against | prompt-injection, tool-misuse, refusal | ## The CI gate The workflow runs the eval set on every pull request, scores it, and blocks the merge under your floor. Nobody has to remember to run it by hand, which is the part that fails first once a team is busy. The tags borrow their shape from [OWASP's Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/). Prompt injection and excessive agency (the agent doing something nobody asked it to) appear in a support agent as often as in a public chatbot. A tagged case catches the regression either way. ## Why not the threshold you already have? A pass-rate threshold cannot see a metric fall while the suite stays above it. The floor in the gate above is a threshold of this kind. The baseline in the [evals-baseline specification](/spec/evals-baseline/1.0) reports every fall beyond that metric's tolerance. Three differences can be checked. - A threshold covers the suite, and a baseline covers each metric. promptfoo's [command-line reference](https://www.promptfoo.dev/docs/usage/command-line/) describes `PROMPTFOO_PASS_RATE_THRESHOLD` as "Set a minimum pass rate threshold (as a percentage)". The README of its [GitHub Action](https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo-action/blob/6a8612f15670b4d5a4d43e0d6fb221d84ab389d8/README.md) describes `fail-on-threshold` as "Required suite pass percentage from 0 to 100". A baseline stores a value and a tolerance for each metric. - A threshold is typed into a workflow line, so nothing in the repository records when the suite last met it. The custom threshold check in promptfoo's [CI guide](https://www.promptfoo.dev/docs/integrations/ci-cd/) fails the build when `$PASS_RATE < 95`. A baseline is committed to the repository with the date it was recorded, and each check that reads it prints that date. - With a threshold of 0.80, a metric can fall from 0.98 to 0.81 and the build stays green. A baseline of 0.98 with a tolerance of 0 reports `below-baseline` for a run that scores 0.81, because the drop, 0.17, is more than the tolerance ([rule 2 of the specification](/spec/evals-baseline/1.0#four-comparison-rules)). A check exits 1 on that finding only with `--strict`, and otherwise it warns and exits 0. The README of promptfoo's GitHub Action disagrees with promptfoo's documentation page about whether the action compares a pull request with its base. The [README](https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo-action/blob/6a8612f15670b4d5a4d43e0d6fb221d84ab389d8/README.md) says: "The action evaluates only the current checkout; it does not run separate base and head evaluations." The [documentation page](https://www.promptfoo.dev/docs/integrations/github-action/) says: "On every pull request that modifies a prompt, the action will automatically run a full comparison". ## A baseline you do not own can be switched off A baseline kept in someone else's [evals](/glossary/evals) service lasts as long as that service allows. Three vendors state their limits on their own pages, each read on 12 November 2026. - [OpenAI's evals guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evals) says: "Evals will become read-only for existing users on October 31, 2026, and the platform is scheduled to shut down on November 30, 2026." - [Braintrust's pricing page](https://www.braintrust.dev/pricing) lists "14-day retention" for its free Starter plan. - [Confident AI's pricing page](https://www.confident-ai.com/pricing) lists "5 test runs per week" for its free plan and adds "additional test runs are locked". [The specification requires](/spec/evals-baseline/1.0#a-passing-check-must-be-expensive-to-fake) the baseline to be a file committed to your repository, and a check to read it without a network or a database. No evaluation vendor's plan, retention period or shutdown date applies to it. ## What it is not It is not a considered eval set on its own. A handful of cases pulled from real conversations tests more than a long list invented at a desk. The starter takes no position on which cases you pick. Choosing the cases still maps to the MEASURE function (one of the framework's four functions) in [NIST's AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework).

rows.text: ## What this is The four documents that answer most of a corporate security review. They are deliberately short: a register nobody updates is worse than no register. The kit also sets out the order in which to call people when an AI system fails. ## What it is not It is not a compliance certificate, and it is not legal advice. It is the paperwork a reviewer expects to see before they look at your architecture. ## Who signs what | Document | What it's for | Who signs it | | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | | AI register | Every AI system in use, who owns it, what data reaches it. | The named AI risk owner keeps it current. | | Acceptable use policy | What you may paste into a tool, and what you may not. | Every employee who uses an AI tool for work. | | Data classification table | Which vendors may see which tier of data. | The AI risk owner, together with whoever owns the data. | | Vendor questionnaire | One answer set procurement can reuse for every new vendor. | Procurement, before anyone signs a vendor contract. | It maps loosely to what ISO/IEC 42001 and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) both expect a company to have on file. It does not require either. ## Vendor questionnaire The other three documents describe how you handle AI. This one asks each vendor how it handles your data. Send the same questions to every AI vendor, and file the answers with the contract. The questions cover these topics: - Whether the vendor trains models on your data, and how you opt out. - Where your data is processed and stored, who at the vendor can read it, and which [sub-processors](/glossary/sub-processor) touch it. - How the vendor announces a model change, and whether you can stay on a fixed version. - How the vendor tells you about an incident, and who answers when you call. - Whether the system counts as high-risk under the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act), and which duties the contract leaves with you. - What happens to your data and prompts when the contract ends. ## Incident response plan When an AI system fails, its owner should not have to work out who to call. Write this call order down beside the register, with a name and a backup against each role. Inside the company, in this order: 1. The system owner named in the register, who limits or stops the system and keeps its logs and model version as they were. 2. The AI risk owner, who decides whether the incident is serious. 3. An executive who can approve a report and a message to customers. 4. Legal counsel, and whoever handles data breaches if personal data is involved. Outside the company, in this order: 5. The provider of the system, which is often the vendor. 6. The importer or distributor, if the system has one. 7. The market surveillance authority. 8. Affected customers, as your contracts require. For a high-risk system you deploy, Article 26 of the EU AI Act asks the deployer to give notice at once when it identifies a serious incident. The order is the provider first, then the importer or distributor and the market surveillance authority. Log the time each person learned of the incident. The page on [serious incident reporting](/glossary/serious-incident-reporting) says which moment starts the clock for a report and sets out the deadlines, so this plan does not repeat them.

rows.text: ## What this is Five axes, scored from zero to three, that give you a rough position before you pay anyone to check it properly. The axes match the ones in the [AI Readiness & Risk Assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment). This is the self-administered version, without the evidence behind it. ## The five axes | Axis | 0 — not started | 1 — informal | 2 — documented | 3 — evidenced | | ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- | | Strategy | No one has named which processes to automate first | Someone has an opinion, nothing written down | A ranked shortlist exists | The shortlist is reviewed by whoever owns the budget | | Data | No one knows what a vendor tool can see | A rough sense exists, not written down | A data classification table exists | The table is checked before a new tool is approved | | Delivery | Every pilot has stalled before production | One pilot is close to live | One system is live, unmonitored | A system is live, monitored, with a rollback path | | People | Only the original builder understands any AI system in use | One other person has read the code | A second person has changed it and shipped | Ownership is written down and handed over on a schedule | | Governance | No [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) exists | A register exists, out of date | A register exists, reviewed occasionally | The register is reviewed on a fixed schedule | ## Scoring it Score each axis from zero to three using the table above, then add the five scores for a total out of fifteen. A low total early on is common. It usually means nobody has written anything down yet, not that the engineering is behind. The five axes are not a substitute for the [NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) or [ISO/IEC 42001](https://www.iso.org/standard/42001). They are a rougher pass at the same territory, built to take an afternoon rather than an audit. ## What it is not It is not the Assessment, and it carries no evidence a reviewer would accept. A self-given three is a claim until someone outside your team checks what you have actually written down.

rows.text: ## What this is A worksheet for one recurring decision: build the workflow yourself, or buy a vendor's version of it. It will not choose for you. It gives the choice a written reason, which is what a board or a buyer asks for later. ## The six criteria | Criterion | Build tends to win when | Buy tends to win when | | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | | Data residency | Customer data cannot leave your infrastructure by contract or by law | A vendor already holds a data-processing agreement you trust | | Customisation depth | The workflow is core to what makes your product different | The workflow looks like everyone else's version of the same task | | Time to a working version | You already have the engineers and the model access | Procurement moves faster than a hiring plan would | | Total cost over years | Usage is high enough that a per-call fee compounds | Usage is uncertain, and a fixed fee caps the downside | | Exit cost | You can rebuild the model calls without rebuilding the product | A second vendor could take over most of the same job | | Ownership when it breaks | An internal team already owns the surrounding process | A vendor's contract has a real answer to who to call | ## Scoring it Weight the six criteria for your situation, score build and buy against each one, and let the total argue with your gut feeling. A bought tool still needs an owner and a place in your [AI register](/glossary/ai-register). [NIST's AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) treats a vendor's model the same as one you trained. That sits under its MAP function (one of the framework's four functions). The risk to your customer does not care who wrote the code. ## Total cost of ownership The Total cost over years criterion needs a total cost of ownership (TCO) estimate, and a vendor quote covers only part of it. Fill in the categories in the table below, for build and for buy. Use the same horizon for both sides, long enough to cover the longest contract you would sign. For each side, add what you pay once to what you pay in every period of that horizon. | Side | Cost category | What to count | | ----- | ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Build | Engineering time | Engineer hours for the first version, and the work those engineers would otherwise ship | | Build | Maintenance | Upkeep as the model API, your libraries and your product change | | Build | Drift monitoring | The [evals](/glossary/evals) and review that catch quality slipping as models and data change | | Buy | Licence | The vendor's fee in the unit they meter it, and how it grows with your usage | | Buy | Integration | Connecting the tool to your data, login and workflows, plus the security review | | Buy | Lock-in | The cost of leaving: moving data out, redoing prompts and workflows, retraining staff | Take every amount from your own quotes and payroll, because this page lists no amounts. Use the same usage forecast on both sides, since the criteria table above shows that usage often decides which side costs less. Lock-in is the cost behind the Exit cost criterion, so fill in both together. ## What it is not It is not a procurement process, and it will not pick the vendor for you. It decides one thing: whether the job belongs inside your codebase or inside someone else's product. This is the call the [Fractional CAIO Retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) reviews every quarter, alongside the [shadow AI](/glossary/shadow-ai) a team already bought without asking.
