rows.text: ## What this is The Handover Playbook is a plan to fill in, not a finished one. It moves AI leadership from an outside lead to a named person inside your company. Most rows ask for a name, a place or a date; the rest ask for a decision. Only your company knows those. The reasons for each table, and how much weight each source carries, are in [How to hand over AI leadership to an internal owner](/blog/handing-over-ai-leadership-to-an-internal-owner). ## Stage 1. The owner and the test Fill this in first. This playbook asks for a written test so that the handover can end on a result, not only on a date. The [pilot article](/blog/why-your-ai-pilot-never-reached-production) says the new owner should have written at least one eval case and watched the rollback rehearsal. The [approach page](/approach) has a related test of whether your engineers can roll back a bad model without waiting on the outside lead. My test has three checks, and I judge each one. The new owner writes an eval case and runs a rollback rehearsal. The new owner also handles one incident without me in the room. | Question | Your answer | | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | | Who takes the role? Write one name. | | | Who decides whether to stop a launch, if that is a different person? | | | What must the new owner do without the outside lead before the role moves? | | | Who judges each check? | | | What counts as a pass? Write it so a third person could judge it. | | | What happens if the new owner is not ready on the planned date? | | ## Stage 2. What moves My handover takes three months, in three phases. The month-one plan sets the end date, not the contract. | Phase | Months | What happens | | ----- | ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------- | | 1 | Months one and two | The new owner and the outside lead work side by side. | | 2 | Month three | The new owner leads. The outside lead reviews. | | 3 | End of month three | The final test and the signatures. | One row per item. Fill in who holds it today, who holds it after, where it lives and the date it moved. The reason for each row comes first, and its source where it has one, so you can drop a row you disagree with. | Item | Why it is here | Held today by | Held after by | Where it lives | Done on | | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------- | ------------- | -------------- | ------- | | Decisions and their reasons | A UK regulator says handover material should include judgement and opinion, not just facts and figures. [FCA handbook](https://handbook.fca.org.uk/handbook/sysc25/sysc25s9), an analogy from financial firms. | | | | | | Work in progress | Status, owner and next action for each open item. [Fractionus](https://fractionus.com/blog/fractional-executive-offboarding), one vendor's advice. | | | | | | Open risks and concerns | The same regulator says the material should include unresolved or possible breaches and unresolved concerns raised by regulators. FCA handbook, an analogy. | | | | | | The list of AI systems | NIST asks for mechanisms to inventory AI systems. [NIST AI RMF](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/5-sec-core/), Govern 1.6, voluntary. | | | | | | Roles and authority | NIST asks that roles, responsibilities and lines of communication are documented and clear. NIST AI RMF, Govern 2.1, voluntary. | | | | | | Runbook, evals and rollback | Google says training for a receiving team can include hands-on exercises in operations. [Google SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/evolving-sre-engagement-model/), the operator's own account. | | | | | | Monitoring and logs | NIST asks for monitoring plans that cover incident response and change management (Manage 4.1). For high-risk systems, deployers will have to keep the logs they control for at least six months. That duty starts on 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. [Article 26](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-26) of the EU AI Act. | | | | | | Outside parties | An interim director helps announce the new leader to funders and peers. [CompassPoint](https://www.compasspoint.org/sites/default/files/documents/Interim%20EDs%20-%20final.pdf), a practitioner's guide for US nonprofits. | | | | | | Vendor and sub-processor contacts | Vendor and [sub-processor](/glossary/sub-processor) contacts are not personal. They are a row in the [AI register](/glossary/ai-register), and the renewal calendar moves with it. | | | | | ## Stage 3. Who signs what NIST AI RMF Govern 2.1 asks that roles, responsibilities and lines of communication are documented and clear. Its voluntary Playbook also suggests documenting delegated authorities. Write that down here for the handover. The rows are examples of decisions that carry a signature; no source lists them. Delete any that do not apply and add your own. For a high-risk system under the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act), ask counsel who must hold [human oversight](/glossary/human-oversight). | Decision | Signs today | Signs after the handover date | Change takes effect on | | ------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ----------------------------- | ---------------------- | | Entries in the AI register | | | | | Risk acceptances | | | | | Policy exceptions | | | | | Vendor and model approvals | | | | | Changes to eval thresholds | | | | | Rollback calls | | | | | Answers to customer security questionnaires | | | | | Serious incident calls | | | | ## Stage 4. Access List every account the outside lead holds. Revoke them in one coordinated step on or before the last day, and do not leave removal to the outside lead. A marketplace that sells fractional executives gives this advice and asks for written confirmation. It is one vendor's opinion. The table lists six categories of account. The client's internal owner or IT lead revokes each one, and the revocation is confirmed in writing the same day. A revoke-all line sits on the last-day checklist. | Account or system | Granted by | Revoked by | Confirmed in writing on | | ---------------------------------------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------- | | The AI register | | The client's internal owner or IT lead | | | The [LLM gateway](/glossary/llm-gateway) | | The client's internal owner or IT lead | | | CI/CD | | The client's internal owner or IT lead | | | The cloud consoles | | The client's internal owner or IT lead | | | The vendor panels | | The client's internal owner or IT lead | | | The SSO admin | | The client's internal owner or IT lead | | ## Stage 5. After the last day Sources agree that some reachable help is useful and differ on how much. Agree it in writing, with its length, scope and who may call. The middle column holds my terms where I have set them. | Question | My terms | Your answer | | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------- | | Will the outside lead stay reachable, and for which questions? | Yes. Questions by email, answered within one working day. | | | For how long, and in what fee shape? | Thirty days after the last day, with one review call on day 30. | | | Who may call? | | | | What is out of scope after the last day? | Anything beyond the email answers and the day-30 call is a separate agreement. | | ## Stage 6. The check after handover Pick the date and the person who asks. The first question comes from one vendor's advice to ask the successor about a month after the exit. The other rows are prompts. Add your own. | Question | Date | Who asks | Answer | | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---- | -------- | ------ | | What do you wish you had known on day one? | | | | | Which decision since the handover was made without the outside lead? | | | | | Which item in the What moves table turned out to be missing? | | | | | Do customer paperwork and the AI register show the new name? | | | | ## What it is not It is not a standard. A search in October 2026 found no standard, law or study that sets out how to hand over AI leadership, and no outcome study of AI-leadership handovers. Nothing shows that these tables lead to better results. It is not legal advice, and it is not a compliance certificate. The [FAQ on how the Retainer ends](/faq/how-does-the-retainer-end) covers how the [Fractional CAIO Retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) ends. No engagement has yet ended in a full handover by the method in these tables.

rows.text: ## What this is A policy file for whichever [LLM gateway](/glossary/llm-gateway) you run, hosted or self-built. It is the config, not the gateway itself. The decisions live in a file your team reviews, not in a script only one engineer remembers. ## The policy schema | Key | What it controls | Example | | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- | | allowed_models | Which providers and model versions a team may call | two named models, not an open list | | redact | Fields stripped before a prompt or response is logged or forwarded | email, national_id, card_number | | rate_limit | Calls per minute before the gateway queues or refuses | a ceiling per team, not per user | | log_retention | How long a request and response pair is kept | matches your data retention policy, not a default | | fallback | What happens if the primary provider is down | a named second provider, or a hard failure | ## Logging and retention The logging schema borrows its shape from [the EU AI Act's Article 12](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ%3AL_202401689), which requires automatic event logs for high-risk systems. Not every call through a gateway is high-risk. The habit costs little to build in now. It is expensive to retrofit once a regulator or a customer asks first. The `allowed_models` and `log_retention` keys map to two [NIST SP 800-53](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final) control families: Access Control and Audit and Accountability. Procurement questionnaires often draw on this catalogue, even when nobody names it. ## What it is not It is not a gateway, and it will not stop a determined engineer from calling a model directly. It makes an unrouted call a [shadow AI](/glossary/shadow-ai) finding. That is the layer the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint) puts in front of a workflow before it counts as production.

rows.text: ## What this is Two weeks. I interview the people doing the work and read your systems and your vendor list. I write one memo you can hand to a board or a customer. I score you on five readiness drivers. The free [AI readiness scorecard](/resources/ai-readiness-scorecard) lets you score the same five yourself in an afternoon. ## What you keep You keep one document, whether or not you continue. It holds the readiness score, the gap list, and the three processes ranked by what automating them is worth this quarter. Before you decide whether to build or buy one of them, use the [build vs buy AI kit](/resources/build-vs-buy-ai-kit). It scores build and buy against six criteria and carries a total cost of ownership table for both sides. If a [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint) follows, the Assessment fee is credited against it. The window and the terms for all three offers are on the [pricing page](/pricing). ## ISO/IEC 42001 gap assessment The gap list compares your company with [ISO/IEC 42001](/glossary/iso-iec-42001), the standard for an AI management system that an accredited body can certify. It shows where you fall short of what the standard asks. This is a gap assessment, not a certification. An accredited body runs the independent audit that grants certification, and the [certification FAQ](/faq/can-you-get-us-iso-iec-42001-certified-or-just-a-working-system) covers the difference between a working system and a certificate. ## Why it is two weeks and not two days A readiness claim you cannot show evidence for is worth nothing in a security review. I read the code, talk to the people who use the tools, and check what your vendors actually do with your data. Two weeks is the shortest span in which I can do all three.

rows.text: In the evals-baseline specification 1.0, a regression is a difference between a baseline and a later run of the same suite. It takes one of three forms: a metric has gone missing, a value has dropped beyond its tolerance, or a sample count has changed. A baseline is a reduced record of one run. A check compares it with a later run, and prints a finding for each regression and for each input it cannot read. By default a finding only warns, and the check still passes. Strict mode is the only way for a finding to make the check fail. An implementation in any language, or a person who reads a pull request, can use the specification to tell whether a result is right. Where an implementation or its documentation disagrees with this specification, the specification wins. This version reads the run files of two tools, promptfoo and DeepEval. ## How to read this specification The words MUST, MUST NOT and SHOULD in a clause carry the meaning that [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119) gives them. Everywhere else the words are plain English. In a message text, a word in angle brackets stands for a value that the implementation fills in. An implementation conforms to a version when it reproduces that version's conformance vectors. The published vectors are the normative annex for exact text: every line a command prints and every file `record` writes. This page gives the form of each message, and a vector gives its words. Where the two differ, the vector decides. A vector marked reference-only is not part of the annex. ## Terms - A **run file** is the file an evaluation tool writes for one execution of a suite. - A **sample** is one scored observation of one metric. A **sample count** is how many samples a run holds for a metric. - A **metric key** names a metric inside one run. For promptfoo it is `<provider label> :: <metric name>`, and for DeepEval it is the metric name. - A **value** is the mean of a metric's samples, on the tool's own scale. This specification assumes that higher is better. - A **baseline** is a reduced record of one run, committed in the repository that owns the suite. - A **tolerance** is a number that is 0 or more, in the metric's own units, stored per metric in the baseline. - A **finding** is one line that begins with a finding id. A **note** is a line that begins with `note:` and never counts as a finding. - A **regression** is a difference between a baseline and a later run of the same suite, as rules 1, 2 and 4 define it. Rule 3 states what is not a regression. - A **reader** turns a run file or a baseline into the data a check compares, or refuses it. - The three **verbs** are `check`, `record` and `show`. The verb `check` compares a run with a baseline. The verb `record` writes a baseline from a run, and `show` prints what the reader extracted from a run. - A `check` runs in **strict mode** when it is given `--strict`, and in **default mode** otherwise. - Strings are **sorted** in UTF-16 code-unit order, the order in which a JavaScript string comparison puts strings. A character above U+FFFF is a surrogate pair, so it comes before the characters from U+E000 to U+FFFF, where code-point order puts it after. Every sort on this page uses this order. That covers metric keys, finding lines, the keys of the rule 3 note, the object keys of a canonical form and the canonical forms themselves. ## Four comparison rules A finding of a rule is one line of the form `<id> <key>: <text>`. The table gives the finding id and the form of the message text of each rule. A rule that fails produces a finding, and the exit codes say whether a finding stops the run. The clauses that follow state the rules exactly. | # | Rule | Compares | Finding id | Message text | | --- | --------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 1 | A metric the baseline names and the run lacks fails | the set of keys in the baseline against the run | `missing-metric` | `the baseline names it (<value> over <n> samples) and this run has no such metric` | | 2 | A value under the baseline, beyond tolerance, fails | baseline value against run value, per key | `below-baseline` | `<run value> is below the baseline <baseline value> by <drop>, more than the tolerance <tolerance>` | | 3 | Metrics present only on the run are ignored | nothing; the keys are listed in one note | none | `note: <n> metric(s) only in this run, not compared (rule 3): <keys>` | | 4 | Unequal sample counts fail | baseline `samples` against the run's sample count, per key | `sample-count` | `the baseline holds <b> samples and this run holds <r>` | 1. For every key in the baseline, a run that holds no samples for that key MUST produce `missing-metric`. If the run holds that metric but the reader refuses it, the finding is `unreadable-metric` instead, and the reader's reason is its text. Rules 2 and 4 are not evaluated for a key that rule 1 reported. 2. For every key present in both, let the drop be the baseline value minus the run value. Let `q(x)` be `floor(x * 1,000,000 + 0.5)`, in IEEE 754 double-precision arithmetic. The check MUST report `below-baseline` when `q(baseline) - q(run) > q(tolerance)`, and MUST NOT otherwise. A value higher than the baseline is never a finding. The message prints the drop to six decimals with trailing zeros removed. Whole numbers are compared because plain subtraction of 64-bit floats can fail a run that sits exactly on its tolerance. For example, 0.92 - 0.9 is 0.020000000000000018, which is more than 0.02. 3. A key present in the run and absent from the baseline MUST NOT produce a finding. The check lists at most ten such keys in one note, in sorted order, then `, and <n> more`. 4. For every key present in both, a sample count different from the baseline's `samples` MUST produce `sample-count`, whichever direction it differs in. Rules 2 and 4 are independent, so one key can produce both. A run exactly at its tolerance passes, and a run one millionth beyond it fails. The table gives a worked example. | Run value, for a baseline value of 0.92 and a tolerance of 0.02 | Result under rule 2 | | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 0.95 | no finding | | 0.92 | no finding | | 0.9 | no finding, because `q(0.92) - q(0.9)` and `q(0.02)` are both 20000 | | 0.900001 | no finding | | 0.899999 | `below-baseline` | | 0.6 | `below-baseline` | ## Binding check The four rules compare numbers. Nothing in them says the numbers were measured on the same cases. A suite in which a hard case is swapped for an easy one keeps its sample counts and only improves. The binding check covers that gap. The baseline records a digest of the case inputs. When the digest of a run differs from the digest in the baseline, `check` MUST report `cases-changed`. The finding says that the baseline no longer describes this suite, so the findings beside it may be meaningless. It is not a regression. In this version the binding check is a warning only. `check` prints `cases-changed` in default mode and in strict mode, and the finding never changes the exit code. The binding check reports a swap of cases that keeps the count equal. It does not punish a person who added a case and has not recorded a new baseline yet. - The digest is the first 12 hexadecimal characters of the SHA-256 of the UTF-8 encoding of one string. That string holds the canonical forms of the case identities, sorted and joined with U+0001. - Canonical form sorts object keys at every depth, keeps arrays in order, writes scalars as `JSON.stringify` writes them and holds no whitespace. So `1.0` is written `1`, `-0` is written `0`, `1e-7` stays `1e-7` and `1e21` is written `1e+21`. - A case identity is, for promptfoo, the `vars` object of the first result for each distinct `testIdx`. For DeepEval it is an object with the keys `input` and `expectedOutput` of each test case, and an absent `expectedOutput` counts as `null`. - Prompts, agent output, scorer definitions, thresholds and metric names are not part of an identity. A change to the agent or its prompt leaves the digest alone and shows only in the values, where rule 2 judges it. Adding a metric leaves the digest alone as well, so rule 3 can ignore the new metric. A check with no findings does not prove that a suite is sound. The binding check does not catch three things: - a scorer weakened in place, for example a promptfoo `contains` value changed so that it always passes - two offsetting changes to single cases that leave the mean unchanged - a fabricated but complete run file ## Findings and notes The three findings of the rules report regressions. The six findings in this table are not regressions, and each one counts as a finding. | Id | When | | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | `no-baseline` | the baseline path does not exist, and nothing was compared | | `bad-baseline` | the baseline cannot be read: it is not JSON, it has an unknown, missing or repeated key or a bad value, or it names a specification the reader does not read | | `bad-run` | the run file cannot be read, or it is from a different tool than the baseline | | `unreadable-metric` | the baseline names a metric that the reader refuses to read | | `cases-changed` | the digest of the run differs from the digest in the baseline | | `internal-error` | the reader or the comparison threw something that is not a refusal, and the text is the error's message | A check that compared nothing MUST NOT print `no findings`. These ids make that impossible: a missing or unreadable input is itself a finding, and by default it warns without failing the run. A note is printed as `note: <text>` and never counts as a finding. Notes exist for these cases: - a metric that appears only in the run, as given in the table of rules - samples the tool itself counted as errors - a metric that the reader refuses and the baseline does not name - a tool version that differs from the baseline's, as `the baseline was recorded by <tool> <version>; this run was written by <version>` Only promptfoo writes its version into its output, so only a promptfoo run can raise the version note. ### Printed lines 1. Text that came from a file MUST be printed with some characters replaced. These are U+0000 to U+001F, U+007F to U+009F, U+061C, U+200E and U+200F, U+2028 and U+2029, U+202A to U+202E, and U+2066 to U+2069. A `[` that directly follows `##` is replaced too. Each becomes `\u` followed by four lowercase hexadecimal digits, so a newline becomes `\u000a`. This covers a metric key, a tool name, a path and a reader's reason. Data therefore cannot start a line, begin a CI workflow command, send a control sequence to a terminal or forge a finding. An implementation prints no escape sequence of its own. 2. Every finding line starts with its id, apart from the two spaces that indent a finding under `replaced:`. Every note line starts with `note:` and a space, and every metric line of `show` starts with `metric` and a space. So `grep` selects each class, and no line starts with text from a file. 3. The `date:` line comes before every finding line, and `cases-changed` comes before the other findings. Finding lines are sorted by key, and for one key they follow the order of rules 1, 2 and 4. The note lines come after the finding lines. 4. The last line of a `check` is its summary, and it is one of four. In the three that count findings, `<findings>` is `1 finding` for one and `<n> findings` for two or more. - `evals-baseline: no findings` when there is none. - `evals-baseline: <findings>; warning only, exit 0 (pass --strict to exit 1)` in default mode, when at least one finding is not `cases-changed`. - `evals-baseline: <findings>; exit 1 (--strict)` in strict mode, under the same condition. - `evals-baseline: <findings>; warning only, exit 0 (cases-changed never fails --strict)` in either mode, when every finding is `cases-changed`. The third form would name an exit code the check did not use. The second would invite a reader to pass `--strict` and get exit 0 again. 5. The first line of a report is the banner, `evals-baseline <package version> (specification <MAJOR.MINOR>)`, followed by the verb and a description that the vectors show. `--version` prints the banner alone. An implementation prints its own package version where the vectors show `<package version>`. 6. A count takes the plural of its noun unless it is 1, as in `1 finding`, `2 findings`, `1 sample` and `4 samples`. Four texts print `(s)` as written, whatever the count: - the note of rule 3, `<n> metric(s) only in this run` - the note for errored promptfoo tests, `<n> errored test(s)` - the note for errored DeepEval samples, `<n> sample(s)` - the reason for a metric whose verdicts contradict higher-is-better, `<n> sample(s)` 7. A number in a message is written to six decimals with the trailing zeros removed, and without a decimal point when nothing follows it. The numbers printed for a value, a drop and a tolerance are rounded with `q`. ## The baseline file A baseline holds one run of one suite from one tool. It is a JSON file with two-space indentation and a final newline. The metric keys are in sorted order, so recording a run that changes nothing produces no diff. A number is written as `JSON.stringify` writes it, so a whole value is `1` and never `1.0`. A JSON Schema for this file is published at [/spec/evals-baseline/1.0/baseline.schema.json](/spec/evals-baseline/1.0/baseline.schema.json). It checks the shape of the file only; the rules on this page decide the rest. A baseline recorded from a promptfoo run with two metrics and four cases looks like this: { "spec": "1.0", "source": { "tool": "promptfoo", "toolVersion": "0.125.1", "shape": "promptfoo-results-3" }, "recordedAt": "2026-09-02T09:00:00.000Z", "cases": { "count": 4, "digest": "e6c6ecf167ab" }, "metrics": { "agent :: accuracy": { "value": 1, "samples": 4, "tolerance": 0 }, "agent :: format": { "value": 1, "samples": 4, "tolerance": 0 } } } | Field | Meaning | | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `spec` | the specification version the file follows, as `MAJOR.MINOR`; the machine-readable form of a citation | | `source.tool` | `promptfoo` or `deepeval` | | `source.toolVersion` | the version string the tool wrote into its own output, or `null` when the output carries none (DeepEval's does not) | | `source.shape` | the output shape the reader recognised: `promptfoo-results-3` or `deepeval-test-run` | | `recordedAt` | ISO 8601 UTC, to the millisecond; the only clock in the file | | `cases.count`, `cases.digest` | the number of cases and their digest, as defined for the binding check | | `metrics.<key>.value` | the mean of the metric's samples, rounded to 6 decimals, from -4000000000 to 4000000000 | | `metrics.<key>.samples` | the sample count, a positive integer | | `metrics.<key>.tolerance` | a number from 0 to 4000000000 | ### Reading a baseline A reader MUST refuse a file as `bad-baseline` when any of these holds: - it is not a JSON object - it has a key beyond those in the table, or lacks one of them, at any level - it has a key that appears twice in one object - it holds a value that does not fit its field - its `spec` is not two whole numbers joined by a dot, with no third number and no leading zero, so `1.0.0`, `1.0.7`, `01.00` and `1.00` are refused - the major number of its `spec` differs from the major number the reader implements, or its minor number is newer - it names no metric, because it guards nothing The refusal text names the first problem the reader found. A reader reads a baseline of the same major and an older or equal minor. Run files are read leniently, because the tools add fields freely. An unknown key in a run is ignored. A missing key that the reader needs makes the run `bad-run`. So does a key that appears twice in one object. So does a metric value outside the range set under Values, sample counts and metric keys. ### Recording a baseline The verb `record` MUST do the following: - read the run with the reader that `check` uses - refuse a run that it cannot read, a run that holds errored samples, a run that holds no case and a run that holds no metric, and write nothing when it refuses - refuse to record over a baseline that exists and that it cannot read, because the tolerances in it cannot be kept, and write nothing - leave out a metric that the reader refuses, and say so in a note - keep the tolerance that the previous baseline holds for a key of the same tool, and give any other key the tolerance from its `--tolerance` argument, or 0 when there is none - write nothing when everything except `recordedAt` and `source.toolVersion` equals what the file already holds, so that `recordedAt` stays the date on which the numbers last changed - print under `replaced:`, before it writes, the findings that the baseline it replaces would have reported against the new run Recording over a regression is allowed, and it is never silent. ## Values, sample counts and metric keys The comparison of values and the comparison of sample counts each take one number per metric from the run. The specification fixes which numbers those are, because two implementations agree only if they read the same numbers from a run file. The table fixes them for each output shape. | Shape | Metric key | Value | Sample count | A sample the tool counted as an error | | --------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | | `promptfoo-results-3` | `<provider label> :: <metric name>` | the sum of the metric's scores divided by its weight total if present, else by its count | `namedScoresCount` of that metric: the assertions carrying `metric: <name>` that contributed a score | not counted, so the count falls | | `deepeval-test-run` | `<metric name>` | the arithmetic mean of the metric's `scores` | the length of the metric's `scores`: the samples that have both a score and a verdict | not in `scores`, so the count falls | The sample count is the metric's own count, never the number of cases. Counting cases would hide a sample lost to an error. - For promptfoo it is `namedScoresCount[m]`, the number the value was averaged over. A test with two assertions on one metric contributes two, and a test with none contributes nothing. So deleting an assertion changes the count even when the number of tests does not. - For DeepEval it is the length of the metric's `scores` array, which DeepEval builds from samples that have both a score and a verdict. Errors are handled twice. They lower the sample count, so a check reports them as `sample-count` findings. They also make `record` refuse the run, so a run that lost samples can never become the baseline. The value is on the tool's own scale, and it is from -4000000000 to 4000000000. A run's mean is rounded to six decimals before it is held to that range. Inside the range, every value scaled by one million, and the difference of two of them, is a whole number that a double holds exactly. A run with a value outside it is `bad-run`, and a baseline with one is `bad-baseline`. A metric whose scores the tool reports as weighted, as promptfoo does with `namedScoreWeights`, has a weighted mean as its value. A weight total that is not a finite number above zero makes the reader refuse the metric, and a baseline that names it gets `unreadable-metric`. A value is computed in double-precision arithmetic, in this order: - A DeepEval metric sums its scores one at a time from the first to the last, starting from 0. A sum that compensates for rounding error, or adds in another order, can differ in the last place, and the vectors detect that. A promptfoo metric takes the sum that the tool wrote. - The mean is that sum divided by the number of scores, or by the weight total of a weighted promptfoo metric. - The value is `q(mean) / 1,000,000`, and `-0` is written as `0`. The table gives means at or near a tie, with the value that the vectors print for each. A tie rounds toward positive infinity. In the last two rows the double nearest the mean lies beside the tie, not on it, and the value follows the product. | Mean of the scores | Product with 1,000,000 | Value | | ------------------ | ---------------------- | --------- | | 0.0078125 | 7812.5 | 0.007813 | | -0.8984375 | -898437.5 | -0.898437 | | 5e-7 | 0.5 | 0.000001 | | -5e-7 | -0.5 | 0 | | 0.0001245 | 124.49999999999999 | 0.000124 | | 0.0001265 | 126.50000000000001 | 0.000127 | The reader is chosen by the content of the run file, never by its name or by a flag. A run file is promptfoo output when it holds an object `results` with a numeric `version`. It is DeepEval output when it holds the arrays `testCases` and `metricsScores`. A file that matches both or neither is `bad-run`, and the text names the top-level keys the reader saw. A run file from a different tool than the baseline's is `bad-run` too. ### promptfoo run files In these rows, `metrics` means `results.prompts[i].metrics` for the same `i`. | Need | Field read | Note | | ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Shape | `results.version` | must be 3, and any other number is `bad-run` | | Columns | `results.prompts[i].provider` | the provider label; a label that repeats is `bad-run`, so this version reads one prompt per provider | | Value of metric `m` | `metrics.namedScores[m]` divided by `metrics.namedScoreWeights[m]` when present, else by the sample count | `namedScores` is the sum of the scores of the assertions that carry `metric: m` | | Sample count of `m` | `metrics.namedScoresCount[m]` | the number of assertions that contributed | | Errors | `metrics.testErrorCount` | a value greater than 0 is a note, and makes `record` refuse | | Case identity | `results.results[j].testIdx` and `.testCase.vars` | the digest of the binding check | | Tool version | `metadata.promptfooVersion` | stored as `source.toolVersion`, and `null` when absent | The metric key is `<provider label> :: <metric name>`, for example `agent :: accuracy`. Only assertions that carry a `metric` produce a named score, so a suite with none has nothing to guard, and `record` refuses it. A metric name that appears in `namedScores` with no entry in `namedScoresCount` is a derived metric. It has no sample count, and the reader skips it. ### DeepEval run files | Need | Field read | Note | | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Shape | `testCases` and `metricsScores`, both arrays | the file carries no schema-version field | | Value of metric `m` | the mean of `metricsScores[i].scores` for the entry whose `metric` is `m` | | | Sample count of `m` | the length of that `scores` array | DeepEval counts a sample into `scores` only when it has both a score and a verdict (`success`), and otherwise adds it to `errors` | | Errors | `metricsScores[i].errors` | a value greater than 0 is a note and makes `record` refuse; a metric with no threshold has no verdicts, so it has no samples and all errors | | Case identity | each `testCases[j]`'s `input` and `expectedOutput` | the digest of the binding check | | Polarity witness | each `testCases[j].metricsData[k]`'s `name`, `score`, `threshold` and `success` | read by the polarity witness | | Tool version | none | `source.toolVersion` is `null` | The metric key is the metric name, for example `Accuracy`. A run in which `conversationalTestCases` is not empty is `bad-run`, because this version reads no multi-turn run. A SQLite file is not JSON and is `bad-run` too. ### Polarity of DeepEval metrics The comparison treats a lower value as worse, but DeepEval metrics are not all higher-is-better. The reader therefore uses DeepEval's own verdicts as a witness. For each sample with a numeric `score`, a numeric `threshold` and a boolean `success`, `success` MUST equal `score >= threshold`. A metric with at least one sample that breaks this rule is refused. The reader leaves it out, and a baseline that names it gets `unreadable-metric` with the text `DeepEval's own verdicts contradict higher-is-better in <n> sample(s) (success=<s>, score=<x>, threshold=<t>); this implementation reads higher-is-better metrics only`. The verbs `show` and `record` print the same text as a note. So a lower-is-better metric cannot be guarded in this major version. The witness proves a contradiction, never a polarity. A metric whose verdicts never contradict the reading, because every sample passed whichever way, is read as higher-is-better and could be wrong. ## Exit codes A command ends with one of three exit codes. | Code | When | | ---- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 0 | The command ran and the arguments parsed. `check` exits 0 whatever it found, unless `--strict` is given | | 1 | `check --strict` printed at least one finding other than `cases-changed`, `record` refused and wrote nothing, or `show` could not read its run | | 2 | A usage error: an unknown verb, an unknown flag, a flag that the verb does not take, a flag given twice, a flag without its value, not exactly one run file, or a `--tolerance` that is not a number from 0 to 4000000000 written as digits with an optional decimal point. The text goes to stderr | Every line of a report goes to standard output, whatever the exit code. A command that exits 1 prints its refusal there and leaves standard error empty. Only a usage error writes to standard error, and it writes nothing to standard output. `check` MUST NOT throw. An exception inside reading or comparing is reported as the finding `internal-error`, with its message. The exit code then follows the rules for any other finding. A bug in an implementation must not turn a build red on a day nothing in the repository changed. This specification defines no input that must raise an internal error, so its vectors are reference-only. ## Three properties every implementation keeps An implementation MUST keep all three properties. Each has a limit, and the limit is stated with it. ### The strict stop is opt-in The default is a printed, dated finding. - Unless it is given `--strict`, `check` MUST exit 0 whatever it finds. Strict mode is the only way for `check` to exit 1. - A check that read a baseline MUST print a line that starts with `date:`. The line states when the baseline was recorded and how old it is, so an ignored finding stays visible. The owner of a suite can delete the step that runs the check. An implementation cannot stop that and does not pretend to, because the visibility is the point. ### Nothing exits non-zero on a clock - The findings and the exit code MUST be functions of the baseline and the run alone. The date is display, and it MUST NOT enter the comparison. - An implementation MUST NOT define an expiry, an age limit or a finding for an old baseline. The field `recordedAt` is written by the implementation. It is not checked against the history of the repository, so the date is printed as recorded and labelled `date:`. ### A passing check must be expensive to fake Every check binds to a referent, something that already sits inside the repository that owns the suite. - The baseline MUST be a committed file in that repository, and a check MUST read nothing from outside it: no network and no database. A hand edit to a number or a tolerance then shows as a diff in that file, beside the number it relaxes. - A baseline that does not exist is the finding `no-baseline`, which warns by default and fails under strict mode. - The `cases` digest binds the numbers to the cases that produced them. - `record` MUST refuse a run that holds errored samples, and MUST print what it replaces, as the clauses on recording a baseline require. - A reader MUST refuse a shape it does not know. The limits of the binding check stay in force. A scorer weakened in place is not caught, and a reviewer sees it in the diff of the suite, not in the report. A fabricated but complete run file is not caught either. The reader needs a complete file in the tool's own shape, and the baseline's `source` must match. ## Permanent refusals These refusals are permanent. An entry leaves the list only through a new major version of this specification. | Refused | Why | | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | A hosted service, dashboard, account, database, or any network access | A hosted part brings an operational duty, and `check`, `record` and `show` open no connection | | A neutral run format, a third reader, or a reader for another tool's output (Inspect, Ragas, LangSmith, Braintrust and the rest) | A format that no tool writes has no files to read, and each reader is a part that goes stale against someone else's release schedule | | Statistical significance, confidence intervals, retries, flaky-test handling | The baseline keeps no per-case data, and a reviewer can read a number in a diff but not a p-value | | Relative, global or auto-adjusting tolerance, or a tolerance given at check time | A tolerance is absolute and stored per metric in the baseline, beside the value it relaxes | | Updating the baseline automatically, on a pass or on a fail | An automatic update makes the baseline whatever the last run was, and so makes the check meaningless. The baseline changes only when a person runs `record` and commits the result | | Calling a model, a judge or any paid API | The check must run with no key | | Telemetry, an update check, any outbound request | A request is a failure that depends on a network and a day | | Pull-request comments, bots, chat messages, badges, status APIs | Each needs a token and a service | | Failing on a date, on baseline age, or on expiry | Nothing exits non-zero on a clock | | Lower-is-better metrics, or a per-metric polarity setting, in major version 1 | The reader reads higher-is-better only, and it refuses a metric whose verdicts contradict that | | A configuration file or environment variables | The baseline is the only configuration, and a second place is a second place for implementations to disagree | | JSON, SARIF or JUnit output of the report | Each format is another contract to keep. The report is line-oriented so that `grep` and the exit code are the interface, and the baseline is JSON for anyone who needs structure | | More than one run or suite in a baseline, merging baselines, per-branch baselines | One baseline holds one run of one suite, so each has one `source` and one `cases` digest | | Saying which case regressed | It needs per-case data that the reduced baseline does not keep | | A `--ci`, `--fail`, `--exit-code` or similar flag that makes failure the default | The strict flag is the only one | ## Versioning A version of this specification has two numbers, MAJOR and MINOR, written MAJOR.MINOR, each a whole number with no leading zero. There is no third number, because a patch to a specification is either editorial, which changes no citation, or normative, which is a new minor. | Number | Changes when | | ------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | MAJOR | a rule, the baseline schema, a finding id, an exit code or the metric key of a shape changes so that an older baseline or an older reading gives a different answer | | MINOR | an output shape is added (a newer promptfoo results version, say), so older baselines are still read and nothing already readable changes meaning | A published version never changes its behaviour. Its page changes only by an editorial correction, which covers wording, examples and added vectors. An editorial correction changes no behaviour and no citation, it leaves the version number alone, and the changelog records it with its date. Any change of behaviour is a new version, published at its own address beside the old one. A baseline names the version it follows in its `spec` field. An implementation reads a baseline of its own major and an older or equal minor. Each version has one page, at an address that holds both numbers, such as `https://meshin.co/spec/evals-baseline/1.0`. That address carries no trailing slash. This site answers the slash form with a redirect, and an address that redirects is one step from being rewritten by whoever quotes it. Only versioned pages are cited. The [evals-baseline series page](/spec/evals-baseline) lists every published version, names the current one and holds no normative text. The version sits in the address so that a later version publishes beside the first and never rewrites what people already cited. ## Changelog | Version | Date | Change | | ------- | ---------- | ----------------- | | 1.0 | 2026-11-12 | First publication | ## Conformance vectors A conformance vector is one run of the command. It names the arguments, a pinned instant, and the baseline file and the run file that the command reads. It holds the exact lines the command prints, its exit code and the text of any file `record` writes. An implementation conforms to this version when it reproduces every vector that is not marked reference-only. The vectors are published as one file, [/spec/evals-baseline/1.0/vectors.json](/spec/evals-baseline/1.0/vectors.json). Under the key `files` it carries the exact text of every baseline file and run file that a vector names and that exists. A path that is not a key of `files` names a file that does not exist. The file alone is enough to run every vector. The [baseline schema](/spec/evals-baseline/1.0/baseline.schema.json) at `/spec/evals-baseline/1.0/baseline.schema.json` describes the shape of a baseline file. Published files, below, gives the digest of both files. Version 1.0 has 165 vectors. 116 run `check`, 21 run `record`, 22 run `show`, 1 asks for the version, and 5 are usage errors that exit 2. The 116 check vectors are drawn from 57 distinct pairs of a baseline and a run. | Covered | Vectors | Distinct pairs | To reproduce | | ------------------------------------------- | ------- | -------------- | ------------ | | Rule 1, `missing-metric` | 8 | 4 | 8 | | Rule 2, `below-baseline` | 10 | 4 | 10 | | Rule 3, the note for a metric only in a run | 8 | 4 | 8 | | Rule 4, `sample-count` | 8 | 4 | 8 | | The binding check, `cases-changed` | 8 | 4 | 8 | | `no-baseline` | 2 | 1 | 2 | | `bad-baseline` | 26 | 13 | 26 | | `bad-run` | 28 | 14 | 28 | | `unreadable-metric` | 2 | 1 | 2 | | `internal-error` | 2 | 1 | 0 | A vector appears in a row for each finding its report names, so the rows do not partition the 165. Vectors that name two findings stand in two rows, and there are 4 of them. Of the 165, 67 name no finding and stand in no row. Of those 67, 18 are `check` runs that must stay silent. The other 49 run `record` or `show`, ask for the version, or are usage errors, and none of them reports a finding. The silent checks include the same suite recorded and checked twice, and a value exactly at its tolerance. The rows therefore total 102. A row counts the vectors that prove it, not the vectors it exhausts. The last column counts the vectors of a row that an implementation must reproduce. The row for `internal-error` has none, because this specification defines no input that must raise an internal error. No implementation is asked to reproduce the reference-only vectors, which number 4 of the 165. Of those 4, 2 print the message a runtime raised, which is not this specification's text. The other 2 print the reason line before a usage error, which this specification does not fix. Three things an implementation sets for itself. Its own package version, which the banner line carries and which this specification never fixes. The clock, which each vector pins, so an implementation that cannot set its clock compares every line except the one beginning `date:`. The order in which it reads files, which changes nothing a vector records.

rows.text: Choice comes first, and it is mostly a filter. A candidate process needs volume, a measurable outcome, and a tolerable failure mode. A tolerable failure mode, because the first version will be wrong sometimes and you need to know what that costs.

rows.text: Adoption telemetry for AI tools usually reports seats, logins, active users and prompts. That is an inference from the sources cited here. None of them shows any of those counts predicting a business result. Self-reports can mislead too. In METR's 2025 trial, 16 experienced developers expected a 24% speed-up. Afterwards they believed they had been 20% faster. Their tasks took 19% longer. METR now marks that result out of date. In an NBER working paper issued in February 2026, nearly 6,000 senior executives reported that 69% of firms use AI. Nine in ten reported no impact on employment or productivity over three years. That is also self-report. A smaller set is easier to defend: coverage, retention by team, one agreed outcome, delivery health, cost per outcome and a trust survey read as opinion. That set is a synthesis, not a finding any source states. Collect it by team, and screen any per-person view first.

rows.text: A pilot stalls in the space between working once and working every time. Most proof-of-concepts skip four things production always needs. Two of them are a named owner who still answers a year after launch and a decision about which data may leave the building. The other two are a number that says whether the system is working, and an automatic check that catches a regression before a customer does.

rows.text: AI governance sits above the technology itself. It covers who owns each AI system, what data it may touch, which use cases are off limits, and who signs off before a system reaches customers. That shows up as a register of the systems in use, a policy engineers actually follow, and a review step before anything new goes live.

rows.text: Article 43 sets this split by Annex III area, the EU AI Act's list of high-risk use cases. Every area except biometric identification uses Annex VI, the self-check route with no notified body involved. Harmonised standards are the detailed technical rules the Commission recognises as proof of compliance.

rows.text: Formally Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Act entered into force on 1 August 2024. It sorts AI systems into a risk ladder, from banned practices, to a high-risk category, to a lighter set of transparency duties. High-risk covers things like hiring, credit and law enforcement. The lighter duties apply to systems such as chatbots. The Act leaves everything else largely unregulated.

NIST adds that the process should be iterative.

An organisation may select some categories and subcategories or apply all of them. NIST’s Playbook adds suggested actions for each subcategory, and an organisation may borrow as many or as few suggestions as fit its use case. Read a subcategory’s full wording before you claim a document answers it.

It can show a system is running while saying nothing about whether one specific answer, given to one specific person, was actually right. rows.text: Article 72 requires a documented monitoring system, sized to the technology and the risk of the specific system. It has to actively and systematically collect and analyse data on how the system performs once it is actually in use. Deployers feed into it directly, since Article 26 requires them to monitor the system on their end and report back to the provider. That way, the provider is not relying on its own visibility alone.

rows.text: Direct injection comes from whoever is typing into the box, phrased to override the model's own hidden starting instructions, its system prompt. Indirect injection is the more dangerous form. It arrives inside content the model retrieves on its own: a webpage it is summarising, a resume it is screening. No attacker ever touches the model directly. Multimodal systems add a further variant, since an instruction can hide inside an image processed alongside ordinary text.

rows.text: The document store is usually a vector index. The system converts passages into embeddings, numerical representations of meaning, and matches a query against them by similarity, not exact keyword. Matching on meaning lets the system find a relevant passage even when the question shares none of the same words as the document.

Both risks sit inside the retrieval layer, invisible to anyone reviewing only the model or the prompts it receives.

rows.text: Procurement asks “is this RAG, or did you train on our data,” because the two have different data-handling implications. RAG typically sends only retrieved snippets to the model at query time, rather than baking a customer’s content into the model’s own weights. It also comes up once someone questions accuracy. A wrong answer usually traces to a retrieval problem, not a flaw in the model itself.
